chapters.title: Chapter 1863 Shattered Reality
paragraphs: *Chu.*
Kaede made herself keep watching. Evidence demanded collection.
The last icon of Fujimori dignity was licking a man's chest in the ancestors' hall, purring between passes.
Kaede's knees, drilled through years of formal seiza, nearly went out from under her.

'She is... My sister is currently...' The assessment refused to fit anywhere inside her, no matter which way she turned it. And none of it explained the red marks. On that single question, the investigation stayed open.
Then Ayame's hand wandered somewhere with unmistakable intent, and Quinlan moved first.
*SMACK.*
His palm cracked across her silk-bare backside.
"Kyaa!?"
The yelp came out at full noble volume. Kaede's body locked solid, and behind the doorframe, the investigation closed.
Confirmed. Struck, bare-handed, on the body, in front of the ancestors, and every doctrine Kaede owned held precisely one procedure for that event: steel, drawn, before the echo finished.

The Ayame she had grown up beneath would have answered an uninvited touch with a blade through the offending wrist, and if that Ayame was in no state to answer, the duty fell to whatever family stood in reach.

The family in reach owned no steel. It owned an incense stick, a servant's gray, and a debt, and it would have to do. Kaede's grip firmed around the stick, her weight rolled onto the balls of her feet, and the disgraced Fujimori made her peace with the ancestors on the way to the door.
"Mmnn~... Again."
Kaede stopped, one step short of the doorway.
The purr had come from her sister. She replayed it, syllable by syllable, and it did not improve on review.
She had spent this entire vigil listening for the sounds a domestically abused woman makes, and no abused woman in the history of the world had ever made that one.
"Behave."
"Make me~"
Kaede stood frozen on the threshold of her own charge and let the evidence re-file itself. The red marks, the melting, the purr, the demand, and it had unmistakably been a demand, for another one.
Nobody in that hall was beating anyone. Her sister, the heir with perfect form at dawn, the measure Kaede had spent her whole life failing to reach, was enjoying it. Asking for it.
Her amazing big sister.
Was a hopeless masochist.
Kaede's worldview held its shape for one more second, out of pure habit. Then it caved in, all at once, and quietly.
And then, at last, the counterattack came.
She saw it start: Ayame pushed herself upright astride him, and for one shining moment the heir of the Fujimori was back, chin high, gaze leveled in judgment over the man beneath her.
"Right~" said the genius girl of the Fujimori. "That's twice this morning you've struck a noble of this house. There will be retribution."
Behind the doorframe, Kaede dared one last time to hope. 'Yes. There she is. There she...'
Ayame reached down and grabbed him by the dick.
"Confiscated~" she announced. "Until further notice."
"When does the tribunal convene?" Quinlan didn't move a muscle.
"The tribunal will issue its demands shortly~"
Kaede stopped hoping.

Her framework contained a place for submission and a place for counterattack. It contained nothing for a counterattack conducted by confiscation. By her sister enthroned on the man, holding him hostage while both parties tried not to laugh and failed.
She attempted the thought three times, and it refused to finish on every attempt.
She left.

She did not run, because one did not run on the ancestors' ground. She walked, in flawless form, spine straight, steps measured, face crimson to the ears, back across the courtyard and around the corner of the outer wall.
Only there, in complete privacy, did the nominal leader of the Fujimori clan slide down the stones into a crouch and press her face into both hands. Properly, this time. No gaps.
From the hall, faint with distance, came another *SMACK*, another "Kyaa!? Respect the tribunal or else- Hnggh?!?!", and another round of the most carefree laughter in the world.
The incense stick in her lap had folded in half.
Inside the dojo, Quinlan noted in passing that the mortified presence marinating by the doorway these past minutes had finally withdrawn.
It had carried no killing intent, only escalating quantities of spiritual damage, and interrupting Ayame's audit for anything short of an assassination attempt had been out of the question.
'She'll recover,' he decided generously, on no evidence whatsoever.
"Your sister is gone," he reported to the woman on his chest. "You knew she was standing there this entire time. Why let her watch?"
"What's there to hide?" Ayame propped her chin on her folded arms. "We're adults. You're my lover. Besides, enjoying this sort of thing is perfectly normal for people of noble privilege~"
"Somehow, I doubt she holds the same opinion."

The grin that answered him grew a size. "Then it's high time she grows up. That damned body of hers is already a grown woman's..." A small scoff escaped her there, and her eyes dropped, for one sour moment, to her own chest, which her little sister's had overtaken years ago. "She should learn these things or someone will take advantage of her again."
Quinlan merely smiled at that, electing not to comment.
Then Ayame pushed herself upright and spun around on top of him, coming face to face with the confiscated property, which stood tall, entirely unmoved by its own legal predicament.
She licked her lips.
"It's time to dethrone Lucille~" she declared. "That bitch has been far too smug about her throat GOAT title. I'll have you revoke it promptly."
Quinlan slid both hands under his head, arranging himself into the resting pose of a man with no unresolved problems in this world.
"Good luck."
It was past midday when the two of them, washed and dressed and almost respectable, walked the silent corridors of the family wing.
"One last stop~" Ayame announced, leading him deeper down a lantern-dark hallway. "There's one thing in this place I'm not leaving behind."
She stopped at the double doors at its end without reaching for the frame.
"My room," she said.
The bratty woman and the lewd lover both had gone out of her voice somewhere in the last ten steps.
Quinlan said nothing and let her take her time.

She slid the doors open on the chamber of a duchy's heir: wide and high-ceilinged, a canopied bed sized for a noblewoman, a full-length mirror in a lacquered frame, a writing desk beneath the shuttered windows, all of it wearing an even shroud of dust.

And in the far corner, spared by every redecoration her growing years had demanded, a small island of childhood remained: a practice stand with one child-sized wooden sword across its pegs, and a low little desk with clumsy name-strokes carved under its lip.
Nobody had lived in this room for years, and nobody had emptied it either. It had been shut the way a ledger is shut, and left.

She crossed the wide floor past the cold bed, knelt at the corner, and drew a line through the dust on the little desk, her fingertips stopping at a shallow notch in its edge, the scar of some ancient practice accident.
"The last time I was in this room," she said, conversational, to the desk, "I couldn't stand up."
Quinlan's eyes cooled.
They had let her lie here, her body too poisoned to rise, while her house priced her and drew up the contract.

When they finally came for her, she had left this room between two guards. The heir's room, the heir's bed, the heir's little desk with her clumsy name-strokes carved under its lip, and by the end not one splinter of it had been hers. She had been an item leaving a house.
She rose off her heels.

Now she stood in the same dusty room as the true owner of the house. Of the estate around the house, the city around the estate, the duchy around the city, and every stone the Fujimori name had ever stacked on another stone.
All of it, from these floorboards to the borders, answered now to the family she had built out of nothing with her own two hands and one extremely shameless man.
She stood with that for a while.

Quinlan crossed the room, folded his arms over her collarbones from behind, and let her have it for as long as she wanted. She leaned back into him and said nothing, and neither did he, while the dust drifted through the shutter-light around the two of them.
Then she wriggled loose, plucked the wooden sword off its stand, and gave it one short test swing.
*Fwip.*
The dust on the desk relocated.
"My first sword," she declared, holding it up. It was notched along its whole edge and sized for a child. "Father made me swing it until my palms bled. I hated it more than anything alive."
"And you kept it in a place of honor."
"Obviously." She spun it once and put it away into her pocket ring. "This blade has drawn more of my blood than any enemy ever managed. It's place is in our home."
"A priceless memento," Quinlan nodded, smiling softly.
"Mm!" Ayame beamed, happy that he thought so.
At the door she paused, one hand on the frame, and looked back once, at the little bed, the dust, the closed shutters.
"I'll have someone open those," she decided. "It's done being a closed box."
And she walked out ahead of him, boss of everything, brat of one man.

She crossed the wide floor past the cold bed, knelt at the corner, and drew a line through the dust on the little desk, her fingertips stopping at a shallow notch in its edge, the scar of some ancient practice accident.
"The last time I was in this room," she said, conversational, to the desk, "I couldn't stand up."
Quinlan's eyes cooled.
They had let her lie here, her body too poisoned to rise, while her house priced her and drew up the contract.
When they finally came for her, she had left this room between two guards.
The heir's room, the heir's bed, the heir's little desk with her clumsy name-strokes carved under its lip, and by the end not one splinter of it had been hers.
She had been an item leaving a house.
She rose off her heels.
Now she stood in the same dusty room as the true owner of the house.
Of the estate around the house, the city around the estate, the duchy around the city, and every stone the Fujimori name had ever stacked on another stone.
All of it, from these floorboards to the borders, answered now to the family she had built out of nothing with her own two hands and one extremely shameless man.
She stood with that for a while.
Quinlan crossed the room, folded his arms over her collarbones from behind, and let her have it for as long as she wanted.
She leaned back into him and said nothing, and neither did he, while the dust drifted through the shutter-light around the two of them.
Then she wriggled loose, plucked the wooden sword off its stand, and gave it one short test swing.
*Fwip.*
The dust on the desk relocated.
"My first sword," she declared, holding it up.
It was notched along its whole edge and sized for a child.
"Father made me swing it until my palms bled.
I hated it more than anything alive."
"And you kept it in a place of honor."
"Obviously." She spun it once and put it away into her pocket ring.
"This blade has drawn more of my blood than any enemy ever managed.
It's place is in our home."
"A priceless memento," Quinlan nodded, smiling softly.
"Mm!" Ayame beamed, happy that he thought so.
At the door she paused, one hand on the frame, and looked back once, at the little bed, the dust, the closed shutters.
"I'll have someone open those," she decided.
"It's done being a closed box."
And she walked out ahead of him, boss of everything, brat of one man.

chapters.title: Chapter 1864 Hard Working Elder
paragraphs: The ducal keep had not slept.

Quinlan and Ayame felt it from the outer gate: courier horses streaming through the yard, boots taking the stairs in relays, and the great hall, when they entered it, converted wholesale into a war camp of paper.
Trestle tables ran in ranks down its length, stacked with documents in sorted tiers, and clerks moved between them at a pace one report shy of running.
At the center of it all, installed behind a desk the size of a modest fortification, sat Elder Chizuru of the Fujimori, governing.

Her brush did not stop while she spoke. "Denied. The garrison's pay is not a negotiation, and neither is its schedule; if the river treasurer finds it burdensome, he may find a new profession. Approved. Grain moves at first thaw, under escort, and the toll stations reopen with it. Denied. Denied. Approved, contingent on inspection. Where is the western granary count I demanded at dawn?"
Papers left her desk in two even streams, one to each flank, into the hands of clerks who received them with a bow to the Elder and ran.
Captain Rin materialized out of the traffic at a jog, helmet gone, an entire courier office compressed into one person. She caught sight of the visitors and braked hard.
"My lady. My lord." The salute she gave the two of them had lost its parade polish overnight and kept all of its sincerity.

"It's... Forgive me. It's working. The towns are answering again. Three garrisons' pay rode out under escort this morning, the river tolls are staffed, the..." She caught herself mid-report, reddening. "You didn't ask. Did you require the Elder?"
"Just admiring the view," said Quinlan, and meant it.

Behind the mountain range of paperwork hung a map of Silverwind with pins migrating across it, roads inked open one by one, and beside it a list of towns losing entries by the hour. The duchy had stopped bleeding, and every person working in that hall could feel it.
Elder Chizuru did not rise.
She finished the stroke she was on, set the brush down with the care owed a relic, and waited behind her desk with the warmth of a courtroom.
"Elder." Ayame stopped in front of the desk, parade-even. "Report."
For one second, nothing came. The sourness surfaced first, pulling the Elder's mouth into a thin line while obedience and loathing finished their negotiation somewhere behind it.
Then compliance arrived the way Chizuru paid every debt: in full, on time, hating every coin.

"Silverwind stands at seven parts in ten of full function and will pass nine within the week." The numbers came without a single glance at any ledger. "The treasury is reconciled through spring. The northern roads reopen with the thaw, and the granaries will carry the towns until they do. The nearest of the emptied ones are already filling again. The duchy will not require your attention."

Every word of it was correct, courtly, and polished to a shine. Her eyes delivered the second report: leech, usurper, gagger of elders. The face around them stayed composed. She had bitten into something sour years ago and kept it there out of principle.
"Magnificent work, Elder," Quinlan beamed at her. "The duchy looks better already."

The Elder took her brush back up. "The keep is honored," she pronounced at ceremonial volume, to a point on the wall above his head, and the next petition received its Denied with a fraction more wrist than the word required.
"We'll be gone from your hall soon~" Ayame promised. "One matter first."
She turned.
By the far wall, in servant's gray with her sleeves tied back, the nominal leader of the Fujimori clan waited at the foot of a sorting table, binding answered petitions into bundles with string.
She looked miserable, and none of it was performance: neck bowed, eyes on her string, tying knot after knot as if the work were the only thing in the keep she still had any right to touch.
"Kaede."

The string went still. Kaede set down the bundle, crossed the floor, and bowed to her sister, deep, hands flat on her thighs. She had not once looked fully at either visitor since they entered the hall.

"You should stay in Silverwind." Ayame's voice was level and public, a posting being read out. "I'd like you to oversee the governance of this duchy, and everything that passes through this hall passes under your eyes."
Kaede straightened by degrees as the posting sank in, and for one unguarded moment the servant's gray sat on her like a uniform again.
Then the moment ran into the obvious.
"But..." Her gaze flicked to the desk, where the brush had resumed issuing verdicts, and dropped again. "Forgive me. The Elder cannot disobey you. What would I be watching for?"

"[Subjugation] is mighty, but it is not foolproof." Ayame raised one finger. "It compels obedience, not diligence. She answers what she is asked and volunteers nothing, which means someone in this keep has to know what to ask." A second finger. "And she will be borrowed from time to time. Black Fang enjoys her company."
Behind the desk, the brush stopped mid-stroke and stayed stopped for three full seconds before it went back to work.
Kaede was nodding before the list ended, and the nodding had color in it, purpose taking hold in real time on a face that had spent a season expecting none.

Quinlan drew Ayame against his side, hand settling proud and easy on her waist, and said nothing at all. The Elder could not betray them, not even work badly; that had never been the question. Ayame was merely helping her little sister by giving her something useful to do instead of just being miserable.
'A big step forward,' Quinlan noted.
"And one task from me," Ayame added.
Kaede came to attention.

"The dawn dojo took heavy damage when I dueled Quinlan." Not one muscle moved anywhere in Ayame's face. "I'd like you to restore it. Every board, every rack, every stone, exactly as it was. Oversee the work yourself."
'... Okay, maybe just half a step,' Quinlan chuckled inwardly, holding his little vindictive lover even closer.
He couldn't care less what Ayame decided to do with Kaede; the decision was left fully in her hands. He'd be okay with torture, swift execution, or full redemption. Whatever made Ayame happy.
Kaede's breath snagged halfway down and stayed there.
She had seen the dawn dojo that morning. She had seen things in the dawn dojo that morning that no restoration effort would ever sand out of her.
"Yes, s..." The word gave out before it could finish. She bowed lower over her own hands, to Ayame's shadow on the floor. "...It will be exactly as it was."
She had nothing but questions, an entire keep of them, bundled and strung and stacked to the rafters.
She asked none of them.
Ayame had already turned away.
"Will you..."
It was out before Kaede could fold it. Of the entire keep of questions, the one that escaped was the smallest. "...Will you visit? Sometime."
Ayame stopped where she stood, her back to the hall, and stayed that way long enough for the courier traffic to notice and detour around her.
Then she looked back over her shoulder, head tilted, and smiled.
"When I have the time."
Kaede bowed so fast and so deep that her low-bound hair swung forward over her shoulder. "The duchy will be worth inspecting!"
"Girl." It arrived from behind the desk, Chizuru's brush already moving again. "The eastern accounts. When your celebrating concludes."
"Watch your mouth, bitch! I'm done being your servant!"
Every brush in the hall stopped at once. Somewhere in the traffic, Captain Rin walked into a trestle table.
Chizuru's head came around with the speed of a siege engine being re-aimed. "I must have misheard."
"You heard me well, you senile sack of hypocrisy!"
Ayame raised an eyebrow. She was almost as dumbfounded as Chizuru herself. Almost. The difference was the corner of her mouth, which had already decided how this story would be retold.

Kaede marched on the desk she had spent her life bowing toward, and no trace of the misery survived the first step. "You murdered my father. You wanted to do the same to my sister! I wear this gray for my share of what happened."

Her voice wobbled at the edges and kept going anyway. "Yours starts today. Hear my first ruling as your overseer: your workload is tripled. Your tea privileges are revoked. Every Denied that leaves this hall crosses my table first. And I will question every. Single. One."
Then, in front of the entire hall, the overseer of Silverwind climbed onto the governing desk of the duchy. A sorted tier avalanched. Over by the sorting tables, a clerk made a small wounded sound.

Kaede planted her feet on a week of verdicts and leaned down into the sour old face that had authored her entire ruin. Oversee, the posting had said. She had decided to begin with the literal reading.
Chizuru held her seat through the avalanche, spine straight, eyes promising a reckoning her mouth was no longer allowed to order.

"Your remaining days belong to me now, bitch. Except when Black Fang sends for you." A small, terrible smile broke over her face, the first anyone in the keep had seen on her. "I hope she sends for you often."
The hall held its breath. Chizuru regarded the girl in servant's gray for a long, glacial moment.
<Obey her,> Ayame ordered.
"...The eastern accounts," the elder said at last, "await the overseer's review."
"They'll wait until I decide they're reviewed." Kaede snatched the stack off the desk. "Which is now. Because I decided it."
"..." It visibly took Chizuru all she had not to sneer back.
"Well then, we're off," Quinlan grinned.
Kaede merely waved without even turning around, busy asserting dominance.
Rin bowed deep to the two of them. "U-um, thank you for your hard work!"
And just like that, the villain and his beloved samurai left the hall.

chapters.title: Chapter 1865 Alexios, You Dare?!
paragraphs: The keep's outer courtyard had been trampled flat by courier traffic, and the early afternoon light lay thin across it.
Black Fang was already there.
She held the courtyard's far edge with her arms crossed, on post. Nobody had assigned her anywhere, and nobody mentioned that, either.
Ayame's grin made it halfway toward a comment, met the violet head-on, and elected to live.
"The capital, then," said Quinlan.
The war of paper waited there, and somewhere behind it, a king holding him to a promise.
He raised his hand, and the [Warp Gate] bloomed in the middle of the courtyard, tall and patient, the air of another city rolling through it.
Black Fang left her post and walked through first, ahead of both of them, offering no explanation to anyone.
Quinlan and Ayame traded a look over the space where she had been. Neither said one word. Some lessons only need learning once a day.
Then Ayame took his arm, the last of Fujimori lands at her back and none of her attention on it, and grinned up at him with the shine he knew best.
"Now then~ Let's go see how that hopeless workaholic is doing."
They stepped through together.
In the Ravenshade ducal seat, the crown's requisition arrived between the fish course and the wine, and Duke Tharion Ravenshade let it wait through both.

He read it afterward in his study, once, at his own pace, in a room where the maps of the duchy hung in frames worth more than the villages they described. The inkwell at his elbow was dwarven silverwork, older than the dynasty it had been bought to outlast.
Fine paper, heavy seal, correct in every particular. But the hand was no clerk's, and neither was the voice.
'To His Grace Tharion Ravenshade, Duke of Ravenshade.
Brother.
The crown has undertaken a full accounting of its roads and its tolls. The oldest books in the kingdom sit in your border holdings, and it seemed only proper to honor them first.
The crown therefore requests and requires the complete toll archives of your border holdings, in their original copies, forty years deep, surrendered to the bearers of this letter.
The commission of audit will see to their transport and their keeping. Nothing is asked of your house but what every house owes the crown: the truth of its own records.
I am told the years have been kind to your archives. I look forward to finding them complete.
Alexios Valorian, King of Vraven, by his own hand.'
"Requests," the duke read aloud, to no one. "And requires."
"Alexios..." The name came out of him low, and he kept the rest of it behind his teeth.

His chancellor had carried it in personally, at a dignified walk, because a man seen running through the halls of Ravenshade was making a statement no servant could afford. He stood in front of the desk now and managed his breathing.
"They asked after the missing years, my lord." His voice held level on every word but the last.
"There are no missing years. There are years the river took when the archive flooded. It is a matter of record."
"Yes, my lord. Only..." The chancellor's thumb found the seam of his sleeve. "They knew which years, my lord. Before a single crate was opened."
The fire ticked in the grate.
It took a moment to reach the bottom of him. When it did, it settled deep.
Audits were for fishmongers and millers, for merchant houses grown too fat too fast.
No king had ever audited a great house, and none had ever dared audit Ravenshade.

His sister had worn a crown. Every royal heir alive carried Ravenshade blood. His house had paid for the realm's balance marriage by marriage, and now that same realm wanted forty years of his toll books, as if Ravenshade were a cheese merchant suspected of shorting the excise.
"He dares?!" he shouted at last, fists trembling. "He calls me brother and dares?!"
Then the shout finished echoing, and the duke sat back down, because shouting was for the room and thinking was for the house.

He understood the signature well enough. Alexios had spent his entire reign balancing the great houses, because he could afford nothing else. That man did not grow a new spine at his age. Spines like this one were on loan, and the whole continent knew the lender.
The worst of it was that he could not even ask his own blood what was moving in the capital. Morgana belonged to the Villain now, publicly, before half a battlefield of witnesses.

Lilith had sent no word his way in years. The house had spent generations seeding the capital with its own people, and in the hour it finally needed eyes there, every one of them had gone dark or gone over.
Across the desk, the chancellor held his station and made no more sound than the furniture.
What the crown thought it was fishing for, he could not say. Probably nothing. Audits were how a new power shook a tree, to see what fell out and who ran to catch it.
But the border holdings were the wrong tree to shake.

"Cooperate," he said to the chancellor. "Open the crates yourself. Catalog every page, wrap the lot in oilcloth, and deliver it three days early. If the crown wants forty years of tolls, Ravenshade will hand them over in better order than the royal archive has ever kept anything."
The chancellor bowed to him, deep and grateful.

"Two things more. Find me whoever runs this commission. Kings sign what is set in front of them; I want the hand that set it." The duke drew the candle closer. "And have fresh paper brought up. The good stock."
The doors closed. The duke sat alone with the fire and the framed maps, and then he wrote the letter himself.

An invitation, nothing more. The winter hawking in the western woods was at its best while the snow held; Count Corvane's company had been missed at the lodge since spring; he should come at his earliest leisure, and bring no one, for the lodge staff would see to everything.
Tharion read it over once, blotted it, and sealed it with the raven.
He had written it the way he wrote every letter that truly mattered: in his own hand, and warmly.
The chancellor's knock came back before the wax had cooled.
"My lord. The commission's men..." The dignified walk was gone from his voice. "They are not waiting for the crates. Their riders took the north road at dusk, under crown seal, moving fast."
The duke looked down at the invitation in his hand, sealed and still warm.
He had written it three days too late.
Then the stillness broke, and the chair went over behind him.
Fear, when it finally reached the Duke of Ravenshade, came out as orders.
"Call them!" He was on his feet and shouting like a garrison sergeant. "Call every count of the border RIGHT NOW! They must ensure everything is in order!"
The chancellor flattened himself against the map wall as his lord crossed the study at a pace no servant would ever be permitted to describe.
The invitation went into the fire whole.
"And Corvane." The duke stopped at the window, where the dark had already swallowed the north road. "Corvane comes to me. Tonight. My seal and an escort, and if he hesitates, the escort doubles."
The shouting, this time, was for the house.
The last call the duke made himself.
The communication artifact came up from the desk drawer, and the mana he forced into it made the crystal whine. Then it pulsed, and pulsed, and Ravenshade learned what waiting felt like.
"Alexios!" The bare name, at a volume the framed maps had never heard. "Riders on my land in the dark, under your seal! You audit fishmongers, Alexios! You audit millers grown too fat!"

The duke's fist came down on the desk, and the dwarven inkwell jumped. "You do not audit the house that put a queen on your arm and heirs in your line! You owe this house more than paper, so you will say it to me! What is this?!"
The artifact hummed, patient, while his breathing filled the study.
"The letter says all the crown has to say." The king's voice came through level, old, and completely unbent.
"What about Felicity?! I'll-"
The connection died in his hand.
Reckoning was upon the final true bastion of the Vraven Kingdom.
Meanwhile, the other notable factions of the Iskaris Continent were activating themselves as well, making preparations brought by the Primordial Villain's rise!

The commission of audit will see to their transport and their keeping.
Nothing is asked of your house but what every house owes the crown: the truth of its own records.
I am told the years have been kind to your archives.
I look forward to finding them complete.
Alexios Valorian, King of Vraven, by his own hand.'
"Requests," the duke read aloud, to no one.
"And requires."
"Alexios..." The name came out of him low, and he kept the rest of it behind his teeth.
His chancellor had carried it in personally, at a dignified walk, because a man seen running through the halls of Ravenshade was making a statement no servant could afford.
He stood in front of the desk now and managed his breathing.
"They asked after the missing years, my lord." His voice held level on every word but the last.
"There are no missing years.
There are years the river took when the archive flooded.
It is a matter of record."
"Yes, my lord.
Only..." The chancellor's thumb found the seam of his sleeve.
"They knew which years, my lord.
Before a single crate was opened."
The fire ticked in the grate.
It took a moment to reach the bottom of him.
When it did, it settled deep.
Audits were for fishmongers and millers, for merchant houses grown too fat too fast.
No king had ever audited a great house, and none had ever dared audit Ravenshade.
His sister had worn a crown.
Every royal heir alive carried Ravenshade blood.

His house had paid for the realm's balance marriage by marriage, and now that same realm wanted forty years of his toll books, as if Ravenshade were a cheese merchant suspected of shorting the excise.
"He dares?!" he shouted at last, fists trembling.
"He calls me brother and dares?!"
Then the shout finished echoing, and the duke sat back down, because shouting was for the room and thinking was for the house.
He understood the signature well enough.
Alexios had spent his entire reign balancing the great houses, because he could afford nothing else.
That man did not grow a new spine at his age.
Spines like this one were on loan, and the whole continent knew the lender.
The worst of it was that he could not even ask his own blood what was moving in the capital.
Morgana belonged to the Villain now, publicly, before half a battlefield of witnesses.
Lilith had sent no word his way in years.
The house had spent generations seeding the capital with its own people, and in the hour it finally needed eyes there, every one of them had gone dark or gone over.
Across the desk, the chancellor held his station and made no more sound than the furniture.
What the crown thought it was fishing for, he could not say.
Probably nothing.
Audits were how a new power shook a tree, to see what fell out and who ran to catch it.
But the border holdings were the wrong tree to shake.
"Cooperate," he said to the chancellor.
"Open the crates yourself.
Catalog every page, wrap the lot in oilcloth, and deliver it three days early.
If the crown wants forty years of tolls, Ravenshade will hand them over in better order than the royal archive has ever kept anything."
The chancellor bowed to him, deep and grateful.
"Two things more.
Find me whoever runs this commission.
Kings sign what is set in front of them; I want the hand that set it." The duke drew the candle closer.
"And have fresh paper brought up.
The good stock."
The doors closed.
The duke sat alone with the fire and the framed maps, and then he wrote the letter himself.
An invitation, nothing more.

The winter hawking in the western woods was at its best while the snow held; Count Corvane's company had been missed at the lodge since spring; he should come at his earliest leisure, and bring no one, for the lodge staff would see to everything.
Tharion read it over once, blotted it, and sealed it with the raven.
He had written it the way he wrote every letter that truly mattered: in his own hand, and warmly.
The chancellor's knock came back before the wax had cooled.
"My lord.
The commission's men..." The dignified walk was gone from his voice.
"They are not waiting for the crates.
Their riders took the north road at dusk, under crown seal, moving fast."
The duke looked down at the invitation in his hand, sealed and still warm.
He had written it three days too late.
Then the stillness broke, and the chair went over behind him.
Fear, when it finally reached the Duke of Ravenshade, came out as orders.
"Call them!" He was on his feet and shouting like a garrison sergeant.
"Call every count of the border RIGHT NOW!
They must ensure everything is in order!"
The chancellor flattened himself against the map wall as his lord crossed the study at a pace no servant would ever be permitted to describe.
The invitation went into the fire whole.
"And Corvane." The duke stopped at the window, where the dark had already swallowed the north road.
"Corvane comes to me.
Tonight.
My seal and an escort, and if he hesitates, the escort doubles."
The shouting, this time, was for the house.
The last call the duke made himself.
The communication artifact came up from the desk drawer, and the mana he forced into it made the crystal whine.
Then it pulsed, and pulsed, and Ravenshade learned what waiting felt like.
"Alexios!" The bare name, at a volume the framed maps had never heard.
"Riders on my land in the dark, under your seal!
You audit fishmongers, Alexios!
You audit millers grown too fat!"
The duke's fist came down on the desk, and the dwarven inkwell jumped.
"You do not audit the house that put a queen on your arm and heirs in your line!
You owe this house more than paper, so you will say it to me!
What is this?!"
The artifact hummed, patient, while his breathing filled the study.
"The letter says all the crown has to say." The king's voice came through level, old, and completely unbent.
"What about Felicity?!
I'll-"
The connection died in his hand.
Reckoning was upon the final true bastion of the Vraven Kingdom.
Meanwhile, the other notable factions of the Iskaris Continent were activating themselves as well, making preparations brought by the Primordial Villain's rise!

chapters.title: Chapter 1866 Left Behind
paragraphs: The [Warp Gate] bloomed in the central reading hall of the Vraven royal archive, and the war of paper barely broke stride.
Quinlan stepped through with Ayame on his arm. The nearest clerk saw the light, hugged his tray to his chest, and kept walking. The hall had adapted.

Black Fang had walked through ahead of everyone, and by the time the gate closed behind them she was already deep in the stacks, in the wing where the crown kept its files on the continent's criminals. Hers occupied most of a shelf.

She pulled her own dossier without asking anyone, opened it against one arm, and read it unhurried, grading the crown's intelligence for accuracy. The aisle emptied of clerks in under a minute. Authorization had not been sought. The archive elected not to bring it up.
"Stop arriving like that," said Alexios from behind a desk that had annexed two of its neighbors, without looking up from what he was signing.
"You said that last time."
"Yes. And?"
"I thought you'd get used to it. It's about time, no?"
"...You truly have an innate talent."
"For elemental magic, among many things, yes."
"Such as getting on my nerves."
Quinlan elected not to hear that, already scanning past him toward the center of the hall.
The center was missing.
Iris's table sat stripped bare, the border maps gone, only knife holes left in the wood where their corners had been pinned.
Only the folio kept its post under the clean sheet of glass, where every runner in the hall passed it a hundred times a day. Damian Ravenclaw, in fresh dark ink, leading the record.
The riders who had taken the north road at dusk rode under Stormlord's command, but Iris was given full permission to lead the investigation itself.
A wry smile climbed onto Quinlan's face and settled in.
"She didn't even tell me she left," he said. But despite the verbal complaint, the pride in it was warm and complete, the kind he never bothered to hide.
For long years the world's paper had agreed that her family had never existed, and she had carried that silence as a powerless child and then as an outlawed adventurer.
Now she was back in Ravenshade lands as the crown's hired investigator, tearing the true story out of the ground with both hands.
"Things are finally moving, huh, Iris?" he said to the empty table, to the name under the glass, to a red-eyed menace far away who couldn't hear him.
Beside him, Ayame looked at the stripped table and smiled.
The cheek stayed home, and so did the tease she would have filed for later, and the whole armory she kept stocked against her rival on principle.
Her frenemy had stopped circling her wound and started hunting it, and Ayame was, from the bottom of her heart, glad.
"Good," was all she said.
"Where is she exactly?" Quinlan asked, drifting toward the desk. "I'd like to pay her a visit."

"Terrorizing my border holdings." Alexios signed another page. "She rode out the night you left and has gutted two toll stations since. The commission's protocol prescribed a month of document review before any field work. She reinterpreted the protocol. I chose to indulge her."
"How generous."
"..." Alexios remained silent. It was evident he had a soft spot for the girl who had been wronged so thoroughly in his kingdom.

But, to save face, he quickly added, "The paper stalled, so she went to question the people who wrote it. She interviews the keepers personally. My chief archivist has requested hazard pay. In writing. Citing precedent."
"Pfft." Ayame's grin went fond.
"And Felicity?" Quinlan asked. "I half expected an ambush at the gate."
"She rides with the commission." The pen kept moving. "The crown needs a face in the field for such a major event, and..."
'My chosen heir needs a name in the field, and Vraven has to watch her make it. A bubbly princess is not enough.'
He didn't say that out loud.
Quinlan's eye found a ledger table abandoned mid-column, its chair shoved back hard enough to have traveled. "And Lilith?"
"The Scarlet Lilies took a crown contract. Commission security, field wing." Alexios reached for the next stack. "Lilith called the pay insulting."
"Aren't you like turbo rich? Pay the woman, you damned coin pincher. In fact, you should double the pay of every person who's present."

The hall's rhythm stumbled. Quills stopped mid-stroke, a runner froze with a crate half lowered, and every clerk in earshot performed the same maneuver: perfect outward composure, ears straining backward. Nobody spoke to their king like that. And no one, ever, had proposed doubling their pay while doing it.
Then hopeful glances began to gather on the crown from every direction, one desk at a time.
Alexios stared at his thoroughly unwelcome guest, and for a long moment the driest man in Vraven was simply, honestly appalled.
The shameless creature was courting the loyalty of the crown's own staff, in the crown's own archive, in front of the crown, while smiling at him.
"...Back to work," the king said, and the hall resumed at double diligence, powered by hope.
Ayame leaned into Quinlan's shoulder, delighted. "You're going to get your bounty raised again."
"It's basically infinite already," Quinlan said. "They stopped offering money for me a while back. It's a royal boon now. Ask the crown for anything."
Her grin widened. "It can always go to two royal boons~"
Quinlan decided this was the right time to move on, so he turned to Alexios and asked, "How loud is the howling?"
"Half my court believes I've lost my mind. No king has ever audited a great house," Alexios replied after signing a document. "The other half is quietly measuring Ravenshade's furniture."
"So you're in control."
"Naturally," Alexios scoffed. "My vassals are no longer powerful enough to force my hand."
Saying that one line seemed to make the man lose centuries of age.
Alexios might've acted nonchalant, but he was making the biggest moves of his career right now, in the middle of a paperwork flood he had signed into being himself.
He had taken the seat out from under Alastair with enough evidence and enough noble backing that nobody could call it a grab, and put it up for bidding.
He had named the Fujimori Elders traitors and sentenced every one of them to death, then gone out and taken a head himself.
And now the last dirty house in Vraven was on his desk, and the old king looked truly happy about it.
Even a certain shameless scumbag's arrival couldn't fully sour the mood.
Quinlan nodded and watched him work for a while after that.

For decades the old king had ruled with a deadline hanging over him, dying a little more each year, and he had kept every appointment anyway. Then a pill forged from a primordial's blood struck him in the chest, and the deadline itself died. His aging simply stopped.
And this was what he did with forever.
Sleeves rolled before dawn, signing warrants against the mightiest house in his kingdom, hunting decades of rot through toll ink.
He could have passed that second life on a sunlit balcony, being toasted by grateful generations. He went straight back to work instead, and worked harder, because now the work would actually finish.

Quinlan had opened his own veins for this man through a whole night and drained his family's reservoir to the floor for him. Looking at the rolled sleeves and the merciless pace of that signature, he'd do every second of it again.
Despite their constant grumbling, the two had managed to earn each other's respect.
"You work too much, old man."
"And whose fault is that."
Neither of them smiled where the other could prove it.

chapters.title: Chapter 1867 Crumbling House
paragraphs: The escort returned to the Ravenshade ducal seat at dawn, and it returned without Count Corvane.

"His gates were shut, my lord." The escort captain stood at attention in the study and looked at a framed map instead of his duke. "The count sends his regrets. He is... indisposed. His men were courteous, my lord. Courteous, and... they were on the walls."
"Indisposed." Tharion repeated the word from behind his desk, level. The level was work.

"There is more. The ferry village across from his seat reports wagons on the count's roads past midnight. Heavy ones, moving without lanterns. And the record-house chimneys... They were still burning when we rode out, my lord."
The last word reached the bottom of the duke's stomach before his face moved, and his hands flattened slowly on the desk.

The count had built his whole service on executing before a thought finished forming, always a step ahead of the whistle. Now the whistle had blown, formally, under ducal seal, and the dog had heard it, and gone back to burying things.
The wagons were the count's affairs moving somewhere darker; the chimneys, his papers becoming smoke. He was cleaning, unordered, at speed, and every fire he lit told anyone watching where to dig.
And Tharion could not order him to stop.
An order would exist. Ink, a courier, a road, a witness: a thread running upward from the count's fires into this study.
The old arrangements had been built, over patient centuries, so that no thread ran upward, and that distance had kept him safe his entire tenure.
Now it worked exactly as designed, in the wrong direction: he could not reach down without leaving a handprint. He could only watch his own instrument panic from the far end of his own lands.

The escort captain had not moved. He stood where he had stopped, eyes still on the framed map, waiting on a duke who had not answered. Somewhere behind him the doors had opened, and the chancellor was already at the desk's corner with a fresh sheet.
Fear, in the Duke of Ravenshade, had only one shape. It came out as orders.

"Riders to every road out of the count's seat!" He was on his feet and the study had become a parade ground. "Name lists at every ferry and every gate. If Corvane travels, I hear of it before his boots cool. If a wagon leaves his lands, I want its weight, its cargo, and the name of the man driving it!"
The chancellor wrote at a speed that endangered the pen.

"And a survey party to our own border archives!" His fist came down, and the wax seals jumped in their tray. "If the crown wants a war of records, Ravenshade's will be in perfect order. Perfect! Find me clerks who can read forty years of toll ink, and find them by noon."
The chancellor began a question, met his duke's eyes, and retired it.
Back in the royal archive, mid-signature, Alexios reached into a desk drawer instead of the next stack.
What came out was old parchment, creased from months of intense copying: a crown warrant for the criminal Devil, in fading ink.
Alexios had signed it himself a lifetime of headaches ago, and had never once gotten around to canceling it.
He canceled it now: one stroke, void, stamped, initialed. He slid it across the desk without a word and went back to signing.
Quinlan flicked two fingers and the dead warrant lifted off the desk, riding a curl of air up to eye level while he read through his own crimes, warming at every charge. "It's not even my birthday."
Alexios did not look up at him. He looked, briefly, at Ayame.
She grinned back, shameless as her lover.
"Take your allies and get out of my archive," said the king. "You're thoroughly unpleasant."
"Aww..." said Quinlan, visibly hurt.
He left the way he'd arrived, the gate blooming mid-stride, Ayame taking his arm with one last fond glance at the stripped table.
Two aisles over, Black Fang tucked her own ledger containing centuries of criminal filing under her arm and walked out of the royal archive with it, committing one more crime in broad daylight.
No one stopped her.
The smoke report reached the royal archive before its seals had fully cooled.
"Fires over the Corvane seat since midnight," Alexios read aloud. "Still rising at dawn."
He crossed to the correspondence table and set the page down in front of the one person in the hall who had grown up reading Ravenshade smoke.
Morgana's pen did not stop. "Record-house chimneys," she said. "Burning a full night." Her crimson eyes crossed the report once, unimpressed. "How utterly boring."
"The commission maps every blaze. Location, duration, order." Alexios took the page back. "Your house is drawing us a treasure map in smoke."
"My house?" The venom in the two words could have inconvenienced an antidote. "I merely donated the blood."
The Duke of Ravenshade gave his day to the crystal, and the day shrank with every call.

The count of the river marches answered from behind sealed archive doors, wobbling on every third word. "They were polite, Your Grace. They had a warrant. It had numbers in it. They knew the years, Your Grace. They knew them before they opened a single crate."

The next call was answered by a steward. He read his master's regrets off a page his master had not written, and he read them twice, because he lost his place. Tharion set the crystal down before the third pass.
One call did not answer at all. Another came back with an apology and, between its lines, a new employer.
By late afternoon a single lever remained, and it was the best of them: Duskmere, the neighboring duchy across a shared border, the oldest friendship Ravenshade had.
He composed himself before making that call. He even sat.
The crystal lit at the second pulse.
"Tharion." Zaren of Duskmere's voice arrived warm and worried at once. "Old friend. I wondered when you would call."
For the first time all day, the duke's shoulders came down a fraction.
"Zaren. You've heard."
"The whole kingdom has heard."

"Then you understand what it means." Tharion leaned in, and the court voice came back into harness, measured and sure. "Today it's Ravenshade's tolls. Tomorrow it's your marsh levies, and Thornhollow's grain counts, and every ledger every house has kept since the Accord. The crown has forgotten what a great house is. We stand together, Zaren, or we kneel separately."
Silence held on the other end, and Tharion let it work.
Then, faint through the crystal, from somewhere sunlit on the other side of that border, came a woman's voice.
"Dear? The winter roses opened this morning. Walk with me before the light goes."
Tharion knew the voice. Every duke alive knew the voice. Calienne Valorian, eldest daughter of King Alexios, wife of Duskmere.
The blood went out of the duke's hands, and it went cold on the way. She had come in somewhere in the last minute of it, and the last minute was the part a king would want.
"A moment, my heart." Zaren's words arrived muffled, a palm half over the crystal. The palm failed to muffle the smile in them.

He left the way he'd arrived, the gate blooming mid-stride, Ayame taking his arm with one last fond glance at the stripped table.
Two aisles over, Black Fang tucked her own ledger containing centuries of criminal filing under her arm and walked out of the royal archive with it, committing one more crime in broad daylight.
No one stopped her.
The smoke report reached the royal archive before its seals had fully cooled.
"Fires over the Corvane seat since midnight," Alexios read aloud.
"Still rising at dawn."
He crossed to the correspondence table and set the page down in front of the one person in the hall who had grown up reading Ravenshade smoke.
Morgana's pen did not stop.
"Record-house chimneys," she said.
"Burning a full night." Her crimson eyes crossed the report once, unimpressed.
"How utterly boring."
"The commission maps every blaze.
Location, duration, order." Alexios took the page back.
"Your house is drawing us a treasure map in smoke."
"My house?" The venom in the two words could have inconvenienced an antidote.
"I merely donated the blood."
The Duke of Ravenshade gave his day to the crystal, and the day shrank with every call.
The count of the river marches answered from behind sealed archive doors, wobbling on every third word.
"They were polite, Your Grace.
They had a warrant.
It had numbers in it.
They knew the years, Your Grace.
They knew them before they opened a single crate."
The next call was answered by a steward.
He read his master's regrets off a page his master had not written, and he read them twice, because he lost his place.
Tharion set the crystal down before the third pass.
One call did not answer at all.
Another came back with an apology and, between its lines, a new employer.
By late afternoon a single lever remained, and it was the best of them: Duskmere, the neighboring duchy across a shared border, the oldest friendship Ravenshade had.
He composed himself before making that call.
He even sat.
The crystal lit at the second pulse.
"Tharion." Zaren of Duskmere's voice arrived warm and worried at once.
"Old friend.
I wondered when you would call."
For the first time all day, the duke's shoulders came down a fraction.
"Zaren.
You've heard."
"The whole kingdom has heard."
"Then you understand what it means." Tharion leaned in, and the court voice came back into harness, measured and sure.
"Today it's Ravenshade's tolls.
Tomorrow it's your marsh levies, and Thornhollow's grain counts, and every ledger every house has kept since the Accord.
The crown has forgotten what a great house is.
We stand together, Zaren, or we kneel separately."
Silence held on the other end, and Tharion let it work.
Then, faint through the crystal, from somewhere sunlit on the other side of that border, came a woman's voice.
"Dear?
The winter roses opened this morning.
Walk with me before the light goes."
Tharion knew the voice.
Every duke alive knew the voice.
Calienne Valorian, eldest daughter of King Alexios, wife of Duskmere.
The blood went out of the duke's hands, and it went cold on the way.
She had come in somewhere in the last minute of it, and the last minute was the part a king would want.
"A moment, my heart." Zaren's words arrived muffled, a palm half over the crystal.
The palm failed to muffle the smile in them.

chapters.title: Chapter 1868 The King's Gambit
paragraphs: The crystal stayed lit, and Tharion sat holding it while a man he could not see looked at his wife. A garden door opened on the far end of the call. He knew what that sound was worth before it finished.
When Zaren returned, the worry had gone out of his voice. What remained was gentle, and final.

"Tharion. Duskmere's friendship is not in question. It never will be." Zaren drew an audible breath. "But an audit is a small thing for a house with nothing to hide, old friend. Cooperate fully, and it passes over you like weather." The warmth came back, gentler than before. "Give my regards to Ardent."
Pleasantries followed. Tharion heard himself supplying his half of them from somewhere outside his own body. Then the light left the crystal, and the study was quiet.
The capital had sent nothing: no letter, no courier, no whispered instruction.

Calienne Valorian had been promised to Duskmere before she was born, married to its duke when she came of age, and had loved him honestly for all their centuries since, filling his halls and remaining, through every year of it, her father's daughter.

She had worked out what these days were on her own. The whole kingdom had heard. So when Ravenshade's crystal lit in her husband's study, she went out to the garden, checked on the roses, and came back for him.
That was the entire operation.

A daughter, placed in the enemy's house four hundred years before he would need her, so loved by its duke that her lightest wish outweighed another duke's warning, waiting through court season after court season for the one afternoon her father would need a door held shut.

Alexios had spent no soldier, no coin, not even a sentence of instruction. The ally Tharion had spent his tenure building left for a walk among winter roses, and the woman who charmed him away went on that walk with a full heart, doing right by the two men she loved most.
Zaren never learned that anything had happened at all. He simply, honestly, wanted to see the roses with his wife.
In the Ravenshade study, the crystal was still in Tharion's hand.
"ZAREN!"
The scream tore out of him at the dead crystal, at a volume no Ravenshade study had ever heard, and his chest was heaving before it ended.

"Cowards! COWARDS, ALL OF YOU!" The crystal went across the study. It took a framed map off the wall, and both came down together, glass and crystal and the western marches. "A lifetime of friendship, and you fold for a WALK IN A GARDEN?!"
The crash brought a guard's face into the door. Whoever it was read the room and withdrew without orders.
The duke stood over the wreckage, breath sawing in and out, fists opening and closing on nothing.
Then he laughed. One short bark, wrong from the first note, and it frightened him more than the audit had.
Morgana. The Ravenshades sold her to the crown and called it, privately, the finest trade of his tenure.

Ravenshade blood on the throne, a queen's ear in the family, royal heirs of their own line. They had walked out of that negotiation certain they had skinned a weak king desperate to buy peace from the house that could unmake him.
He turned the trade over now, and it showed him its other face.

The crown had bought Ravenshade's blood out of Ravenshade, and let him call it a queen. His sister lived in the capital, belonged to its new order, publicly, and not one line of her hand had reached this study in years.
The finest trade of his tenure had moved his house's heart behind the enemy's walls, and he had been proud of the price.

Calienne. He had counted that marriage as tribute: the king's eldest daughter, paid into the bloc's soundest house to buy its quiet. A frightened man appeasing his betters, marriage by marriage. He had called it a concession won.
His hands had begun to shake. He watched them do it as if they belonged to the chancellor.
She was a garrison, promised before she was born, installed with a wedding, held in reserve through an entire honest marriage, and spent this afternoon, all of her, on one walk among winter roses.
The weak king had aimed her at this exact day before she drew her first breath.
And the succession. Felicity, and the deal that...
The thought arrived at a door, and Tharion did not open it. He turned from it bodily and crossed the study, because a man in motion could be doing something other than finishing thoughts.
His whole tenure at that desk, he had negotiated against a dying man and won every single session, concession after concession carried home in triumph.
He stopped above the wreck of the western marches, glass crunching under his boot, and could not name one prize the old man had not placed in his hand.

Every victory of his tenure had been handed to him across that desk, wrapped, by a man who wanted him to carry it home and be proud of it. And he had been proud. He had set each one down in this study like a trophy, session after session, the sharpest head his house had ever put in front of a king.

The shame came slower than the fear had, and it went deeper, because the fear was about the house and this was about him. He had been finished this afternoon, on a schedule, by a man who had stopped needing to think about him centuries ago.
The weakness had been aim. The dying had been patience.
Alexios Valorian wrote the letters that mattered in his own hand, warmly, exactly as Tharion did. Only the mail differed.
His own fondest letter of the decade had gone into a fire three days too late. The king's had been arriving centuries early, every one of them, since before his enemies knew there was a war.
"CHANCELLOR!"
The doors opened on a man already braced.
"Duskmere's letters. Every page that house has ever sent this study, on this desk by morning."

He was moving along the map wall as he spoke, straightening frames that were already straight. "The correspondence ledgers with them. Who wrote, when, carried by whom, answered how. And the same for every house that has gone quiet on me this week!"
"My lord, that is... decades of correspondence."
"Then light more candles!"
The Duke of Ravenshade had begun auditing his own friendships.
The last report of the day came up from the capital in a merchant's cipher, from the one hand down there that still answered him.
Tharion decoded it himself, alone at the desk, the house asleep around him.

'The commission of audit answers to a woman. Young. Red eyes. She carries no house name, and none can be produced by any inquiry at any price. The royal archive opens to her at any hour, on her voice alone. The king defers to her in all matters of the audit. No further particulars available.'
Tharion read it three times.
"Red eyes," he read aloud, to the empty study. "No house name. A girl." He turned the page over, as if the real report might be hiding on the back. "This is what I pay for? A DESCRIPTION?!"
It gave him nothing. A young woman with no house was nobody: some crown creature pulled out of a gutter and dressed in authority for the work, a tool and nothing more.
Nobodies did not audit great houses.
"And yet the archive opens at your voice," he told the cipher, his thumb pressing a crease into it. "And yet the king defers. To you. Who ARE you?!"
The paper declined to answer.
The oldest house in Vraven stood under audit, dukes' letters went unanswered across the realm, and at the center of all of it sat a red-eyed girl with no name that money could buy.
He fed the cipher to the fire and watched it curl. Then he took fresh paper, the good stock, and wrote one line in his own hand, pressing hard enough that the last stroke tore through.
'Her name. Whatever it costs.'
He sealed it with the raven.

chapters.title: Chapter 1869 Catching Up to the March
paragraphs: The commission's column had been on the border road since the previous night, and Iris ran at the head of it with the third holding's books roped between her shoulder blades.
Nobody behind her had eaten anything warm since the dark, and nobody said so out loud, because the young woman leading them hadn't slowed once and complaining took energy.

The commission's clerks made it worse by surviving. Three archivists swayed in the middle of the column with crate-files strapped where saddlebags should be, sleeping in shifts. One of them was drafting a second hazard-pay request in his head.
Ahead of them, out past the river flats, mysterious fires had been burning since midnight.
Iris had known that since dawn.
She had been moving at this pace ever since.
Stormlord rode the ranks up and down, and backs straightened wherever he passed. "Water at the next rise," he told the sergeants. "We stop for nothing else."

Near the front, Princess Felicity Valorian sat her horse with her visor up and her chin refusing to admit anything. Her stomach growled with the volume of a modest siege engine. She pretended it was the horse.
Then the air split open in the middle of the column, and a [Warp Gate] bloomed between the supply wagons, breathing warmth into the winter road.
"GATE!"
The column turned into a hedgehog in under three seconds. Spears and swords came down in a bristling ring, horses shied, and two riders threw themselves bodily in front of the princess.
Every soldier on the continent knew what came out of gates like that. Necromancer was the polite version.
Quinlan Elysiar strolled out with Ayame on his arm and surveyed the leveled steel with warm approval, as though the crown had turned out an honor guard for him.
Black Fang came through behind them and was even less bothered by the sharp blades aimed at her.
Then Quinlan looked past the spearpoints at the column behind them, and the approval dropped off his face.

Grey faces looked back at him. The horses had been ridden well past the point where a horse argues about it, and behind them the clerks slept sitting up, with the kingdom's evidence roped to their backs.
"Quinlan!"
Felicity burst out from between her own bodyguards, shoved a spear aside with a gauntlet, and arrived at a sprint.
"You're late!"
"Sorry."
"Did you have fun?" she asked, sending a look toward Ayame, having a great many suspicions about what they'd been up to for the past day.
"It was nice seeing Silverwind. Beautiful land."

"Hehe! I bet you did a lot of sightseeing..." She had both gauntlets on his sleeve already. "We left in such a hurry there was no time to stock anything meaningful. Supply lines are trying to catch up."
The look she sent down the column landed on exactly one person.
Iris came back down the line at a run and stopped hard in front of him.
"You're stalling the march."
"They look like they could use a breather." Quinlan hadn't stopped looking at her soldiers. "How long have they been up?"
"Since we left."
"How far to the next destination?"
"They'll make it. They're professionals."
Many flinched at that.
"Hmm." Quinlan grinned, liking how this unhinged baddie was making career soldiers weep silently. "Then let me make it faster."
Quinlan rolled his wrist once, and the road went to work.
Wagons full of files went first.
Then the road itself. Frozen ruts a hand deep sank flat ahead of the wheels, stone knitting where the ice had chewed it open. This let the horses and infantry boots stop fighting the ground.
A wrongness folded open beside the supply train, and Void arrived out of it with her eyes shut, in exactly the posture she had been sleeping in a moment earlier.
"Welcome back..." she murmured, smiling softly.
She lifted one hand at the rearmost wagon without opening her eyes. The wagon left the road, arrived a hundred paces up it, and kept rolling as though nothing at all had happened to it.
And just like that, the Void Mage and the Primordial Villain began hauling the heavy vehicles, drastically increasing march speed.
Iris watched the road unbuild itself in front of her army as she ran, and the thing she had been carrying since the dawn report came loose by a fraction.
"...Thank you..." she whispered under her breath.
Quinlan refused to accept the gratitude, merely grinning back at her, making Iris avert her gaze.
Felicity beamed at the pair of them from Quinlan's elbow, delighted beyond all reason, both gauntlets still on his sleeve.
Stormlord took one look at a road with nothing wrong with it and gave the only order it left him.
"Column! Double time!"
The groan that went up ran the entire length of the formation.
"He fixed the road," a corporal said, and heard his own funeral in it. "Why did he fix the road?"
"So we can run on it faster," said the man beside him.
"He's truly a villain!"
"The Villain!!"
Down the ranks the verdict assembled itself out of forty separate complaints, and it was unanimous.
They had been warned about this man for nearly a year now. And the first thing he had done on meeting them was take away every excuse they had to walk.
"That's how he does it." A sergeant wheezed it between strides. "He improves your conditions... until you die of them."
Quinlan flew at the head of a column that was now openly calling him a slaver, and looked entirely at peace with the assessment.
"Your soldiers are slow," he told Felicity.
'Die, Villain!!' many screamed inwardly.
"They're trying their best!" Felicity chirped.
'We are, princess!!'
"Is that so...? Then let me help them. [Awaken]."
He said it without ceremony.
The winter road opened along both flanks, and the dead climbed out of it.

They rose in the colors they had died in, ring mail scoured and surcoats whole, wearing faces the living had last seen going into the ground. Then they fell in beside the column at a dead run and started picking people up.
A soldier in the third rank was scooped off his own feet by an arm around his ribs, and made a sound no grown man wants recorded.
"PUT ME DOWN YOU FOUL-!"
"No. You're too slow."
"Marlen?!"
"Aye."
Petyr hung over a dead man's shoulder at a full run, staring at the back of a head he had helped burn a kit for. "You were on the wall! I helped burn your kit!"
"Good kit, too." Marlen didn't break stride. "You still owe me four silver."
"You're DEAD and you're still on about the four silver?!"
"Money is money."

It happened the whole length of the column at once. Men who had been two miles from falling over were being carried by men and women they had buried, and the shouting that went up had very little to do with fear.
"Does it hurt?" It came quiet off a dead man's back, with no mockery anywhere in it. "Being... what you are now?"
The soul carrying him considered the question at a run.
"I hated the cold," he said. "Haven't been cold since."
"He killed you," the living man said, careful.
"Aye." The dead man shifted his grip so the living one wouldn't slide. "I've had worse commanders."
Behind them, the sergeant who had explained the improvement of conditions was riding up a rise on the back of a lancer he had drunk with for six hundred years, and had revised his position.
'He's an angel!'
Iris ran at Quinlan's shoulder with the ledgers thumping against her back and told him what was in them.
"Every road in this county pays twice," she said. "Once to the crown, on a schedule that's written down. Once to the count, on a schedule that isn't."
"How far back?"

"Oldest book I've got is thirty years, and it's on every page of it." She jabbed a thumb back at the books strapped between her shoulders. "Three holdings, three sets of books, same second toll. The books don't say whose it is. The keepers do, once you sit them down properly."
"He's got an entire machine running."
"Yes."
Silence returned, the two of them looking at each other for a long moment. Then...
"Look at you~"

"Your soldiers are slow," he told Felicity.
'Die, Villain!!' many screamed inwardly.
"They're trying their best!" Felicity chirped.
'We are, princess!!'
"Is that so...?
Then let me help them.
[Awaken]."
He said it without ceremony.
The winter road opened along both flanks, and the dead climbed out of it.
They rose in the colors they had died in, ring mail scoured and surcoats whole, wearing faces the living had last seen going into the ground.
Then they fell in beside the column at a dead run and started picking people up.
A soldier in the third rank was scooped off his own feet by an arm around his ribs, and made a sound no grown man wants recorded.
"PUT ME DOWN YOU FOUL-!"
"No.
You're too slow."
"Marlen?!"
"Aye."
Petyr hung over a dead man's shoulder at a full run, staring at the back of a head he had helped burn a kit for.
"You were on the wall!
I helped burn your kit!"
"Good kit, too." Marlen didn't break stride.
"You still owe me four silver."
"You're DEAD and you're still on about the four silver?!"
"Money is money."
It happened the whole length of the column at once.
Men who had been two miles from falling over were being carried by men and women they had buried, and the shouting that went up had very little to do with fear.
"Does it hurt?" It came quiet off a dead man's back, with no mockery anywhere in it.
"Being... what you are now?"
The soul carrying him considered the question at a run.
"I hated the cold," he said.
"Haven't been cold since."
"He killed you," the living man said, careful.
"Aye." The dead man shifted his grip so the living one wouldn't slide.
"I've had worse commanders."
Behind them, the sergeant who had explained the improvement of conditions was riding up a rise on the back of a lancer he had drunk with for six hundred years, and had revised his position.
'He's an angel!'
Iris ran at Quinlan's shoulder with the ledgers thumping against her back and told him what was in them.
"Every road in this county pays twice," she said.
"Once to the crown, on a schedule that's written down.
Once to the count, on a schedule that isn't."
"How far back?"
"Oldest book I've got is thirty years, and it's on every page of it." She jabbed a thumb back at the books strapped between her shoulders.
"Three holdings, three sets of books, same second toll.
The books don't say whose it is.
The keepers do, once you sit them down properly."
"He's got an entire machine running."
"Yes."
Silence returned, the two of them looking at each other for a long moment.
Then...
"Look at you~"

chapters.title: Chapter 1870 Bureaucratic Stalling
paragraphs: Ayame had drifted up on his other side, running happily, entirely untroubled by the pace.

"A deserter with a bounty on her head, hiding in the dirt and biting people. And now the King of Vraven signs whatever you put in front of him, and his soldiers run when you tell them to run." She tilted her head. "Your rise rivals Quin's."
"Say it."
"Say what?"
"The part where you think 'somebody' handed it to me."
"Insecure, are we~? I'd never say such a thing," Ayame purred, full of joy.
"Eat shit."
"No, thanks~" Ayame grinned, shaking her head at this impossible girl. "Listen to my wisdom, young lady."
Iris sent her the nastiest of looks.
Ayame blew her a kiss and delivered the wisdom.
"Just enjoy your revenge, shed good blood, bash some skulls, and stop thinking useless thoughts.
Quinlan flew between the two of them and made no attempt to keep the pride off his face.
The girl who had once torn testimony out of a Covenant lord in a frozen basement was taking a duchy apart with paperwork, and the paperwork was losing.
Stormlord drew level on Iris's far side and gave the road one flat glance, then the investigator a longer one, a beat past anything a report required. He said nothing about it at all.
"The crown's escort does not require civilian assistance," he informed Quinlan.
Behind him, two of his own sergeants were riding on dead men's backs.
"Duly noted," said Quinlan.
Walled in grey stone, the Corvane seat rose out of the river flats an hour before full dark.
Smoke came up with it, four columns thick and steady, leaning east with the wind and still fed after a full day.
Nobody said anything about that. The column had run itself hollow to arrive, and it had arrived exactly as late as Iris had known it would.
The gates were open.

The night before, the Duke of Ravenshade's own escort had found those gates shut, with courteous men on the walls. For the crown's commission, riding under the royal seal, the count had opened everything and strung lanterns the length of the approach.
An honor guard in polished ring mail lined the road, and a steward bowed to Princess Felicity at the gate arch and held the bow until the whole column had passed him.
"Your Highness... his lordship... the count waits within, Your Highness."
Count Corvane himself waited in the outer courtyard, a broad man in formal furs with rings on every finger and sweat standing at his collar in the winter air.
Iris had his name off the crown's liege rolls before she ever came east. Her father's barony had answered to this county.
What she had from before the rolls was a dinner table.
'Damn the count. He is pocketing the coins, I'm sure of it.'

Her father, drunk at his own table, complaining about a man he owed money to. She had been far too young for the words to mean anything, but lucky for her, Quinlan - who saw the same memories - was more than old enough to understand and relay those words to her.

When the barony died, the county it sat inside got bigger. However, that did not imply criminal behavior; with the family members' deaths and Iris's own disappearance, it was only natural that the barony returned to the count.
However, thirty years of a second toll, and the fires that were visibly burning before their very eyes...
It did not paint a favorable picture of the count, whose welcome had been drilled since morning. The welcome survived until his eyes found the tall man strolling loose at the column's flank.
The bow he offered Princess Felicity was flawless. It also gave him somewhere to put his eyes that was nowhere near Quinlan Elysiar.

Felicity dismounted, and Stormlord brought his horse up at her right shoulder. Iris drifted to the escort's flank and leaned there, arms folded. The princess had practiced in the saddle most of the afternoon, quietly, lips moving.

"Count Corvane. In the name of my father, Alexios Valorian, King of Vraven, the commission of audit requests and requires the toll archives of your holdings, in their original copies, surrendered to its bearers."

The count's voice was rich and warm and a shade too quick. "Your Highness honors my house beyond its worth. Rooms have been prepared, and my kitchens... Your riders must be frozen through. Vraven remembers hospitality, whatever else these strange days take from us."
"The archives. Now, please."
"Of course. Immediately." He paused. "Of course."
The count spread his hands, rings glittering.

"There is only the small matter of the catalog. By statute, a holding surrenders records under seal with a certified inventory, and my seneschal, who has kept that inventory thirty years, is abed with winter fever. To hand Your Highness loose crates, uncounted, unsealed... the crown itself would rebuke me for sloppiness."
Somewhere behind the inner wall, burning timber let go with a crack, and a fresh gust of sparks climbed into the evening.
The count listened to it sideways, without turning his head, and lost half a sentence to it. "The... yes. The inventory. Forgive me."
Felicity held her voice level. "Count. There's a fire burning in your holding."
"A chimney accident, Your Highness. Old flues, older timber." He dabbed his neck. "My men contained it swiftly. No documents were harmed, I've been assured."
Above his head, the smoke went on rising, uncontained, in four places at once.
"Then your men can show mine the archives. Right now."

"By daylight, Your Highness, gladly, joyfully. Night work breeds errors, and errors in a royal audit stain the innocent alongside the guilty." He bowed to her again, deeper. "You have my full cooperation. I ask only that it be done properly."
"A fire broke out." Felicity's voice came up, and every scrap of courtesy left it at once. "The same night my father's letter reached this duchy."
"A regrettable coincidence, Your Highness."
"I've heard enough."
Her hand had found the seal at her breastplate without her deciding to.
"You open those doors now, or I tell my father that Count Corvane refused the crown's commission to his princess's face."
The count did not flinch, and that was worse than flinching. He inclined toward her as though she had raised a point of law.
"Your Highness accuses. That is Your Highness's right." The warmth stayed in his voice, and there were teeth under it now.

"An accusation is not a finding. A finding wants evidence, evidence wants an inventory, and the inventory wants my seneschal, who is ill. I have refused the crown nothing at all. I have asked for daylight and a clerk."
He spread the rings again, catching lantern light with them.
"If Your Highness wishes to name me traitor tonight, before witnesses, without one page in her hand, I will of course submit. My advocates will meet the charge in the morning."
This was where Iris quit listening.

Her eyes had gone to the smoke instead of the man, and they had stayed there through every word of the parley. Through the chimney accident that burned in four places. Through the count's aching regard for exactness.
An ash flake drifted down and settled on her sleeve. She tilted her arm into the lantern light.
Paper. It was snowing paper.
She came off the flank walking, straight past the parley, and the courtyard's temperature followed her.
"I'm done waiting." Her voice stayed low and her stride didn't break. "Move."
Count Corvane worked it out a half second ahead of everyone else in that yard. The woman coming through the parley was coming at him.
"Your Highness." His voice finally cracked in the middle. "Your Highness, control your-"
Stormlord's horse crossed her path first, and then Stormlord swung down off it and planted himself in her way.
"Stand down, investigator."
"Move."
"No." The word landed iron-flat, and what sat behind it had nothing to do with the count.

"That man is a vassal of my king. Until a court or damning evidence says otherwise he has the crown's protection, and I am the crown's protection." His eyes didn't leave hers. "You deserted under my watch once. I have worn that embarrassment in front of my king ever since. You will not wreck a second mission under my watch."
"Your watch." Iris looked up at him, and her voice went bored. "Your watch is why a fat loser's chimneys get to outrank a royal seal."
*Shing.*
