chapters.title: Chapter 1871 Black Fang's Move
paragraphs: *Shing.*
The sound crossed the courtyard alone, small yet absolute.
Iris held the drawn sword low at her side, red eyes level on the man who had once commanded the outpost she walked out of.
"I don't have time for you." Her tone stayed conversational. "I'll kill you first."

The courtyard went wrong in stages. Hands found hilts along the honor guard, one after another. The escort discovered it had no idea where to point its spears, at her or for her, and settled on trembling in place.
Up on the walls the count's men stopped pretending to be furniture, and a warning left one of them as a squeak. A dropped spear rang on the stone like a bell. It stayed where it fell.
"Now this is more like it~"
Ayame arrived at Iris's shoulder with her thumb already resting on her katana's guard, and gave Stormlord a smile with nothing polite left in it.
"You're already embarrassing yourself by refusing to act. We all know what's going on here. Stop being pathetic."
Her chin tipped at the four columns standing over the inner wall.
"A man with nothing to hide doesn't light four buildings in one night. He's already confessing, just doing it with chimneys instead of words."
Stormlord did not look at it. "It's smoke. Fires happen. This is not damning evidence."
"I see." Steel whispered a centimeter out of Ayame's sheath.
One drawn investigator had been a crisis. Two of the continent's monsters standing shoulder to shoulder was a sentence, and every armed man present had just heard it read aloud.
Stormlord stayed exactly where he was.
"I'll not forgo written protocol because some outsiders demand it. If he's lying, he'll be prosecuted, as the law demands."
His gauntlets creaked at his sides, and his feet did not move, a king's captain planted between two women because his king had put him there.
Count Corvane had gone grey above his collar. "Gentle... honored guests, surely..."
Not one head turned his way. That, at least, was new.
Felicity had gone still in the middle of all of it, her prepared sentences dead in her mouth.

She had asked for this post. Begged her father for it, actually begged, hands folded, the whole performance. Iris was finally close to the thing she'd been hunting, and Felicity had wanted to be part of handing it to her, certain her presence would count for something as a royal who was on her side.
She knew what the answers meant to her friend. Iris had only ever given her pieces of it.
And she had done everything right, every form, every courtesy, and the count had eaten her words one bow at a time while his chimneys ate the truth.

Now Iris and Stormlord stood a centimeter of steel apart in the courtyard of the house they had come to audit, and Stormlord had been guarding Felicity since she was light enough to ride on his shield arm.
All of it was hers.
The stall, the standoff, the whole curdled evening, because a princess with a royal seal and a practiced speech hadn't been able to buy Iris one open door.
The guilt landed all at once, hot, under her breastplate where the seal hung.
Her eyes began to sting, her throat working hard.
Then a hand settled on her shoulder.
It came down light, and half the courtyard flinched harder for it, because the whole yard knew who it belonged to.
The Primordial Villain stood beside the princess of Vraven in the falling ash.
"Hey," he said, only to her. "You did good helping Iris. You're a great friend."
The shout died in her throat.

Felicity looked up at him. His hand stayed easy on her pauldron, and behind him a courtyard full of steel waited for somebody to move first, and he had turned away from every bit of it to say those words to her.
The sting went out of her eyes, and her fists came open at her sides.
She smiled instead, small and soft, as if she had known from the very start that everything was going to be fine.
But Quinlan had promised Alexios he'd do this the right way.
Was ignoring Stormlord, Alexios's military representative, the right way?
'Hmm. Let's do "that" then-'
Black Fang was already ahead of him.
The Venomborne Terror reached into her sleeve and drew out a communication artifact.
The crystal pulsed twice before a voice climbed out of it, thin with distance and thick with age.
"...This channel has not opened in a very long time."
"It's me."
Silence.
Then the old man's voice came back at a volume that made the artifact buzz against her palm.
"BLACK FANG?! You- after everything, after every message I sent, you finally-"
"I need you to tell me what our archives have on a Ravenshade noble."
Something creaked at the far end of the connection. Something else was set down on a workbench.
"Haaah... Not one word in months, and the first one is an order to your elder." A dry sound followed it. "You have not changed even slightly. Which noble."
"Corvane."
"...Ah." All the wryness in the world arrived at once. "Corvane. Of course it is Corvane."
"What do you have?"

"What do I have." The old man said it back to her slowly. "That man, and the operation he represents, is the reason we do not operate properly in Ravenshade. That, and the skellies. So yes. We have files on Corvane. We have files on Corvane's files."
Quinlan leaned into range of the artifact.
"Can you bring it here?"
On the other end, whatever the old man had been doing stopped.
"...Is that Devil."
"Hello, boss."
Technically, Quinlan was still a Vesper Phenom.
"You shameless- Ehem. The Consortium's pride, standing in a duchy that is not his, on an open channel, while Black Fang holds the-"
"Time is of the essence, old man."

"...Everything is of the essence, young man. Discretion matters. Preparation matters. A dossier of that weight, properly copied, properly bound, properly-" the old man slowed, reaching for a comfortable number, "-I could have it ready by tomorrow evening."
"Now."
The old man went quiet.
"... You're making an impossible request of this old man."
"Corvane is burning his papers. We need proof of him being a criminal scumbag so Stormlord stops barking at us."
"Ah. You should've started with that. My weary knees suddenly feel alive again."
"I'll help you bring it to us."
Count Corvane had prepared for a princess. He had prepared for an investigator. There was no statute anywhere in the kingdom that covered the third thing.
The [Warp Gate] bloomed in the middle of his courtyard.
What stepped through was an old man in dark robes, grey beard down his chest, back stooped from a millennium of work, a leather case held under one arm.
He took two steps onto Corvane stone and blinked at the lanterns, then looked around a yard where a whole column of exhausted soldiers was being held upright by the dead.
Then he found Stormlord, adjusted the case, and produced a bow of respectable depth.

"Stormlord of the Aegis Vanguard." He straightened and held the case out to him. "Our noble establishment's documents on this county, and on that wonderful man over there. Most of them written by his own people and... 'acquired' by mine."
Behind the honor guard, Count Corvane had gone completely motionless.
"Huh?"
He had come through the crown's letter, the princess, the investigator, the drawn steel, and he had held his shape through every one of them.
He looked at the man in the dark robes, and his rings began to rattle against each other.
He knew that face.

"Corvane.
Of course it is Corvane."
"What do you have?"
"What do I have." The old man said it back to her slowly.
"That man, and the operation he represents, is the reason we do not operate properly in Ravenshade.
That, and the skellies.
So yes.
We have files on Corvane.
We have files on Corvane's files."
Quinlan leaned into range of the artifact.
"Can you bring it here?"
On the other end, whatever the old man had been doing stopped.
"...Is that Devil."
"Hello, boss."
Technically, Quinlan was still a Vesper Phenom.
"You shameless- Ehem.
The Consortium's pride, standing in a duchy that is not his, on an open channel, while Black Fang holds the-"
"Time is of the essence, old man."
"...Everything is of the essence, young man.
Discretion matters.
Preparation matters.
A dossier of that weight, properly copied, properly bound, properly-" the old man slowed, reaching for a comfortable number, "-I could have it ready by tomorrow evening."
"Now."
The old man went quiet.
You're making an impossible request of this old man."
"Corvane is burning his papers.
We need proof of him being a criminal scumbag so Stormlord stops barking at us."
"Ah.
You should've started with that.
My weary knees suddenly feel alive again."
"I'll help you bring it to us."
Count Corvane had prepared for a princess.
He had prepared for an investigator.
There was no statute anywhere in the kingdom that covered the third thing.
The [Warp Gate] bloomed in the middle of his courtyard.
What stepped through was an old man in dark robes, grey beard down his chest, back stooped from a millennium of work, a leather case held under one arm.
He took two steps onto Corvane stone and blinked at the lanterns, then looked around a yard where a whole column of exhausted soldiers was being held upright by the dead.
Then he found Stormlord, adjusted the case, and produced a bow of respectable depth.
"Stormlord of the Aegis Vanguard." He straightened and held the case out to him.
"Our noble establishment's documents on this county, and on that wonderful man over there.
Most of them written by his own people and... 'acquired' by mine."
Behind the honor guard, Count Corvane had gone completely motionless.
"Huh?"
He had come through the crown's letter, the princess, the investigator, the drawn steel, and he had held his shape through every one of them.
He looked at the man in the dark robes, and his rings began to rattle against each other.
He knew that face.

chapters.title: Chapter 1872 A New World
paragraphs: Count Corvane knew that face.
The knowledge was written all over him, and every soul in the torchlit courtyard could read it.
Stormlord took the case from the old man's hands.

"NO!" The word tore out of the count before wisdom could catch it. "I will not... This is outrageous! Stolen ledgers! Forgeries, peddled by cutthroats and poison-merchants! Your Highness, this... this creature offers you criminal contraband and calls it evidence! No court in Vraven would seat the word of the Vesper Consortium against a peer of the realm!"
Ash drifted between the lanterns. On the wall, one of the count's own men shifted his grip, armor creaking in the hush.
Felicity tilted her head. "The Vesper Consortium?"
"Count." Her voice came out small and clear, and it carried to every corner of the yard. "I get the impression that you knew him on sight."
Corvane's mouth stopped working.
"Care to explain yourself?" The princess took one step forward, gauntlets loose at her sides.
Silence.
"Do answer, my lord." The old man leaned on nothing in particular, grey eyes politely interested, hands folded into his sleeves. "I confess I am curious myself."
"B-Black Fang called him! She's well known-"
"Black Fang can call in favors with many people. I asked where you know his face from."
The count's answer began three separate times, and each attempt died faster than the one before it, because every road out of that question ran through the same gate, and the gate was a confession.
Felicity watched him drown for exactly as long as he deserved, then turned her head and looked at Stormlord.

She did not say a word. She had spent every courtesy she had on this courtyard, every form observed, and the count had swallowed all of them. The look she gave her father's commander was the end of that patience, a princess of Vraven done asking.
Stormlord met her gaze for a moment before he opened the case.

He read standing, unhurried, while the count found his voice again and spent it at volume on jurisdiction, on statute, on the indignity of a royal commission entertaining gutter documents on noble stone. Stormlord turned pages through all of it without lifting his eyes once.
"Investigator." He held out one gauntleted hand, still reading. "The third holding's books."
Iris pulled the rope off her shoulders one-handed, sword still naked in the other, and threw the whole bundle across the courtyard.
Stormlord caught it without looking up from the page.

He set the crown's seized ledger beside the Consortium's copy on the flat of the case. His eyes went left, right, left again, down thirty years of parallel columns written by different hands, agreeing with each other to the coin.
Corvane ran out of statute somewhere in the middle of it. Nobody in the courtyard breathed especially well after that.
Then Stormlord closed the case and looked at the count, and delivered his verdict with the same iron flatness he had used to block a drawn sword.
"I said a court or damning evidence." He handed the case to the sergeant at his shoulder. "This is damning evidence."
Somewhere behind him, Ayame grinned. "Finally."
"You cannot..." Corvane began.

"Count Corvane. On suspicion of levying an unlicensed toll upon crown roads across thirty years, on suspicion of commanding criminal enterprises in your lands, and of burning records demanded under royal seal." Stormlord's voice rose to fill the yard, pitched for fields far larger than this one. "By the authority of the commission of audit, you are detained for the crown's judgment. Take him."
The courtyard moved, and it moved away from him.

His honor guard, the polished men in polished ring mail who had lined his approach with lanterns, stepped backward out of the light in ones and twos, hands finding their way off their hilts. They left a wide, respectful, empty lane between their lord and the commission's soldiers.
His steward had already vanished somewhere between one shout and the next.
By the time the crown's men reached him, Count Corvane stood entirely alone in the middle of his own courtyard.

"Hands off me! HANDS OFF!" The composure that had survived a princess, an investigator, and two drawn blades came apart all at once. "I am a COUNT of VRAVEN! My house has held these borders for generations! You are arresting the WRONG..."
They took his arms. His boots furrowed the gravel.
"I have friends! You have no idea what you are touching! There are people who will... who..."
"What friends?" Felicity asked sweetly. "Are any of them named Ravenshade?"
The count's sentence went nowhere, at full volume, in front of everyone.
"Corvane's holding stands with the crown!" someone called from the wall, quite loudly, twice.
"COWARDS! TRAITORS!" The count's head whipped toward his own walls, and somewhere in the whipping, the understanding finally landed: nobody was coming.
His face went from red to grey in the space of one breath, and the sweat at his collar turned cold.
The fright, when it took him, took him completely.

"Wait." His voice came out at half its size, cracking in the middle. "Wait, wait, WAIT! I can pay. Whatever the crown believes it is owed, my vaults... I will open my vaults! I am an old man, I have served, I have served..."
His legs stopped carrying their share of him, and the two soldiers adjusted their grips without breaking stride. His rings rattled against their vambraces like dice in a cup.
He found Felicity's face and aimed everything he had left at it. "Your Highness! I appeal to the crown! Mercy! I demand... I BEG the crown's mercy!"
Felicity didn't even reply, merely watching with a soft smile as the man was taken away.
The guardsmen half-carried him through the gate arch of his own keep. The screaming thinned into begging, and the begging got smaller and smaller until the night took it entirely.
*Shink.*

Iris's sword went home for the first time since the parley began. She rolled the shoulder the ledgers had been chewing on all day, unimpressed, as if the evening had merely finished catching up to her schedule.
Beside her, a centimeter of steel clicked back into Ayame's sheath.
"Mm~" was all the samurai said, deeply satisfied.

Stormlord turned to his sergeant and issued orders past the arrest without pausing for breath. "Send word to the capital; I want this seat logged as commission ground before dawn. Every servant confined to quarters, every fire crew under escort, and nobody touches a page without the investigator's leave."
The yard broke into motion around him, and the commission poured inward.
Quinlan fell in with the flow, then peeled out of it at the east wall, where Black Fang had reclaimed her patch of shadow.
His hand settled on her waist, warm and easy.
"Thanks for the save."
Black Fang looked at the middle distance. "It was nothing." She walked on, robes whispering, and took up a new post ten paces deeper in.
Quinlan grinned at her back, looking entirely too pleased with himself.
By the gate arch, the Mediator observed the entire exchange without appearing to observe anything at all.
'...She let him keep the hand after that?'

He had watched the greatest assassin on the continent end men for standing in her light. The Consortium kept a great many incident reports on its sharpest blade, and as of tonight, every last one of them required revision.
'This continent is doomed,' the old man concluded serenely. 'Truly, thoroughly doomed.'

Then he gathered his sleeves and turned for the arch, because the case was delivered, the crown had what it needed, and the yard was filling with royal soldiers who would shortly run out of urgent tasks.
He offered the nearest sergeant a small bow on his way past. "My compliments to your commander. The Consortium's business here is concluded."
The sergeant, who had no instruction covering any part of this evening, saluted the old man back.
"Aren't you curious?"

Quinlan had stopped at the inner doors, holding one open, firelight from the bailey beyond catching the edge of his grin. He tipped his head toward the keep's interior, the invitation aimed at the old man by the gate arch.
The Mediator regarded him.
A count's inner holding stood open past that door.
Crown soldiers guarded its thresholds, a princess of the blood walked its corridors, and the most wanted man alive stood holding its door, inviting him in to watch the evidence get read.
He had entered noble houses before, a long lifetime of them. Through servant doors, through coin-bought windows, through tunnels dug under treasuries by men whose names no record kept.
His people had entered such houses the same way for generations, because front doors were not built for people of their blood.
'Thank the Goddess,' the Mediator thought, adjusting his sleeves with great dignity, 'that we are on the right side. For once.'
"Curiosity," he said aloud, shuffling forward with his beard preceding him, "is the one appetite age has left me. Lead on, young man."
The inner bailey was snowing.

Paper ash came down in fat grey flakes, thicker with every courtyard they crossed, catching in hair and dulling the lantern light. Ahead of the commission, the record-houses of the Corvane seat glowed against the night sky like four open hearths.
They felt the heat a full courtyard before the doors.
Iris walked at the front of it all, ash gathering on her shoulders, red eyes fixed on the nearest of the burning archives. Suffering and a continent of scum had stood between her and this place.
She was one door away now.
The doors were iron, and they were hot, and behind them lay whatever the count had considered worth burning last.
'Damian... Mother... It'll end soon.'

A mile beneath the dwarven capital, Brokk, First Hammer of the royal smithy, came into her hall on the morning shift and found her smiths crowded around the gallery mouth. A notice had been nailed up there in the night.
The paper bore the seals of four claimant lords who agreed on nothing else in this world.
They had agreed on this.
"Read it out!" someone called from the back tiers. "Not all of us have eyes to read the gibberish in these council letters!"
Young Vorn was already standing on a bench with the thing in both hands, and his voice cracked twice getting through it.

"By joint order of the council of claims, for the defense of the mountain." He swallowed. "First. Every forge in the capital is turned to the pattern-book. Axes, helm blanks, mail links, warhammers, to quotas the council will set and revise at need."
"...Standing commissions are suspended," Vorn read on. "Masterwork is suspended. Apprentice trials are suspended for the duration."

"The pattern-book." The master with the copper wire braided through his beard said it slowly, and put his weight on it. "Forty years at that anvil. And they want me to instead make mass-produced axes."
"Second."

chapters.title: Chapter 1873 Tyranny
paragraphs: "Second." Vorn's voice was climbing. "A general levy is raised upon every household of the under-tier, called by district, beginning with the galleries. Smiths are exempt, being required at the anvil."
"Exempt." Old Dain said it from his bench, both hands on his cane, testing whether the word worked any better out loud. It did not. "They'll take my sister's boys, and leave me here to arm them."
"Third. Wages of all crown craftsmen are to be paid in scrip until the war is decided." The hall's rumble began somewhere around the word scrip.
"Which war?!" a journeyman shouted down from the second tier. "We haven't got an army! We buried it in the passes!"
"Fourth," Vorn said, and then he stopped.
He had read ahead.
"Read it, lad."

"The elves." Vorn's voice came out flat and careful. "Having broken faith with the mountain and delivered their whole race unto the Primordial Villain, are declared treacherous, and hold no treaty of ours."
The rumble stopped.
"And the Villain is declared enemy of the mountain, to be resisted and eliminated, for he will come with the long-ears at his back to break our gates and put our people in chains."
At the back of the hall, Brokk's thumbs went into her belt.
"Ah."
"They're preparing for war against him."
"With what?!" a smith growled, hurling his wadded shift-rag at the post. "Our armories are not fit for war!"
"This is so pointless! Have they lost their minds?! Everyone knows numbers mean nothing against his Necromancy, and they plan to throw our friends and families at him?!"
Line by line, at full volume, the hall took the notice apart.
A shield-veteran named Halvar came down with the off-watch, still in his harness, and the stair behind him filled with more of the same.
"They cut the passes' pensions," he reported to the hall at large. "Scrip. For the living. The widows get... they get nothing. And now they're raising a levy off the same galleries."

Journeymen drifted in behind the soldiers, then porters, then a pair of tunnel-wardens still carrying their lamps. Every trade of the under-tier was collecting in the one hall where somebody they trusted held authority.
"Treacherous," one of the tunnel-wardens repeated, setting his lamp down on a cold anvil.

Vorn was still up on his bench with the paper in both hands, and he had gone a color no apprentice should ever see on a master. The smith who raised him from his first nail had marched out with the army and never marched back.

"Kaelira chose hearth-steel," Vorn said. "With the crown's adamantite lying open right behind her. Because... because the piece has to deserve the metal." He shook the notice once. "She hammer-tested by ear. In our hall. And she taught it to anyone who asked." His voice went. "That's not a traitor."
"And this." Old Dain didn't move off his bench. "This says the man is coming to put us in chains."
"Ahaha! Those imbeciles don't even know that he was already here!"
"They're clueless," a master agreed. "He stood where you're standing and asked me about my flue draw."
"And when he went, he left the hammer."

Old Dain set both hands back on his cane. "He could've killed every soul in this hall, but instead he asked us about quench oil." He looked up at the notice. "You don't leave a gift on the anvil of a place you mean to chain."
"Where's Elowen?" an apprentice said, from somewhere along the second-tier rail.
The hall looked around itself and found a gap in it.
Then something came up out of the tunnel-wardens' alcove, which answered the separate question of where the wardens' good barrel had gone.
Elowen of the elven royal guard arrived at the top of the steps at a list, one hand on the rail, the other around a dwarven drinking horn that had not been issued to her by anybody.
"I heard," she announced to the entire under-tier, with enormous care, "a WORD."
"Which word, lass?"
"Treacherous." Her ears went flat. "Treach... treh..."
*Buuurp.*
"...Forgive me."

"I was ON that bench." She swung the horn at the guests' bench and lost a third of it over the stone. "I watched them fold those damned metals, and then they left it sitting on that anvil and went home. And your lords have written down that he is coming to CHAIN you."
"Aye!"
"He was here for a whole DAY!" One finger came up, on the second attempt. "If he wanted your mountain he would simply have taken your mountain, you magnificent short people!"
Half the gallery mouth started laughing.
"He takes what he wants," Elowen went on, warming to it, gesturing broadly enough to endanger the nearest apprentice. "That is the entire..."
She stopped.
Her own words caught up with her, slowly, the way things do at the bottom of a horn.
"...He forgot about me."
"Aye, lass."
"He left me HERE." The ears came up. "That MOTHERFUCKER left me here!"
The royal smithy of the dwarves roared its approval, and a second horn was pressed into her free hand before she could put the first one down.
Brokk had not said one word since the gallery mouth. She stood in the middle of her own hall and read the notice for herself, top to bottom, while every soul in it watched her do it.

Behind her, the Copper Vaults' siege-plate order sat racked by the quench basin, ground and fitted and waiting on the final quench. That call was hers, and nothing left this mountain as finished steel until she made it.
A master smith cleared his throat and put it to her formally, the old form, with a nod at the racked plate.
"The Vaults' order's suspended, First Hammer. Council wants the pattern-book on these anvils by the next shift." His beard worked once. "They'll want your call on the first crate."
Brokk looked at the plate, then at the notice, then at her hall.
Her thumbs came out of her belt.
"Light the forges."
Nobody moved.
"All of them," Brokk said. "Every hearth on every tier, and dig the old die racks out from under the sand bins."
She was already walking toward the nearest cold hearth.

"First Hammer-?!" Vorn was down off his bench without noticing he had left it, the notice crumpled in his fist. "They want axes! You heard what they wrote about her. You heard what they wrote about him. And you're going to-"
"Move, lad."
"You'll stamp out their axes, then." Old Dain said it from his bench with no heat in it at all, and the hall went quieter than any shouting could have made it.
Brokk stopped.
She came back through her own smiths and put her boot on the notice where it had fallen.
"They want us to make weapons."
She let them have that.
"So be it. We'll make weapons."
The hall went still.
"And every one of them will be used to protect our loved ones and the future of the dwarven people."
"First Hammer!" The roar started at the racks, took the second tier with it, and did not stop until it had the rail.
Brokk talked straight through it, and it fell away to let her.
"They take!"
"AYE!"
"And Take!"
"AYE!"
"And take even more!"
"AYE!"
"And when there's nothing left to take, they write down that we owe them more, and they sign it the defense of the mountain! I'm done."
"Done." Old Dain got his cane up off the floor and held it there with both hands shaking on it.
"And then what?"
It came from a journeyman near the front, and it was not a heckle. The lad looked frightened, and he said it anyway.
"Who rules us at the end of it? You, First Hammer?"
"No. I don't have the strength nor the will. But there's a man who already beat them," Brokk said.
Three hundred smiths knew exactly who she meant, and not one of them said the name.
"He asked me what we could make." Her thumbs went back into her belt. "No lord has ever asked me that. They tell me their demands."
"And when the talk came round to my smiths, he said we sounded like the kind of people any sane ruler would want to support."
Then the First Hammer of the royal smithy put it to them flat, tier by tier.

This time the hall answered her.
"YES!"
Brokk let them have it for as long as it took her to cross her own floor.

Her smiths opened out of her path without being asked, and the noise went out behind her tier by tier as they worked out where she was walking, until three hundred dwarves were following her with their eyes and nothing else.
At the heart of the hall stood an anvil nobody had worked in a season.
Everwright, squared to the light where an elf had set it down before she went home. It had been humming there through every shift-bell since.
The First Hammer's fingers closed, and she lifted the Villain's gift off the anvil.
Three hundred smiths pulled in one breath and held it.

She raised it over her head. The elf had stood on this same floor to do that, with her ears blazing and her spine straight, and the lamplight ran the length of the water-grain now exactly as the forge-light had run it then, waking the rune-script where it crossed.
"Magma."
Brokk reached into the hammer instead of into herself. She had watched it done from four feet away, once, and she had not forgotten a single thing about it.
The rune-channels answered a dwarf.
The head woke red, then deeper, then molten, and the light came up the grain until the whole tool ran the color of a fresh pour and brought the First Hammer's face up out of the dark.

Brokk brought Everwright down.
*KRAAANG!!*

sentences.text: "Second." Vorn's voice was climbing.
"A general levy is raised upon every household of the under-tier, called by district, beginning with the galleries.
Smiths are exempt, being required at the anvil."
"Exempt." Old Dain said it from his bench, both hands on his cane, testing whether the word worked any better out loud.
It did not.
"They'll take my sister's boys, and leave me here to arm them."
"Third.
Wages of all crown craftsmen are to be paid in scrip until the war is decided." The hall's rumble began somewhere around the word scrip.
"Which war?!" a journeyman shouted down from the second tier.
"We haven't got an army!
We buried it in the passes!"
"Fourth," Vorn said, and then he stopped.
He had read ahead.
"Read it, lad."
"The elves." Vorn's voice came out flat and careful.
"Having broken faith with the mountain and delivered their whole race unto the Primordial Villain, are declared treacherous, and hold no treaty of ours."
The rumble stopped.
"And the Villain is declared enemy of the mountain, to be resisted and eliminated, for he will come with the long-ears at his back to break our gates and put our people in chains."
At the back of the hall, Brokk's thumbs went into her belt.
"Ah."
"They're preparing for war against him."
"With what?!" a smith growled, hurling his wadded shift-rag at the post.
"Our armories are not fit for war!"
"This is so pointless!
Have they lost their minds?!
Everyone knows numbers mean nothing against his Necromancy, and they plan to throw our friends and families at him?!"
Line by line, at full volume, the hall took the notice apart.
A shield-veteran named Halvar came down with the off-watch, still in his harness, and the stair behind him filled with more of the same.
"They cut the passes' pensions," he reported to the hall at large.
"Scrip.
For the living.
The widows get... they get nothing.
And now they're raising a levy off the same galleries."
Journeymen drifted in behind the soldiers, then porters, then a pair of tunnel-wardens still carrying their lamps.
Every trade of the under-tier was collecting in the one hall where somebody they trusted held authority.
"Treacherous," one of the tunnel-wardens repeated, setting his lamp down on a cold anvil.
Vorn was still up on his bench with the paper in both hands, and he had gone a color no apprentice should ever see on a master.
The smith who raised him from his first nail had marched out with the army and never marched back.
"Kaelira chose hearth-steel," Vorn said.
"With the crown's adamantite lying open right behind her.
Because... because the piece has to deserve the metal." He shook the notice once.
"She hammer-tested by ear.
In our hall.
And she taught it to anyone who asked." His voice went.
"That's not a traitor."
"And this." Old Dain didn't move off his bench.
"This says the man is coming to put us in chains."
"Ahaha!
Those imbeciles don't even know that he was already here!"
"They're clueless," a master agreed.
"He stood where you're standing and asked me about my flue draw."
"And when he went, he left the hammer."
Old Dain set both hands back on his cane.
"He could've killed every soul in this hall, but instead he asked us about quench oil." He looked up at the notice.
"You don't leave a gift on the anvil of a place you mean to chain."
"Where's Elowen?" an apprentice said, from somewhere along the second-tier rail.
The hall looked around itself and found a gap in it.
Then something came up out of the tunnel-wardens' alcove, which answered the separate question of where the wardens' good barrel had gone.
Elowen of the elven royal guard arrived at the top of the steps at a list, one hand on the rail, the other around a dwarven drinking horn that had not been issued to her by anybody.
"I heard," she announced to the entire under-tier, with enormous care, "a WORD."
"Which word, lass?"
"Treacherous." Her ears went flat.
"Treach... treh..."
*Buuurp.*
"...Forgive me."
"I was ON that bench." She swung the horn at the guests' bench and lost a third of it over the stone.
"I watched them fold those damned metals, and then they left it sitting on that anvil and went home.
And your lords have written down that he is coming to CHAIN you."
"Aye!"
"He was here for a whole DAY!" One finger came up, on the second attempt.
"If he wanted your mountain he would simply have taken your mountain, you magnificent short people!"
Half the gallery mouth started laughing.
"He takes what he wants," Elowen went on, warming to it, gesturing broadly enough to endanger the nearest apprentice.
"That is the entire..."
She stopped.
Her own words caught up with her, slowly, the way things do at the bottom of a horn.
"...He forgot about me."
"Aye, lass."
"He left me HERE." The ears came up.
"That MOTHERFUCKER left me here!"
The royal smithy of the dwarves roared its approval, and a second horn was pressed into her free hand before she could put the first one down.
Brokk had not said one word since the gallery mouth.
She stood in the middle of her own hall and read the notice for herself, top to bottom, while every soul in it watched her do it.
Behind her, the Copper Vaults' siege-plate order sat racked by the quench basin, ground and fitted and waiting on the final quench.
That call was hers, and nothing left this mountain as finished steel until she made it.
A master smith cleared his throat and put it to her formally, the old form, with a nod at the racked plate.
"The Vaults' order's suspended, First Hammer.
Council wants the pattern-book on these anvils by the next shift." His beard worked once.
"They'll want your call on the first crate."
Brokk looked at the plate, then at the notice, then at her hall.
Her thumbs came out of her belt.
"Light the forges."
Nobody moved.
"All of them," Brokk said.
"Every hearth on every tier, and dig the old die racks out from under the sand bins."
She was already walking toward the nearest cold hearth.
"First Hammer-?!" Vorn was down off his bench without noticing he had left it, the notice crumpled in his fist.

You heard what they wrote about her.
You heard what they wrote about him.
And you're going to-"
"Move, lad."

chapters.title: Chapter 1874 Talk Around The Fire
paragraphs: In the heartlands of the Beastman Confederation, Skarn of the wolfkin had not slept a full hour since the four columns came home.

The camps told the story to anyone with eyes. The tribes had returned from the war to their own ground, and they still pitched apart: wolfkin ridges, tigerkin river-lands, the bearkin deep woods, the dogkin vales.
A confederation that won a battle in utter glory, its enemies decimated, had come home carrying itself like it lost.
Their four lords met at the war-lodge fire, as they now did whenever the continent coughed, and the continent had been coughing without pause.
A scout crossed the lodge and bowed low to the four lords together, and her report broke apart in her mouth.
"Word from the human kingdom, great lords. The king has... forgive me. It reads wrong, but it reads the same from three runners."

She steadied herself. "The human king has put his own mightiest remaining house under the knife. A royal audit, lords, against his own blood-tied duke. And the Villain's gate opens in the royal capital... daily, great lords. The clerks don't even look up anymore. I don't know what to make of that."
Silence sat over the lodge for a moment, and then Skarn came up off his haunches and began to pace.
"We walked home." The words scraped out low and raw; this was not the first time the fire had heard them.

"The elves knelt and called it faith. The humans are about to kneel and call it statecraft. The whole continent is going to its knees, and the predators of Iskaris turned around and walked home in our own dust, with our tails up like nothing happened!"

"Aww." Rajah lay along a fallen trunk on the fire's far side, amber eyes half-closed, tail tip ticking. "This fire has heard that speech more often than it has heard my name." The tail stopped. "Say the true part, wolf. He made you small, and he did it while we watched."
Skarn's head snapped around, and the snarl climbing out of his throat died there, because the tigerkin lord was not wrong and they both knew it.
"He dangled my own oath in front of my teeth," the wolfkin lord said instead, "and smiled while I nearly bit. In front of the armies!"
His claws flexed once, fully, and retracted. "The pact is a toy to him. He keeps it while it amuses him, and his patience runs like a bleeding bitch's temper."
"Mm. Awfully accurate words, my friend." Rajah had gone very still along the trunk. The amber eyes opened the rest of the way, and nothing lazy survived in his voice.
"I stood on that field while a human king called me 'little kitten' in front of my army, wolf. Then I turned around, took my soldiers, and carried the word home with me. I understand your dismay."

The drawl slid back on like a coat. "And so we prepare. When the other lands run out of entertainment for him, he will come for the wilds, and the mountain will not lift a hammer for us when he does. Let him find something with teeth."
"Walking home was correct." Gorruk said it into the fire without lifting his head, and the rumble rose through the ground ahead of the words. "Every lord here knows it. That is why it sits so badly."
None of them called it fear. The preparations screamed it for them.
Drill-fields churned to mud before every dawn. Fletchers and tanners worked torchlit shifts that ended when the torches did, and every trail in the wilds had its watcher.
The lodges filled with cots down the aisles, and the greybeards turned away at the door returned at first light to stand in it.
Through all of it, Vargis Ironfang sat with his giant war axe across his knees and a whetstone making slow circles along its edge.
He had sat through fire after fire in that same silence, until the other lords stopped inviting his counsel and he stopped offering it.
The whetstone stopped.
Three heads turned, because nobody at that fire could remember the last time it had.
"The oath has held," said the dogkin lord.

"Kingdoms fall to that man on a schedule. Whole races kneel to him by choice. And in all of it, he has not moved on one wolf, one tiger, one bear, or one hound. The fox went for his women, and the reckoning stopped at the fox."
He let that sit for a breath. "Skarn handed him the excuse himself, in front of both armies, and he declined to take it."
"Ironfang-" Skarn began.

"We have never asked him for terms. Not once." The war-chief spoke over him without raising his voice. "Every lord at this fire has spent a season preparing to lose a war nobody has declared, and all four of us have walked past the door to do it."
He looked around the flames at the three of them. "I say we send for him."

"And say what?!" Skarn's laugh had no floor under it. "I had terms, dogkin. I had a blood oath sworn in my own hand, and he lifted it to see whether I would bite." He was pacing again. "You would roof the Confederation with that man's mood."
"Say that the pact no longer fits the man who swore it." Vargis sighed, and the slow circles started again while he spoke.
"He signed it when he was weak, with our claws forcing his hand, and it has been nothing but a restriction on him since. A pact that only takes is a pact waiting to be dropped."
"So we ask him what the wilds can offer that he would want. We make it fit both sides, and then it is not his patience holding our roof up."

"There's nothing to ask. He'd take, take, and take. And there is the other matter." Rajah had not moved from his trunk. "He keeps what he kills. The ranks we would march beside are full of dead men carrying their killer's banner." The tail lay still. "Predators do not run with thralls, dogkin."
"Gorruk." Vargis turned to the bearkin. "You caught the trap he set for Skarn. You saw what he did after."
Gorruk regarded him for a long moment.
"I did."
"And?"
"And I will not put the Confederation's throat inside a fist I cannot reach." The rumble stayed level. "Ask me again when I can."
Skarn's pacing had run out a while ago. The dogkin had gone past him to Gorruk, and two lords were deciding the wilds' future between them while the wolfkin lord stood there and listened.
Skarn came around the fire, and he did not lower his voice for it.
"Your daughter lives in that man's house, Ironfang. You have not spoken at this fire in a season, and the first time you open your mouth, you open it for him."

He put his weight forward onto the balls of his feet. "Tell this council what your counsel is worth." The wolfkin lord's voice dropped into the register he saved for prey. "Are you even still on our side at all?"
The whetstone stopped mid-circle.
Vargis Ironfang set the war axe and the stone aside without one wasted motion, stood, and the lodge got smaller.
"My daughter chose that man, and I let her keep the choice." He said it level, and it landed heavier that way. "I weighed him longer than any of you cared to look at him. That is all."
He crossed the ground between them, and Skarn did not give way. Chest met chest, and neither lord yielded a finger's width.
"Say the word you mean, wolf." The dogkin lord's voice did not rise. "Say oathbreaker, and say it where the fire can hear you."
Loyalty was the marrow of the dogkin, sworn and kept on more fields than the Confederation had songs for, and Skarn had spat on it across a council fire.
Vargis had walked off every one of those fields with his loyalty taken as given.
He had let his daughter keep the man she chose because he trusted his own eyes, and Skarn had just picked her up and used her as a knife.
The fire snapped. Somewhere along the wall, the scout stopped breathing.
"Take it back," Vargis said, very quietly. "Or say it again with your claws out."
Skarn held where he was, and the whole lodge waited to see whether the word or the claws came first.
Gorruk rose, and his shadow put half the lodge in the dark.
"Enough."
The rumble arrived from somewhere beneath the flames, and it did not ask. He looked from one chest to the other until there was room to breathe between the two lords again.
"Border dens report at each moon, watchers go on the passes, and the stores fill before the cots do, because a den full of warriors and empty of grain is a siege we lose in a week."
"We prepare for the worst, and we rebuild what the march emptied while we do it."
His voice went around the fire and stopped at nobody. "And Ironfang's door stays open. Whether we walk through it, and how, this fire decides together. Not tonight."
Vargis returned to his log and set the stone to the edge without breaking the look. Skarn lowered himself onto his haunches, and Rajah's tail took up its tick again, delighted.
"...He told us he would reach out," Rajah said to the flames. "If he does, we will learn what his word is worth."
Quinlan had offered reparations at the end of the war, for their help in bringing about victory.
Dwarven engineers, elven coin and all. He had given Gorruk his word he would raise it again anyway.
"Whatever the future holds, the Confederation prepares as one," Gorruk said.
That night, from den to den and ridge to ridge, the deep drums of the Confederation woke and said the same thing until dawn: sharpen, stockpile, drill.

The iron doors of the last record-house had not cooled by a single degree since Iris stopped in front of them, and through the metal, underneath the fire's voice, came the sounds of men still working.
Racks crashed over somewhere inside. Orders reached them through the iron, muffled, and somebody in there was sobbing while he worked.
Iris listened to every bit of it without moving. Somewhere behind that iron, men were feeding her brother's answer into a fire, and she could hear them doing it.
"Barred from the inside, Highness," the fire-warden captain reported to Felicity, and kept a full spear-length back from the investigator while he did it.
Behind the commission, chains rattled across the bailey stones.

They had brought the count back in irons, because a man who had screamed an offer of his vaults in front of the whole yard was going to honor it, and Corvane had walked quietly enough until he saw which doors the investigator had stopped at.
Then he began to fight the two soldiers holding him, thrashing on the end of their grip like a hooked fish.
"There is nothing in there! Tax rolls! Duplicates! I swear it on my mother's memory, do not waste the crown's time on..."
Iris put her bare hands flat on the iron.

He had given Gorruk his word he would raise it again anyway.
"Whatever the future holds, the Confederation prepares as one," Gorruk said.
That night, from den to den and ridge to ridge, the deep drums of the Confederation woke and said the same thing until dawn: sharpen, stockpile, drill.

The iron doors of the last record-house had not cooled by a single degree since Iris stopped in front of them, and through the metal, underneath the fire's voice, came the sounds of men still working.
Racks crashed over somewhere inside.
Orders reached them through the iron, muffled, and somebody in there was sobbing while he worked.
Iris listened to every bit of it without moving.
Somewhere behind that iron, men were feeding her brother's answer into a fire, and she could hear them doing it.
"Barred from the inside, Highness," the fire-warden captain reported to Felicity, and kept a full spear-length back from the investigator while he did it.
Behind the commission, chains rattled across the bailey stones.

They had brought the count back in irons, because a man who had screamed an offer of his vaults in front of the whole yard was going to honor it, and Corvane had walked quietly enough until he saw which doors the investigator had stopped at.
Then he began to fight the two soldiers holding him, thrashing on the end of their grip like a hooked fish.
"There is nothing in there!
Tax rolls!
Duplicates!
I swear it on my mother's memory, do not waste the crown's time on..."
Iris put her bare hands flat on the iron.

chapters.title: Chapter 1875 Burning Books
paragraphs: The heat bit through both palms in one breath, deep and total. She took all of it in without a sound, one more payment into a very old account.
*KRRUNK.*
The hinges gave before the door did. This one she threw, and it went tolling across the bailey like a dropped bell, and the commission got its first look inside.
The count's men had built a pyre in the center aisle out of the archive's own racks and were feeding it by the armful.
A dozen of them, stripped to shirtsleeves, black to the elbow, faces cooked red by a night of it.
At the far end, two more hauled crates out of the deep racks, where a night of burning had not reached yet.
For the space of one breath, everything stopped: the burners with their arms full, the commission in the doorway, the fire eating in the middle.
Then Corvane wrenched one arm free and screamed past his own guards with his voice tearing in half.
"BURN IT! BURN THE REST! If you love your children, BURN IT ALL!"
And his men chose the fire.

The initials squared away in those books were their own, and whatever waited above Corvane for men who let his paper be read frightened them worse than anything standing in that doorway. Armfuls went up. Torches came around toward the untouched racks.
None of it landed.
Ayame crossed the hall in one straight line, and the nearest torch hit the floor still gripped by a hand that no longer had an owner.
Her second cut went through the neck of the man mid-throw beside him, so quickly that his armful of ledgers was still climbing when he died.
"Feed it! FEED IT, you cowards!" The foreman got that much out before he saw what was walking up the aisle at him, and the rest of it turned into a noise with no shape to it.
"Quin!" Ayame shouted.
The ledgers never landed.
Gusts of wind materialized from nothing, under every thrown volume, beside every burning armful, plucking the count's history out of the air and out of the flames themselves.
Down in the deep racks, the two men with the crates found a shadow standing between them, and neither finished turning toward it.
Black Fang flicked her blade clean and stepped over what fell without looking down.
Iris took the last pair herself, the two who lunged for the pyre with the final crate between them.
She caught the first by the wrist and broke it, then took him off his feet with it and put the second face-down into the stones hard enough to crack them. She stood on him and looked around for more.
There were no more.
The rest were already on their knees with their arms up, and the hall went down to fire-noise and one man being sick against a rack.
Quinlan finally got around to the pyre on his way past it. The air over the center aisle folded in on itself, the flames went flat, and the hall dropped into a smoking quiet with nothing left to eat.
He squared his tower of rescued ledgers on a scorched reading table and gave the stack one satisfied pat.

"Walk the surrenders out to the yard, captain, and keep the wounded under guard until I say otherwise." Stormlord said it without stopping, already stepping through the wreckage. "The crown will want every one of their testimonies."
Corvane made a sound in his chains that had no words left in it.
Hands folded into his sleeves, the Mediator came up to the reading table and looked over the stack still warm from the fire.
"This is the part that interests me, Your Highness. A man with one night to work in burns the dangerous paper first, and these are the ones that remained."
He sounded amused, as if staring down an intriguing philosophical question. "Or perhaps they were in such a hurry that there was no order to the chaos at all?"
Felicity ignored his ramblings.
The stack ran to forty-odd volumes, scorched along the edges, spines marked by year, every one of them taken out of the air on its way to the fire.

Felicity worked them in silence, the newest book open under the sergeant's lantern, then one volume from each decade, then the oldest down at the bottom of the pile, checking a single thing in every one of them.
"What he took. What he kept. What he sent up." Her gauntleted finger rested beside the cipher at the head of a page written before her grandfather's grandfather was born.
"Thirty years is what we accused him of." Her voice was small in the hush. "This column's been climbing out of these lands for hundreds of years. It's older than even Mom."

"Well, yes, this syndicate we're dealing with is older than even the king. By quite a bit." The Mediator worked down the stack from the other side of the table, grey eyes going down the columns with unmistakable professional attention.

"Immaculate. Better kept, I confess, than several of my own branch offices. And in all those accounts, this house wrote down everything except who it was paying, year after year, in a hand this careful. Excellence is a dangerous habit."
He closed a cover softly. "That is what I would call testimony, Your Highness."
"And stupidity." Felicity closed the book on her thumb. "They were so brazen, keeping such records..."
The Mediator's beard did not move. Behind it, his professional composure fought for its life.
'The princess royal of Vraven,' he thought, with great serenity, 'has just spoken to me as if we were on the same side...'
"Caution costs money, Your Highness, and the crown never bothered to sniff properly before today..." he mused aloud.
"...Yeah..." Felicity sighed, dejected.
She pressed the book flat against her chest. "We audited an entire duchy and its administrating families on suspicion. After tonight it's evidence."
Black Fang had taken one of the scorched volumes off the far end of the table and was reading it with a perfect poker face.
Iris had stopped hearing any of them somewhere around the vellum.
She went through the stack from the bottom, pulling volumes and dropping them, not gently, until the year she wanted landed in both hands.
Ravenclaw.
The page blurred, steadied, and held.
The word stood at the head of a fresh section in that same tidy hand, and under it, entry by entry, her whole world had been bought: the lands, the mills, the river tolls, the granaries.
Every piece of it had gone into the Corvane holdings at salvage prices, sold against debts a ruined barony could never argue with. Each entry carried its initials, and each column had been squared.
'Where...'
There was no entry for the people.
She had spent her whole life hunting a face.
What waited at the end of the hunt was a set of initials and a price, entered by the man in chains out in the hall.
'They didn't bother writing down the names...? Of what they'd done to us...? They wrote down so much, and yet...'
Everything she had been carrying since she was a child had arrived, and there was nowhere left to put it down.
Her hands shook hard enough to buzz the page.
'Was that too inconsequential? Not worth the ink?'
Killing intent rolled off her in slow waves then, filling the burned hall wall to wall, and the two soldiers nearest the door discovered urgent duties in the bailey.
A short laugh got out of her, one wrong little sound with nothing funny in it. She read the section again. Then she read it again.
Ayame arrived at her elbow, read the heading, and for once in her life said nothing sharp at all, which from her was a shout. "Breathe, Iris."
"Don't tell me what to do..." the Child of Reckoning scoffed, voice trembling.
Quinlan came up behind her and looked at the page over her arm for a long moment. Whatever he thought of it stayed off his face.
His hand landed on her shoulder and patted it twice.
"Maybe they burned the files with victim names first," he said, quietly, just for her, with none of the dressing-up she would have hated.
Iris's eyes came off the page for the first time since she had found it. "Then I'll go get those too," she said, and it came out steady.
"There's no need, Iris."
Quinlan straightened. "Let me help you."
The warmth went out of his voice as if it had never existed, replaced by a tone of dread that made royal soldiers tremble from head to toe.
"I promised Alexios I would investigate this properly." He walked away from the table unhurried as he said it, past the kneeling surrenders, between the gutted racks.
"I did. The evidence is gathered, the forms are observed, the law is honored." One short gesture took in the table, the ledgers, the whole ruined night.
"The old bastard must be satisfied by now."
He stopped in front of Count Corvane.
"So now it's time to finish this investigation my way."
Corvane got as far as opening his mouth.
The boot took him in the teeth.
Dozens of teeth skittered away across the stones, and the count went out cold before his back met them, chains and all.
The two soldiers who had been holding him were left holding air. "Wah?!" One of them made a very small sound.
Back at the table, Iris scrubbed her eyes once with the heel of her hand.
'You just can't help but make a scene, can you?...'
A gorgeous, soft smile settled on her face.
"Quinlan..."
The Primordial Villain set his boot on the unconscious count's chest and said one more word.
"[Subjugation]."

chapters.title: Chapter 1876 Damning Confession
paragraphs: "[Subjugation]."
The word settled over the gutted record-house.
They had spent the last months hearing what the Primordial Villain did to the people who crossed him.
Every soldier along the walls looked at the unconscious count in his chains and arrived at the same understanding in the same breath: they had just watched a peer of Vraven stop belonging to himself.
Nobody moved.
Until Stormlord's warhammer rang free of its harness.
The commander of the Aegis Vanguard took one step with the hammer already in his fist, and there was nothing hot in his face at all.
He had watched a detained vassal of his king enslaved in front of a royal commission, and his whole body had turned into the next line of protocol.
But before he could take the next step, the temperature at his throat changed.
Black Fang had not moved from the far end of the reading table, the scorched volume still open against her arm.
Her blade stayed in its sheath and her mouth stayed shut. She was watching the space past him, at angles and distances already measured.
Stormlord stopped.

He was one of the strongest men in Vraven, and every instinct that had kept him alive for centuries was reporting the same thing: a serpent sat coiled at his throat, and it would arrive before he reached the Villain.
He did not step back.

His gauntlet tightened on the grip, and he stayed exactly where his last stride had put him, a king's commander refusing to yield ground to the most dangerous woman on the continent over a matter of law.
"Release the count," he said, to Quinlan, past her. "He is the crown's prisoner. What you have done to him is not in any statute I serve."
Quinlan looked back at him with mild interest and said nothing at all.
The hall held its breath around the three of them.
One drawn hammer, one unsheathed nothing, one villain, and a floor of soldiers who had stopped pretending they knew where to point their spears.
"Stormlord."
Felicity's voice was not loud.
The princess of Vraven stood beside the scorched reading table with her visor up and ash in her hair, and every eye in the record-house went to her.
"You did your duty. Now stand down."
"Your Highness." Stormlord did not move. "The count is under crown protection until the crown's judgment. What was done here..."
"Was watched by the crown." Her voice stayed simple and clear. "I saw everything. I'll tell Father everything, and if he's angry, he can be angry at me."
She tipped her head back, and looked up at the man who had guarded her since before she could walk.
"I'll take responsibility for what happened here."
The hall watched the commander of the Aegis Vanguard look down at his princess for a long moment.
Then the hammer settled back against his spine, and the serpent at his throat was simply elsewhere.
Stormlord stepped back to Felicity's shoulder and planted himself there, facing the villain he had just been ordered to permit.

And that was the picture the commission would carry back to the capital, every soldier in the hall a witness: the princess of Vraven, fourteen years old, ordering the king's own commander to stand his weapon down while the Primordial Villain enslaved a peer of the realm in front of her.
The princess had not blinked while it happened.
"Wake up." Quinlan's cold voice sobered the whole hall.
Corvane's eyes opened.

He was awake all at once, whole, aware. The command reached down into wherever the beating had sent him and hauled him out of it by the spine, and the count of the Corvane holdings lay flat on the scorched stones of his own record-house, awake because he had been told to be.

His mouth was a ruin. His rings were gone into some soldier's custody, his furs soaked with melt-water and ash, and when he tried to speak, what came out through the gaps where his teeth had been was wet, whistling, and shapeless.
"Whh... what..."
Then he felt his own body sitting up, though no one had touched him.
Quinlan had lifted two fingers in a lazy come-up flick, and the count had obeyed it before his mind finished screaming that it wouldn't.
Corvane looked down at his own obedient hands, and the fright that took him made the arrest look like composure.
"No. No, no, what did you... what is this... what did you do to me?!"
"You'll answer every question put to you in this hall, truthfully and completely," Quinlan said. "Start with the toll."
"I refuse! I..."
The refusal was still leaving his mouth when the answer started.

"The second toll..." His own voice climbed his throat like a bucket dragged up a well, and his eyes went wide and white around it. "...my grandfather set our share of it. The chain above us was already old by then. The crown's schedule is written in the state's official ledgers. Ours was never written in theirs."
He got a hand over his own mouth, trying to suppress the treacherous words.

It changed nothing. The words came through his fingers anyway, wet and whistling. The burned record-house stood in silence and listened to a man testify against himself in a voice he was losing to, inch by inch.

"Collection runs up through the tax farmers. The farmers pay the assessors. The assessors pay a man I was never..." The word fought him on the way up and came out sideways. "...never permitted to know. And the coin goes up. The coin always goes up. Since before the Accord."
"Who is it for?" Felicity asked quietly.
"I don't know."
"You levy an unlicensed toll on the king's roads," she said, "and you don't know who you're collecting for?"
"That is the design." Sweat stood on his face in beads. "Nobody knows the next name but his own handler. Initials in the ledgers. Ciphers on the orders."
His throat worked against the admission and lost it whole.
"A caught man can sell nothing but himself. I know my handler's mark. I know the chain is long, and that's it."
By the reading table, the Mediator's grey eyes had gone still over the ledgers.
"Every branch blind to the one above it," the old man observed, with great serenity. "We build ours the same way. There's a reason we still stand-"
"Stop bragging." Ayame shut him up quickly.
"The tolls buy what?" Stormlord's voice came iron-flat from Felicity's shoulder.
"Everything." Corvane laughed, one wet syllable with no humor in it. "You think the coin is the point? The coin is the harvest. The machine is the point."
"Explain," Quinlan said.
And the count's own voice explained it, one sentence at a time while its owner sweated, fought, and lost, and the commission's clerks wrote until their hands cramped.

"Debt." His tongue found the gaps in his teeth around the word. "Debt is the plow. A baron falls behind, and we are already there, smiling, with terms. A merchant house grows past its place, and its creditors sell us his paper, because we ask nicely. Twice."
"Nobody but a barbarian takes a man's lands at sword-point these days. We take them at the signing table, at salvage prices, with the law nodding along beside us."
"What if your target doesn't play along?" Iris asked.
It was the first question she had asked since Quinlan put his boot through the count's teeth.

She stood with her hand still resting on the stack of rescued volumes, red eyes level on the count. Her voice came out flat and conversational, and every hair on Felicity's neck stood up at the sound of it.

"The ones who won't sign get help," the count's voice said. "A granary burns. A bridge fails. A caravan meets men on a quiet road. A wife hears what happens to children whose fathers are stubborn. Blackmail where there are letters, extortion where there aren't." His hand pressed harder over his mouth, and the words came anyway. "...the Ravenclaw solution."
The name landed on the hall like a dropped torch.
Felicity's hand rose halfway to her mouth and stopped there.
Iris did not move at all.
"Explain," Quinlan repeated, lower this time.

"An example." Sweat ran into the count's collar. "The old writ says lands held by miscreants and debtors revert to worthier hands. It has said so since our lands existed. The 'how' is left to the man on the ground. That is the design. That is always the design."
"Were you ordered?"
"No. It's how we always operate. If the first two solutions don't work, then go for the third..."
He gulped, then...
"Ravenclaw was MINE." The count stopped fighting, then, and the first crack of mania came through the wet ruin of his voice.
"Do you know what that little barony cost me? Gilbert Ravenclaw, the honest baron, the beloved baron, sitting on his muddy border crossing like a toad on a coin purse."

"He would not sell. He would not sink. He kept current, he kept his nose clean, and then he started saying it out loud, at his own table and at everyone else's, to any neighbour who would sit still for it: that the levies I set on his roads never once reached my county's coffers."
The laugh came again, wetter.
"He was right! Of course he was right! And a baron who is right, and loud, and beloved, and is not on our side, is to be burned."
"He went and found his own criminals for his little roads. Men like that are never hard to find once a man is already drowning."

"We bought their paper off them inside the month, cheap, because they wanted coin and we wanted land, and the road he broke himself building ran to a city that was already mine. That was the machine, functioning as designed. And when it came due..." His shoulders heaved, breath whistling through the gaps in his teeth. "...collection."
"You sent the collectors under the Covenant of Eternity's name," Ayame whispered.
"Everyone sent collectors under the Covenant's name!" The count's manic edge climbed. "That is what the name was for! The skeletons never cared. Why would they?"

"They wanted corpses, tunnels, their dark little workings under this duchy's own dirt. They had no use at all for surface land, for tolls, for barley. They took the underworld and left the surface to us, and no fool ever went looking for a debt behind that name, because who hunted the Covenant?"
He wheezed. "We rented their shadow for the price of never lighting a candle in it."
The Mediator's beard shifted over the ghost of a smile. "Fascinating. A tenant below ground, a landlord above it, and neither party ever knocking. I confess we never managed anything half so tidy..."
The words reached Iris on a delay.
