The princess of Vraven stood beside the scorched reading table with her visor up and ash in her hair, and every eye in the record-house went to her.
"You did your duty.
Now stand down."
"Your Highness." Stormlord did not move.
"The count is under crown protection until the crown's judgment.
What was done here..."
"Was watched by the crown." Her voice stayed simple and clear.
"I saw everything.
I'll tell Father everything, and if he's angry, he can be angry at me."
She tipped her head back, and looked up at the man who had guarded her since before she could walk.
"I'll take responsibility for what happened here."
The hall watched the commander of the Aegis Vanguard look down at his princess for a long moment.
Then the hammer settled back against his spine, and the serpent at his throat was simply elsewhere.
Stormlord stepped back to Felicity's shoulder and planted himself there, facing the villain he had just been ordered to permit.

And that was the picture the commission would carry back to the capital, every soldier in the hall a witness: the princess of Vraven, fourteen years old, ordering the king's own commander to stand his weapon down while the Primordial Villain enslaved a peer of the realm in front of her.
The princess had not blinked while it happened.
"Wake up." Quinlan's cold voice sobered the whole hall.
Corvane's eyes opened.
He was awake all at once, whole, aware.

The command reached down into wherever the beating had sent him and hauled him out of it by the spine, and the count of the Corvane holdings lay flat on the scorched stones of his own record-house, awake because he had been told to be.
His mouth was a ruin.

His rings were gone into some soldier's custody, his furs soaked with melt-water and ash, and when he tried to speak, what came out through the gaps where his teeth had been was wet, whistling, and shapeless.
"Whh... what..."
Then he felt his own body sitting up, though no one had touched him.
Quinlan had lifted two fingers in a lazy come-up flick, and the count had obeyed it before his mind finished screaming that it wouldn't.
Corvane looked down at his own obedient hands, and the fright that took him made the arrest look like composure.
"No.
No, no, what did you... what is this... what did you do to me?!"
"You'll answer every question put to you in this hall, truthfully and completely," Quinlan said.
"Start with the toll."
"I refuse!
The refusal was still leaving his mouth when the answer started.
"The second toll..." His own voice climbed his throat like a bucket dragged up a well, and his eyes went wide and white around it.
"...my grandfather set our share of it.
The chain above us was already old by then.
The crown's schedule is written in the state's official ledgers.
Ours was never written in theirs."
He got a hand over his own mouth, trying to suppress the treacherous words.
It changed nothing.
The words came through his fingers anyway, wet and whistling.
The burned record-house stood in silence and listened to a man testify against himself in a voice he was losing to, inch by inch.
"Collection runs up through the tax farmers.
The farmers pay the assessors.
The assessors pay a man I was never..." The word fought him on the way up and came out sideways.
"...never permitted to know.
And the coin goes up.
The coin always goes up.
Since before the Accord."
"Who is it for?" Felicity asked quietly.
"I don't know."
"You levy an unlicensed toll on the king's roads," she said, "and you don't know who you're collecting for?"
"That is the design." Sweat stood on his face in beads.
"Nobody knows the next name but his own handler.
Initials in the ledgers.
Ciphers on the orders."
His throat worked against the admission and lost it whole.
"A caught man can sell nothing but himself.
I know my handler's mark.
I know the chain is long, and that's it."
By the reading table, the Mediator's grey eyes had gone still over the ledgers.
"Every branch blind to the one above it," the old man observed, with great serenity.
"We build ours the same way.
There's a reason we still stand-"
"Stop bragging." Ayame shut him up quickly.
"The tolls buy what?" Stormlord's voice came iron-flat from Felicity's shoulder.
"Everything." Corvane laughed, one wet syllable with no humor in it.
"You think the coin is the point?
The coin is the harvest.
The machine is the point."
"Explain," Quinlan said.
And the count's own voice explained it, one sentence at a time while its owner sweated, fought, and lost, and the commission's clerks wrote until their hands cramped.
"Debt." His tongue found the gaps in his teeth around the word.
"Debt is the plow.
A baron falls behind, and we are already there, smiling, with terms.
A merchant house grows past its place, and its creditors sell us his paper, because we ask nicely.
Twice."
"Nobody but a barbarian takes a man's lands at sword-point these days.
We take them at the signing table, at salvage prices, with the law nodding along beside us."
"What if your target doesn't play along?" Iris asked.
It was the first question she had asked since Quinlan put his boot through the count's teeth.
She stood with her hand still resting on the stack of rescued volumes, red eyes level on the count.
Her voice came out flat and conversational, and every hair on Felicity's neck stood up at the sound of it.
"The ones who won't sign get help," the count's voice said.
"A granary burns.
A bridge fails.
A caravan meets men on a quiet road.
A wife hears what happens to children whose fathers are stubborn.
Blackmail where there are letters, extortion where there aren't." His hand pressed harder over his mouth, and the words came anyway.
"...the Ravenclaw solution."
The name landed on the hall like a dropped torch.
Felicity's hand rose halfway to her mouth and stopped there.
Iris did not move at all.
"Explain," Quinlan repeated, lower this time.
"An example." Sweat ran into the count's collar.
"The old writ says lands held by miscreants and debtors revert to worthier hands.
It has said so since our lands existed.
The 'how' is left to the man on the ground.
That is the design.
That is always the design."
"Were you ordered?"
"No.
It's how we always operate.
If the first two solutions don't work, then go for the third..."
He gulped, then...
"Ravenclaw was MINE." The count stopped fighting, then, and the first crack of mania came through the wet ruin of his voice.
"Do you know what that little barony cost me?
Gilbert Ravenclaw, the honest baron, the beloved baron, sitting on his muddy border crossing like a toad on a coin purse."
"He would not sell.
He would not sink.

He kept current, he kept his nose clean, and then he started saying it out loud, at his own table and at everyone else's, to any neighbour who would sit still for it: that the levies I set on his roads never once reached my county's coffers."
The laugh came again, wetter.
"He was right!
Of course he was right!
And a baron who is right, and loud, and beloved, and is not on our side, is to be burned."
"He went and found his own criminals for his little roads.
Men like that are never hard to find once a man is already drowning."
"We bought their paper off them inside the month, cheap, because they wanted coin and we wanted land, and the road he broke himself building ran to a city that was already mine.
That was the machine, functioning as designed.
And when it came due..." His shoulders heaved, breath whistling through the gaps in his teeth.
"...collection."
"You sent the collectors under the Covenant of Eternity's name," Ayame whispered.
"Everyone sent collectors under the Covenant's name!" The count's manic edge climbed.
"That is what the name was for!
The skeletons never cared.
Why would they?"
"They wanted corpses, tunnels, their dark little workings under this duchy's own dirt.
They had no use at all for surface land, for tolls, for barley.
They took the underworld and left the surface to us, and no fool ever went looking for a debt behind that name, because who hunted the Covenant?"
He wheezed.
"We rented their shadow for the price of never lighting a candle in it."
The Mediator's beard shifted over the ghost of a smile.
"Fascinating.
A tenant below ground, a landlord above it, and neither party ever knocking.
I confess we never managed anything half so tidy..."
The words reached Iris on a delay.

chapters.title: Chapter 1877 The Real Motives
paragraphs: Every rung of the ladder she had climbed since she was a girl had sworn the next one up was the Covenant, and the last Covenant lord alive had told her, laughing, that no such agent ever existed.
Here, at last, was the reason the trail had always dead-ended in skeletons.
And it was such a simple, dumb explanation.
At the table, slowly, her hand came off the ledgers.
"The collection of Ravenclaw's debt," she said. "Explain how you did it."
"It's simple. He had debt, we bought his debt, then made certain the money he borrowed could never turn a single coin. So the debt was called, and he paid it."
The wet laugh got out of him again.

"He paid it. Begged it off every neighbour who would still open a door to him, and it broke his back doing it. After that we did nothing at all. He spent eleven years finishing what we started for him."
His collar was black with sweat now.

"When the line died there was nobody left standing on the ground. So the ground went up to the duchy, the way paper always does, and it came back down to me in writing, a fee for tidy administration. Nobody in this kingdom ever asked why."
"The family..." For the first time, the compulsion had to drag against real weight, and the count's whole face shone with the effort of holding it, and lost. "...the family was priced."
The temperature dropped to freezing. "Priced," Iris said.

"Assets," his voice said. "The mother had a face, and her husband found the buyers himself. Every one of them out of my city, spending my coin. The father had nothing worth taking, so we gave him grief, a bottle, and a decade to dig his own grave. We only stopped filling it in. And the children..."
At Felicity's shoulder, Stormlord's gauntlet closed on the haft until the leather spoke, the same sound it had made in the courtyard, and this time it had nothing to do with the Villain.
The count stopped.
He was looking at Iris.

He looked at her like a sum that would not come out wrong no matter how many times he ran it: the black hair, the slight build a swordbelt had done nothing to soften, the two red eyes over the stack of his own rescued ledgers.
And all of it standing in the burned hall of his own keep, at the head of the king's own commission.
"...No," he said, in his own voice, quite softly.
"The crown sends a red-eyed girl with no name to open my house to the sky," he whistled, "and she stands at the head of it, and she asks after Ravenclaw in specific..."
His breath came faster, and faster, whistling through the ruin of his mouth like wind through a fence.
"There was a daughter. The one who was never delivered." His white eyes climbed to her face. "You. You're the daughter."
And then, sliding back down onto the cracked stones of his own record-house, with the crown's chains on his wrists and a slave-brand on his soul, the count began to laugh.
It was a horrible sound.

It came up through the wreckage of his mouth wet and broken-edged, hitching on the gaps where his teeth had been. It went on, and on, climbing over the fire-noise, a man laughing from a place that had nothing to do with anything funny.
Corvane was lying in chains at a villain's feet, laughing at the ceiling, and the tears sliding into the ash on his face had nothing of grief in them.

"You're alive!" he wheezed. "Oh, that is... after everything, all this, the audit, the princess, the big bad monster standing on my chest, and it comes down to... ahahaha... it comes down to the little Ravenclaw girl, the one loose thread, walking into my own house with the crown at her back..."
"You know me," Iris said.
Her voice stayed flat and conversational while the ground fell out of the world, and the wrongness of that reached every soldier along the walls.
A man like this, who ruined so many lives, who massacred families while pretending to be a normal vassal, remembered a little girl from more than two decades ago.
To say it was odd was putting it lightly.
"Know you." The count turned his head against the stones and looked up at her, and what was in his face now had tipped past fear into somewhere with no floor.

He knew what he was. He knew what was under him, wearing his soul like a signet. He knew there was no version of this night that ended with him keeping anything, and the knowing had burned through the last of his caution. "Girl, I ordered you."
The room went very still.

"The debt was collection. The lands were the writ. But you..." The laugh bubbled up again through the words. "You were never written anywhere. That is the beauty of the thing. I don't sign for what I want."
"The order that went down was a child, any child, deniable as weather."

"But the men who do that work knew what pleased the top of their ladder, and a baron's daughter is a soft thing that grows into a softer one, so they reached for the girl on their own, exactly as I liked, to be raised to my standards. Another ten years, and you would have been..."
What was left of his lips pulled back, and his tongue dragged across the broken ruins of his teeth.
"...perfect."
The word crawled across the hall and fouled the air wherever it touched.
Stormlord's gaze cut to the fourteen-year-old at his side, once, and back to the count, and the iron in his face had gone brittle at the edges.
"Instead," the count said, "they brought me a damned boy."
Iris did not make a sound.

"A boy!" The mania spiked, indignant, a merchant's grievance still alive in it, as though under the fear he were still filing this complaint with the collectors. "A useless, worthless BOY, planting himself in the mud of that estate with his little chin up, telling the men his sister deserved better!"
He punched the floor in frustration.
"I had wanted a bride! And the fools on the ground took pity on a brave little speech, took the volunteer, and left the girl I wanted sitting in the dirt between two dead guards."
His breath sawed. "I was sad. I was truly, honestly sad, and I remember the evening exactly. And then I thought, well."
The tongue found the broken teeth again.
"Waste not."
Ayame's katana came out of its sheath one full hand-span, and the sound it made was the only sound in the world.
"They had him one day," Count Corvane told the ceiling of his record-house, dreamily, while his terror poured off him in sweat and his voice reeled on past every attempt his hands made to stop it.
"Not my men. Write that down properly, girl, your clerks are working so hard tonight. I have never in my life owned a man who carries a knife."
He had to stop and pull air through his own wreckage before he could go on.

"I own the man who owns the man who hires them. The word goes down through cousins and ciphers until nobody at the bottom of it could name me if you flayed him where he stood. That is how a thing like me stays a thing like me."
He looked delighted with himself.
"But men at the bottom guess upward. They guess well. So they washed the boy and brought him to my house that evening, like a gift, and I had my hours with him."
Somewhere along the wall, one of the commission's clerks stopped writing.

"Then I sent him back down where he came from, because I do not keep what I have already used. The fools holding him got into the wine that night and were thorough with him. By morning there was a corpse where my collateral should have been."
The wet syllable of a laugh got out again.

"Four days after that, the father finally scraped my coin together, so we carried what was left of the boy to his own door and put it in his hands. He paid me anyway. Every copper, borrowed off every neighbour who still pitied him. A debt is a debt."
He rolled his head, found her, and smiled at her with everything left of his mouth.
"And do you know what I remember, girl?"
The fire ticked somewhere down the hall, eating what was left of a shelf.

"Nothing came of it. The fool went wailing to his duke, and the duke swore he would look into the matter, and looked into nothing at all, because that is what a duke does with a dead pauper's boy. No writ, no reckoning, not one hand from that whole wide world ever reached down for me."
The smile stretched, ghastly. "That is what your family was worth. One night, a box carried to the door, and a father no one troubled to hear."
And then he tipped the rest of the way over the edge. The last of the fear burned off into pure shrieking spite, because he had nothing left to lose and one knife left to throw, and he threw it.

"If you had just COME WITH US," he screamed at her, chains ringing against the stones, "both of you would be ALIVE! Fed! Kept! He'd be a grown man now with a life! You killed him, girl, YOU, his sister deserved better, and better was MY BED, and he died in your place FOR NOTHING, for NOTHING AT ALL!"
The words hit Iris Ravenclaw with full force.

chapters.title: Chapter 1878 Shaken Conviction
paragraphs: Count Corvane's scream still hung in the smoke of his own burned record-house, the words he had saved for the very end and thrown with everything left in him: that Damian Ravenclaw had died in his sister's place, and that he had died for nothing at all.
The whole hall watched them hit.

Iris stood at the head of the reading table, her hand frozen above the ledgers, and for once the guard failed her. She couldn't keep it off her face, because there are wounds that never close, only wait.

She had carried this one since she was two years old, and every horror that came after, the cage, the basement, the dying scum, had been stacked on top of it until the carrying became the whole architecture of her.
And the man in chains had just reached in with one filthy hand and torn every year of it open at once.
Her face emptied.
The color drained out of it, and her hands, her terrible hands, the ones that had cracked flagstones, began very finely to shake.
'He was a baby.'

The thought didn't arrive as words. It arrived as the thing she had been too young to remember and had built anyway, night after night, year after year: a small chin lifted in front of large men, a voice that had barely finished learning its sentences spending them on her.
'He was a baby, and I hunted a shadow half my life, and the whole time it was this. A monster's appetite. One night. A box carried to our own door.'
Her breath had stopped being automatic. She was doing it manually now, one in, one out.
'They didn't even write his name down. He wasn't worth ink. He was worth one night, and I...'
The shake climbed from her hands into her arms.
Felicity was tearing up.
She had both hands clamped over her mouth, tears cutting clean lines down the ash on her face.
She had begged her father for this posting to help her friend find her answers, and no one had warned her the answers would be like this.
Iris's whole guarded, cursing, unreachable self was a wall built around a small grave, and Felicity had to stand in a burned hall in armor and watch it dug up to a laugh.
Ayame stood with her eyes on the count and her thumb on her blade's guard. The tease and the tilt had burned out of her hours ago. What remained was a samurai livid beyond words.
Black Fang watched Iris.
Only Iris. The count had stopped existing for her entirely, dropped below the threshold of things she deigned to see, and her whole attention rested on the shaking of those two clenched fists.
Quinlan stood.
He had not said one word through any of it.
He had listened to all of it, standing quite still in the middle of the hall he had taken, and the soldiers nearest him had drifted back off him one instinctive step at a time.
He crossed the hall to Iris, put his arms around her, and pulled her in tight.
She didn't fight it.
For the first time, instead of shoving him off or turning it into an insult, she let herself be held, her forehead against his collarbone, her fists caught between them, shaking.
The hall looked away. Even the ones who didn't know why.
<Quinlan.>
Her voice arrived over the link as it never sounded out loud, young and stripped, holding on to its own steadiness with every fiber of her being.
<Tell me something... I don't care what. Everything in my head is his voice and I need... I need one thing in there that isn't.>
Quinlan closed his eyes.
<I'm afraid now's not the time to escape reality.>
Iris went rigid against his chest.
<I lived every hour you lived until the tragedy, so the thing I'm about to say is what my observing eyes have told me.>

His arms tightened around her. <He wasn't taken from you, and he wasn't tricked into it. He looked at the worst thing that had ever walked into your home and chose it, so it would leave without you. Three years old, and braver than every soldier in this hall. That was Damian Ravenclaw.>
A sound came out of Iris then, once, very small, muffled against his chest.

<He didn't die for nothing.> Quinlan's voice over the link stayed level, and underneath the level, far down, his fury lay absolutely still. <He bought you every year you've had since, and every year you'll have from here on out.>
Her shaking wouldn't stop, so Quinlan hugged her fragile frame even tighter. <There's one thing I can say with absolute certainty. It's the single fact I believe with my entire existence.>
Hearing Quinlan's deep, certain voice, Iris couldn't help but look up into his face. Her big, teary red eyes were awaiting his words with desperate need.
He spoke them hard, with no smile anywhere in him, because he believed his next words truly and fiercely.

<He'd do it all over again without blinking and without having regrets. That is who your wonderful brother is, the little hero who earned more of my respect than any living creature ever had and ever will.>
The shaking stopped all at once, like a bell gripped mid-ring.
For a long moment she stayed exactly where she was, her eyes on his face, and when her voice crossed the link again it had found a floor to stand on.
<You're right.>
Then she came off the link and gave her words to the hall.
"He didn't die for nothing. But he didn't die for me either."
It left her quietly and arrived everywhere, iron under every word, a voice that reached the farthest wall of the record-house as though she stood beside every man in it.
Heads came up all along the walls. The last working clerk stopped writing.

"He died because this world is rotten. It lets beings like that foul thing live in it, grow old in it, prosper in it. It let a coin buy my brother, and it went back to its supper. It has done the same in ten thousand halls like this one, and it has never once been made to pay."
Quinlan had lived every hour of that basement from the inside of her skin.
Of every soul alive, only he carried what she carried, the same years in the dark, the same brother, and all night his half of the fury had lain still under its inch of ice.
"Damn right..." The words rose out of him instinctively, unnaturally deep. His half of their shared fury rose to meet her words as she spoke them.

Fire lit between Iris's shoulder blades. It ran the length of the Bloodfather sigil sealed down her spine, every line of the mark waking at once, and against her fists, through the cloth, the hollow above Quinlan's heart kindled in answer. She felt all of it happening to her, and she did not stop.
Neither of them had chosen it. The bond had measured the two furies, found them identical, the same grief in two bodies, and drawn them into one.
"I now know what I want from this world. What I'll do after my vengeance is complete."

sentences.text: Count Corvane's scream still hung in the smoke of his own burned record-house, the words he had saved for the very end and thrown with everything left in him: that Damian Ravenclaw had died in his sister's place, and that he had died for nothing at all.
The whole hall watched them hit.
Iris stood at the head of the reading table, her hand frozen above the ledgers, and for once the guard failed her.
She couldn't keep it off her face, because there are wounds that never close, only wait.

She had carried this one since she was two years old, and every horror that came after, the cage, the basement, the dying scum, had been stacked on top of it until the carrying became the whole architecture of her.
And the man in chains had just reached in with one filthy hand and torn every year of it open at once.
Her face emptied.
The color drained out of it, and her hands, her terrible hands, the ones that had cracked flagstones, began very finely to shake.
'He was a baby.'
The thought didn't arrive as words.

It arrived as the thing she had been too young to remember and had built anyway, night after night, year after year: a small chin lifted in front of large men, a voice that had barely finished learning its sentences spending them on her.
'He was a baby, and I hunted a shadow half my life, and the whole time it was this.
A monster's appetite.
One night.
A box carried to our own door.'
Her breath had stopped being automatic.
She was doing it manually now, one in, one out.
'They didn't even write his name down.
He wasn't worth ink.
He was worth one night, and I...'
The shake climbed from her hands into her arms.
Felicity was tearing up.
She had both hands clamped over her mouth, tears cutting clean lines down the ash on her face.
She had begged her father for this posting to help her friend find her answers, and no one had warned her the answers would be like this.
Iris's whole guarded, cursing, unreachable self was a wall built around a small grave, and Felicity had to stand in a burned hall in armor and watch it dug up to a laugh.
Ayame stood with her eyes on the count and her thumb on her blade's guard.
The tease and the tilt had burned out of her hours ago.
What remained was a samurai livid beyond words.
Black Fang watched Iris.
Only Iris.
The count had stopped existing for her entirely, dropped below the threshold of things she deigned to see, and her whole attention rested on the shaking of those two clenched fists.
Quinlan stood.
He had not said one word through any of it.
He had listened to all of it, standing quite still in the middle of the hall he had taken, and the soldiers nearest him had drifted back off him one instinctive step at a time.
He crossed the hall to Iris, put his arms around her, and pulled her in tight.
She didn't fight it.
For the first time, instead of shoving him off or turning it into an insult, she let herself be held, her forehead against his collarbone, her fists caught between them, shaking.
The hall looked away.
Even the ones who didn't know why.
<Quinlan.>
Her voice arrived over the link as it never sounded out loud, young and stripped, holding on to its own steadiness with every fiber of her being.
<Tell me something...
I don't care what.
Everything in my head is his voice and I need...
I need one thing in there that isn't.>
Quinlan closed his eyes.
<I'm afraid now's not the time to escape reality.>
Iris went rigid against his chest.
<I lived every hour you lived until the tragedy, so the thing I'm about to say is what my observing eyes have told me.>
His arms tightened around her.
<He wasn't taken from you, and he wasn't tricked into it.
He looked at the worst thing that had ever walked into your home and chose it, so it would leave without you.
Three years old, and braver than every soldier in this hall.
That was Damian Ravenclaw.>
A sound came out of Iris then, once, very small, muffled against his chest.
<He didn't die for nothing.> Quinlan's voice over the link stayed level, and underneath the level, far down, his fury lay absolutely still.
<He bought you every year you've had since, and every year you'll have from here on out.>
Her shaking wouldn't stop, so Quinlan hugged her fragile frame even tighter.
<There's one thing I can say with absolute certainty.
It's the single fact I believe with my entire existence.>
Hearing Quinlan's deep, certain voice, Iris couldn't help but look up into his face.
Her big, teary red eyes were awaiting his words with desperate need.
He spoke them hard, with no smile anywhere in him, because he believed his next words truly and fiercely.
<He'd do it all over again without blinking and without having regrets.
That is who your wonderful brother is, the little hero who earned more of my respect than any living creature ever had and ever will.>
The shaking stopped all at once, like a bell gripped mid-ring.
For a long moment she stayed exactly where she was, her eyes on his face, and when her voice crossed the link again it had found a floor to stand on.
<You're right.>
Then she came off the link and gave her words to the hall.
"He didn't die for nothing.
But he didn't die for me either."

chapters.title: Chapter 1879 Child No Longer
paragraphs: "I now know what I want from this world. What I'll do after my vengeance is complete."
Her eyes stayed on Quinlan's face while she condemned everything beyond him.
"Every man who puts a price on a child."
The light climbed her back as she spoke, and a second voice had come up under hers, far down, level, bottomless. Nobody along those walls dared look at the man holding her.

"Every hand that carries the box. Every lord who signs the deed. Every clerk who leaves a dead boy's name out of the book. I am coming for every single one of them. Anywhere they run, however long it takes, I'll find them. One by one, I will cleanse this rotten world of its filth."
The smoke in the rafters had begun to turn, slowly, all of it, one great wheel above their heads.
"I'll not stop until no child has to wait for help that never comes. That is what I want to do."

Quinlan looked at her for a long second before his eyes began flashing, brighter than the sun itself. "I hear your creed, Iris Ravenclaw. Let's scrub this world clean together." The ritualistic words were spoken.
Somewhere above the world, the Soul Records began to write.
And somewhere far beneath it, in the deepest dark of the villain's soul realm, where a careful little warden kept it sleeping, the Seed of Corruption opened.
It did not erupt. It tipped a single drop of itself into the ink, authority no mortal woman was ever meant to hold, and then it settled back down under its warden's care, satisfied.
[The one designated 'Child of Reckoning' is a child no longer.]
[Witnessed and countersigned: Bloodfather.]
[Class Evolved: Demon of Vengeance.]
[Shield of the Innocent. Scourge of the Vile.]
What the hall saw was a man standing in the middle of a burned record-house, holding a woman whose back had become a line of rising light between his hands.
What the hall felt arrive was a demon.

It rolled out from the two of them in one slow wave, heat off an opened furnace door. Where the ember-light threw them against the far wall there was one shadow, tall as the iron doors, and it belonged to neither body casting it.
Soldiers who had held their ground through the count's whole confession found the wall at their backs without deciding to move. Felicity grabbed Stormlord's vambrace and held on.
Ayame's hand pressed flat and low over her stomach, and Black Fang's did the same where she stood, two marks pulsing in time with a sister's.
The red of Iris's eyes lit from far inside, and the tears still standing on her cheeks burned off her skin as fine mist, mid-fall.
Nobody would ever watch Iris Ravenclaw cry again.

Quinlan felt the pride come up through him, pride and something even fiercer under it, because he had just watched the girl from that basement become the thing that would make the world pay for it. His arms stayed exactly where they were, the stillest thing in the hall.
Then it banked. The glow along her back dimmed and went out under the cloth, the one shadow on the far wall folded back into two, and the hall remembered how to breathe.
Her eyes left Quinlan's face and found the count.
She stepped back out of his arms.
The fragile thing had gone into the forging, all of it, and the heat that rose off her in its place reached the walls.
She was the Demon of Vengeance.
Every torn-open year of what had just been done to her had to go somewhere, and she had spent her whole life learning where.
The killing intent poured out of her, steady and total, filling the hall as it had over the ledger page an hour before, except this time it had no bottom.
"You'll pay."
She said it flat enough to walk on, and loud enough for every soul in the hall to carry it home.
"You'll know no mercy. You'll know no sleep. And, for as long as I live, you'll know no death."
Her red eyes never left the count. "You're mine. For the rest of your infinite misery."
[New Ability Acquired!]
Her class had heard every word, and it had already begun keeping them.
Ayame's thumb came off her blade's guard, relinquishing the claim without a word.
Quinlan said nothing at all.
Count Corvane found his voice first.
"No." It came out of his ruined mouth as a croak and climbed with every word. "No. There is due process! I am a peer of the realm! I have rights! I answer to the capital, to the crown, to a court..."
His chains thrashed against the stones as he twisted toward Stormlord. "STORMLORD! You serve the law! Tell them what the law says!"
Iris started walking.
She crossed the burned floor one slow step after another, unhurried and gentle, and the fire leaned toward her as she passed.
Quinlan turned to Stormlord.
"What does your king's law do with him?"
Stormlord did not look at the count. He answered the villain, level and complete, without one wasted word.
"Treason against the crown's roads. Records burned under royal seal. And what he confessed tonight, before a royal commission."
He let one heartbeat pass. "He'd be taken to the capital, tried before the king, stripped of his title, and hanged."
"Hanged," Quinlan repeated.
The word came out of him quietly, and the record-house changed.
The torches simply burned smaller.
The winter reached in through the broken doors and settled along every spine at once. The ash stopped drifting and hung in the air, as though the hall itself had decided not to move.
Then, together, the Primordial Villain and the Demon of Vengeance decreed:
"That cannot stand."
Quinlan smiled. "Guess I'll fail the old man's task after all."
"No."
Stormlord's voice.
The commander of the Aegis Vanguard stepped forward from Felicity's shoulder, the only man in the hall whose spine had not bent a single degree.
He was looking at Quinlan with flat, settled calm. He had made his peace with dying where the law told him to stand long ago.
"You'll fail nothing," he said.
He turned to Felicity, named her formally, and the iron in his voice laid itself down in front of her like a drawbridge.

"Your Highness. The law asks a court for one thing, to establish what was done, beyond doubt, before the crown's witnesses. It was established here tonight, before a royal commission and a princess of Vraven carrying the king's seal.
"A court in the capital would spend a month reading back what this hall already knows."
He drew one breath. "Judgment belongs to the crown, and the crown is standing on these stones. You may render it."
Felicity stared up at him.
"Render judgment... Me?" she said.
"You, Your Highness."
She looked at Iris, at her friend's receding back, for a long moment, tears still cutting through the ash.
One look was enough.
Felicity Valorian turned to face the count, drew herself up, and passed sentence in the smoke of his own burned records, in the plain words of a fourteen-year-old.

"Count Corvane. You're guilty of terrible crimes against not just Vraven but humanity itself." Her voice shook and did not stop. "The crown takes your lands, your title, your name. And the crown takes your life."
She swallowed.
"The execution belongs to Iris Ravenclaw."

chapters.title: Chapter 1880 Welcome to Hell
paragraphs: The name rang off the iron doors, spoken in a crown sentence and under seal: a house restored in the same breath that fed its destroyer to it.
"She can do it however she wants," the princess finished.
For the space of three heartbeats, the hall was perfectly quiet.
Then the count began to scream.

"HANG me!" He fought his knees under him at last, his ruined voice climbing through what was left of its range. "Do you hear me?! Take me to your father and HANG ME! I am a peer of the realm and I DEMAND MY ROPE!"
Nobody answered him.
"STORMLORD!" he shrieked. "You served the LAW, the law says the ROPE, you KNOW the law, MAKE THEM..."
Stormlord looked at him, said nothing at all, and stepped back to his princess's shoulder.
"HANG ME!" the count screamed at Felicity, at the Mediator, at the soldiers along the walls, at anyone, his voice shredding on the gaps in his teeth. "HANG ME! HANG ME! PLEASE!"
So a peer of Vraven begged for his own hanging as a mercy, and the whole commission heard him do it.
Nobody came to him.
That was the first thing Corvane understood, down on the stones with his screams dying in the smoke: no one in that hall was ever going to come to him again.
The soldiers had turned their shoulders, and the princess had turned her back.
Then the hall began to empty, though not truly, and he knew it, distantly, with the last reasoning part of him.
The soldiers still stood along the walls. The princess still stood by her commander.

But the light pulled in on itself, the sounds of the living furled up like paper in a fire, and the great burned cavern of his record-house drew down long, dark, and narrow. All of creation held three people, and two of them were looking at him.
The tall man stood motionless in the ember-light. The small woman was coming for Corvane, step by step, and there was nothing human left in either one.
Corvane's breath stopped working.

He tried to push himself backward across the flagstones, away, anywhere, and his body would not answer him. The arms that had signed a thousand deaths lay where they were and refused him, and that refusal frightened him worse than any grip could have.
The villain's head tilted.
That was all it did.
It tilted, unhurried and considering, and it reached into Corvane's chest and closed a hand around his heart.
He had seen the villain angry and had had the villain's boot on his teeth. That had been weather.
This was the sky coming down, patient and bottomless, resting its eyes on him like something that had eaten kingdoms, found them small, and meant to keep him now for a very long time.
His bladder let go.
He felt the warmth spread under him across his own cracked flagstones, distant and shameful, and no shame came to meet it, because shame needs a future to live in and he no longer had one.
The villain was terror enough to empty a man where he sat.
Then Iris Ravenclaw was close, and the count learned he had not yet met the worst thing in his own hall.
Where the villain's stillness had pulled the world small, her approach shoved it back into his face.

The banked ash lifted off the stones in the wake of her boots and would not settle. His own chains, lying slack, began to ring against the flagstones with no hand near them, and his back teeth ached in his ruined mouth as though the air itself had turned to iron.
Her eyes were swirling.
Red turned within red, slow as syrup, deep as wells, two lit windows onto a furnace that had been banked her whole life and just, finally, been fed.

The pressure came off her and filled the hall to the rafters, thicker than the smoke, older than the tolls. It was a bloodlust with no bottom and no far shore, and it had his name written on every drop of it, his whole name, the one his grandfather had built this house to carry.
His bowels loosened where he sat.

He felt that too, the heat and the reek of it spreading across the stones his grandfather had laid, and he could no more stop it than he could stop his chains from singing. The delicate woman crossing the floor did not slow, did not hurry, did not so much as blink.
One step.
Then the next.

And Count Corvane, who had priced a barony to the coin, left its people out of the book entirely, and slept soundly ever since, understood in the swirling red of a dead girl's living eyes exactly what the rest of his existence was going to be, and that it had not yet even begun.
It began.

"PLEASE." The count broke apart entirely, forehead grinding the stones, bound hands scrabbling at the flagstones in front of her boots. "Please. Not her. The rope. I'll give you everything, I'll testify to anything, before any court, PLEASE..."
His voice shredded down to a wet whisper. "Mercy. Mercy..."
Iris crouched.
She took a fistful of his collar, lifted his ruined face out of his own filth, and gave him the last words he would ever hear on the living side of the world.
"Nobody came for him, either."
Then she opened her free hand above the stones, and the floor of the record-house tore.
"I already told you. You'll know no mercy."
"NO!"
A seam split the flagstones beside the count, wide as a grave and getting wider. Below it there was no cellar and no earth.
Iris then cast her new spell, the first one as the Demon of Vengeance, her powers derived from the perfect culmination of her and the villain's fury, and she sentenced her first target to...
"[Undying Damnation]."
A new dimension materialized before their very eyes.
Black metal ground ran away in every direction under a sky the color of banked coals, and the air of that place rolled hot, in and out. The whole dimension was breathing.
It was empty. It had been born tonight, it belonged to the woman crouched at its rim, and it was waiting for its first tenant.
She gripped Corvane by the throat and threw him into its entrance. The hall heard him scream the whole way down.

He hit the black metal ground of another world. Before the pain of the landing could even find him, words wrote themselves across his sight, patient and courteous, and they did not care whether his eyes were open.
[Welcome to the hell of the Demon of Vengeance.]
[Resident: 1.]
The seam stayed open. She stood at its rim and made the whole hall look.
Down in the ember domain, the ground began to move. It bulged under the screaming count and pushed something up out of itself, grinding, enormous.

What came up was a pillar the height of a watchtower, wrong in every way a built thing can be wrong: rugged black metal, crooked and scabbed, flaking rust in sheets, run down its whole length with fat living veins that pulsed and wept.
Every drop they shed hit the ground hissing.
It narrowed as it rose to a point, it glowed from the inside like a poker left deep in a forge, and the air above it warped with heat.
The count saw it and began to howl fresh.
The demon spoke down into her dimension with the doubled voice, hers riding on top, the villain's authority running underneath, and it spoke straight past the count's mind to his body.
"Climb."

It tilted, unhurried and considering, and it reached into Corvane's chest and closed a hand around his heart.
He had seen the villain angry and had had the villain's boot on his teeth.
That had been weather.
This was the sky coming down, patient and bottomless, resting its eyes on him like something that had eaten kingdoms, found them small, and meant to keep him now for a very long time.
His bladder let go.
He felt the warmth spread under him across his own cracked flagstones, distant and shameful, and no shame came to meet it, because shame needs a future to live in and he no longer had one.
The villain was terror enough to empty a man where he sat.
Then Iris Ravenclaw was close, and the count learned he had not yet met the worst thing in his own hall.
Where the villain's stillness had pulled the world small, her approach shoved it back into his face.
The banked ash lifted off the stones in the wake of her boots and would not settle.
His own chains, lying slack, began to ring against the flagstones with no hand near them, and his back teeth ached in his ruined mouth as though the air itself had turned to iron.
Her eyes were swirling.
Red turned within red, slow as syrup, deep as wells, two lit windows onto a furnace that had been banked her whole life and just, finally, been fed.
The pressure came off her and filled the hall to the rafters, thicker than the smoke, older than the tolls.
It was a bloodlust with no bottom and no far shore, and it had his name written on every drop of it, his whole name, the one his grandfather had built this house to carry.
His bowels loosened where he sat.
He felt that too, the heat and the reek of it spreading across the stones his grandfather had laid, and he could no more stop it than he could stop his chains from singing.
The delicate woman crossing the floor did not slow, did not hurry, did not so much as blink.
One step.
Then the next.

And Count Corvane, who had priced a barony to the coin, left its people out of the book entirely, and slept soundly ever since, understood in the swirling red of a dead girl's living eyes exactly what the rest of his existence was going to be, and that it had not yet even begun.
It began.
"PLEASE." The count broke apart entirely, forehead grinding the stones, bound hands scrabbling at the flagstones in front of her boots.
"Please.
Not her.
The rope.
I'll give you everything, I'll testify to anything, before any court, PLEASE..."
His voice shredded down to a wet whisper.
"Mercy.
Mercy..."
Iris crouched.
She took a fistful of his collar, lifted his ruined face out of his own filth, and gave him the last words he would ever hear on the living side of the world.
"Nobody came for him, either."
Then she opened her free hand above the stones, and the floor of the record-house tore.
"I already told you.
You'll know no mercy."
"NO!"
A seam split the flagstones beside the count, wide as a grave and getting wider.
Below it there was no cellar and no earth.
Iris then cast her new spell, the first one as the Demon of Vengeance, her powers derived from the perfect culmination of her and the villain's fury, and she sentenced her first target to...
"[Undying Damnation]."
A new dimension materialized before their very eyes.
Black metal ground ran away in every direction under a sky the color of banked coals, and the air of that place rolled hot, in and out.
The whole dimension was breathing.
It was empty.
It had been born tonight, it belonged to the woman crouched at its rim, and it was waiting for its first tenant.
She gripped Corvane by the throat and threw him into its entrance.
The hall heard him scream the whole way down.
He hit the black metal ground of another world.
Before the pain of the landing could even find him, words wrote themselves across his sight, patient and courteous, and they did not care whether his eyes were open.
[Welcome to the hell of the Demon of Vengeance.]
[Resident: 1.]
The seam stayed open.
She stood at its rim and made the whole hall look.
Down in the ember domain, the ground began to move.
It bulged under the screaming count and pushed something up out of itself, grinding, enormous.

What came up was a pillar the height of a watchtower, wrong in every way a built thing can be wrong: rugged black metal, crooked and scabbed, flaking rust in sheets, run down its whole length with fat living veins that pulsed and wept.
Every drop they shed hit the ground hissing.
It narrowed as it rose to a point, it glowed from the inside like a poker left deep in a forge, and the air above it warped with heat.
The count saw it and began to howl fresh.
The demon spoke down into her dimension with the doubled voice, hers riding on top, the villain's authority running underneath, and it spoke straight past the count's mind to his body.
"Climb."

chapters.title: Chapter 1881 Down
paragraphs: "Climb."
Count Corvane's body obeyed.

He watched his own hands drag him up the scabbed pillar. "STOP." He was screaming at them now, a lord commanding his last two vassals. "STOP. I COMMAND you. I COMMAND YOU..." They climbed. His knees climbed after them, up through heat that cooked the skin off his palms, all the way to the top.
"Impale yourself," said the Demon of Vengeance.
Along the walls, hardened soldiers grabbed for each other's shoulders.
His body folded him onto the point, and his weight did the rest, one finger-width at a time.
The metal went through his guts straight up from the backside.
It was furnace-hot. It burned him from the inside out as it went, cauterizing nothing, cooking everything, and the blood that had nowhere left to run came up his throat between the screams.
His own muscles held him steady on it, and his own hands stayed flat against the pillar, pressing. That was the obedience.

The point rose through him and came out of his throat, red, then white-hot, then red again. Count Corvane hung on his own length of glowing metal, boots off the ground, and the hall's view of him shimmered in the heat.
The sound he made then had no language left in it.

It came out of him around the metal, wet, doubled, enormous, a wail that climbed past what a throat should be able to survive, and the domain delivered every note of it up through the seam with perfect, loving fidelity.
Men who had stormed walls put their hands over their ears. It did not help. The sound came through their palms.
Then his flesh began to knit.
The oldest soldiers along the walls understood.
The domain rebuilt him around the metal, patient and thorough. It repaired his cooked organs so they could cook again.
It remade his ruined throat around the point so he could scream past it, and he did, instantly.
Then the demon spoke again, in the voice that never rose.
"Reach the bottom."
For one heartbeat, nothing in him understood.

Then his eyes rolled down the length of the pillar underneath him, down the taper, to where the glowing metal thickened toward its base, thick as his thigh, thick as his chest. Understanding arrived, and the wail broke into words.
"NO. NO, NO, NO, PLEASE, NOT..."
His hands turned over, pressed flat above his head, and pushed.
He slid one hand-span down the taper, and everything the point had torn on its way in, the width behind it tore wider.
The scream that came out of him then made the first one sound like practice.
The domain healed him snug around the metal between one movement and the next. That was the trap of it. The healing kept him sealed to the metal, kept his nerves new, kept his blood in.
Every push began from warm, healthy flesh, and healthy flesh feels everything.
He did it again.
His body gave him no choice about it.

The count hauled himself down his pillar hand over hand, and every pull drove the thickening glow deeper through the middle of him. He screamed without one pause for breath, because the domain breathed for him now and had freed his lungs for their real work.
A hand-span. Another. The metal under him went from wrist-thick to arm-thick, and what leaked down the taper hissed and smoked on the glow.
"MAKE IT STOP!" He found pieces of words in the middle of the descent and spent them on the watching hall. "GIRL. PLEASE. MAKE IT..." The scream took him back before the sentence could finish.
Along the walls of the record-house, men had begun to pray, quietly. The Mediator stood with his ledgers forgotten against his chest. Nobody managed to look away.
It went on. That was the thing the hall would carry home hardest, that it simply went on, past every point where mercy or death or madness should have ended it.
Down and down it went, arm-thick, leg-thick, the man stretched wider than a man goes, healed tight around every inch and made to feel the next one from nothing.
And then his boots touched the ground.
Everything stopped at once, the moving, the tearing, the worsening, all of it.

He hung there upright at the base, run through and standing on his own feet, and the stillness that flooded through him after that descent felt like cool water, felt, for one unforgivable heartbeat, good.
Some last ember of the man he had been dared to lift his head and think it. 'Over. It is over. It is finally over.'
"Up."
The word landed on his body, took his hands, and turned them over.

Count Corvane began to climb his own impalement in reverse, and the sound that rose from the bottom of Eternal Suffering was worse than everything the hall had heard yet, because there was comprehension in it now.
He knew the taper. He knew every inch of it by name. He was going to meet them all again from the other side, narrowing, and then...
"Repeat until the end of eternity."
"No... No... NOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO!"

That was all of him now, established in front of a royal commission and sealed under a crown sentence: a man on a pillar in a breathing country, climbing forever, descending forever, healed new around the glow between every push so nothing ever dulled, the moving centerpiece of a world built to hold him.
No mercy, no sleep, no death.
The demon had promised him in front of everyone, and she kept her promises.
[Domain Manifested: Eternal Suffering.]

[A world born of the Primordial Villain's authority and the Demon of Vengeance's vow, fueled by vengeance itself. Those the Demon judges vile, she may grant unending existence within its keeping. Their suffering is her strength.]
[So long as the Demon of Vengeance does not stray from her path, the domain shall endure. Should she fall, the domain shall endure.]
[Vengeance's will does not die.]
Iris let them look until there was no man along those walls who would ever need the story secondhand.
Then she closed her hand.
The seam began to draw shut, and the last thing Count Corvane ever saw of the living world, up through the narrowing cut of it, was the Demon of Vengeance looking down at him.
The red of her eyes had stopped swirling. For the space of one heartbeat, both burned with the same shape her hell had stamped across his sight when he landed: 1.
Then the seam sealed, and the flagstones lay whole again, unmarked, with the screaming gone where no morning would ever reach.
Somewhere along the wall a veteran was quietly vomiting onto the stones, and nobody mocked him.
Stormlord had watched every second of it without moving.
Felicity Valorian, fourteen years old, had made herself watch too, because her seal had bought this and she would not flinch from its price.
The Soul Records had one more thing to say.
[The Primordial Villain has taken his justicar.]
[Iris Ravenclaw, the Demon of Vengeance. Shield of the Innocent. Scourge of the Vile. Keeper of Eternal Suffering.]
[The vile shall fear her name.]

Iris walked back across the silence to the villain's side, and her eyes had banked down to their ordinary red by the time she reached him. When she spoke, it was to nobody in particular, flat and quiet, in her own voice again.
"One down."
She exhaled.
"Next."

chapters.title: Chapter 1882 Invaded
paragraphs: Dimensions above the mortal night, in the radiant heart of her own domain, Goddess Lilyanna was fighting for her existence.
The assault had come in the deep of that night, without herald or declaration.
One heartbeat of stillness, then the stain on her cheek had torn open from the inside, and the Withered Flame had poured through the breach in her own skin.
Ash-scented fire rolled through corridors that had never known heat.
Planes of layered starlight buckled inward one after another, and every surface that failed turned the color of a dying ember before her will forced it back.
The blight on her cheek burned like a hook set in bone. Through it, patient and immense, Sel'Ashra pulled.
"Kekeke..." The laughter arrived from every direction at once, warm as a banked forge. "You feel thinner than last time, Little One. Does nobody pray properly anymore?"
"Leave!" Lilyanna's decree bent the air of her own dimension, and the dimension answered her, folding plane over plane to cut every road the corruption tried to take.
The stain pulsed, delighted, and crawled a finger-width toward her eye.

Pain drove up through her cheekbone and into her skull. At the far edges of her domain, her radiance guttered like candles in a draft. She clamped her authority down over the crawling blight and held it still by sheer will.
"Such a stubborn little girl~"
The pressure doubled. Molten gold light seeped up between the tiles of her innermost sanctum, and the smell of scorched offerings filled a hall that had only ever smelled of dawn.
"You bleed for him on your own floor, and he has never once said thank you. Give me the boy, Little One. I would treat you both so much better..."
"You will not have him!"
The refusal came out at a pitch no divine decree should reach, and it did not care.
The Withered Flame stopped playing.

Everything the Withered Flame had fed into the anchor arrived at once, ember-cracked will in a single hammerblow, and for one appalling instant the Goddess of Purity felt her own domain forget whose it was. One of her knees touched her own floor.
Then it remembered.

This was her ground. Every plane, every silver structure, every grain of starlight had been raised by her hand and answered her will alone. Lilyanna gathered all of it, the whole architecture of her existence, and closed it over the intruder like a fist.
"This is MY house!"
Her dimension rang like a struck bell.
The corruption tore out of the anchor, shrieking backward down its own thread, and Sel'Ashra went with it, cackling into the dark between worlds.
"Kekekeke! Almost got you that time, Little One~ Almost... almost..."
The laughter frayed into distance and was gone.
Silence settled over the domain. The planes crept back into alignment, and the scorched tiles of the sanctum paled, one by one, back to silver.
Lilyanna stood in the middle of it, bent forward, heaving.

Her breath came in gulps no goddess should need, and it took a long moment before she trusted her legs enough to straighten. Her fingers rose and found her cheek. The stain sat where it had sat for far too long now, clamped back behind its old border, quiet again.
Then the Goddess of Purity stamped her foot.
The stomp cracked a plane of layered starlight clean across. It repaired itself immediately and said nothing about it.
"He corrupts me, and then I have to do this for him!" She stamped again, harder. "Divine war! In my own home! I fight for him whether I like it or not, bleeding in my home, and he doesn't even know!"
"What am I, his slave girl?!"
The question echoed off the silver structures of her sanctum.
She heaved once more, pushed her chin up, and smoothed the front of her robe with both hands.
"...Well. He is the Subjugator."
"What a terrible man. I don't even want to see what he's doing right now."
She turned her back on the scrying mirror to prove it.
She retrieved her complaint notebook from where the battle had thrown it, sat very straight upon her throne, and set her pen to a fresh page.
'Complaint #24,318: Evil Boy forced a divine war upon me. He never once apologized or thanked me.'
Her pen stopped after one line.
The resistance lasted the length of a held breath.
Then the Goddess of Purity set the notebook down and spun on her throne.
She checked anyhow.
The scrying surface gathered itself out of starlight and turned its face toward Thalorind.

A burned record-house in the human kingdom. Smoke still crawling in the rafters, soldiers pressed along the walls, and the Evil Boy standing in the middle of the wreckage with the red-eyed girl at his side.
Then the fresh ink of the Soul Records surfaced across the image, lines written that very night, and Lilyanna stopped hearing her own thoughts.
[Class Evolved: Demon of Vengeance.]
"The Demon of... what?"
She leaned in until her nose nearly touched the starlight. "What? How?!"
[Iris Ravenclaw, the Demon of Vengeance. Shield of the Innocent. Scourge of the Vile. Keeper of Eternal Suffering.]
The red-eyed one. The little swordswoman forever orbiting him with a scowl, the one whose mouth belonged on a dock worker.
Then the Records gave her the rest.
[The Primordial Villain has taken his justicar.]
Lilyanna shot to her feet.
"His justicar?!"
Her voice cracked across the sanctum. "He is nowhere near divine! That seed of his has achieved exactly one thing in all these months, and it was assaulting my perfect skin!"
She began pacing the dais, robe snapping at every turn, counting on her fingers.

"An enforcer of the divine requires a seat." One finger. "A domain for the oath to anchor in." A second. "A covenant the Soul Records have ratified." A third. "And the authority to countersign the remaking of a mortal soul."
Her fourth finger stopped in the air.

Nobody alive on Thalorind held that fourth authority. She held it. Her peers held it. It was the exact power that separated a god's arch priestess from every self-anointed prophet shouting in a market square: the signature.
The starlight mirror scrolled one more line.
[Witnessed and countersigned: Bloodfather.]
"A class," the goddess said, in a very small voice. "The Records accepted a countersign from a class."
She did not remember crossing the dais. The complaint notebook was simply in her hands again, and she was tearing backward through her own entries fast enough to bend the pages.
'Complaint #23,882: Gave the samurai water. Why water?'
'Complaint #23,990: Governor girl still hasn't been given the ritual. The foul creature keeps neglecting her!'
'Complaint #24,102: The serpent woman's victims rise and fight for her. This is necromancy by proxy. He has found a way to commit sacrilege through other people's hands.'
Her pen-hand went slack.
Entry after entry, the same shape stared back at her out of her own tidy grievances: mortal women wearing power with no divine source behind it, granted, anchored, and growing.
Then she realized: 'They were already his blessed. All of them. All this time.'
'I have been keeping the registry of his faith for months, and I called it complaints.'
Her own word snagged her mid-thought.
'...No. Wrong word.'
'Faith, as the divine understand it, is a covenant with divinity. A seat above, worship rising to meet it, and the Records keeping count between.'
'He has no divinity. He has never carried a single drop of it.'
'That is the anomaly sitting in my registry.'
'He is a primordial. Even now, after the physique, after the classes, after transformation upon transformation... a primordial nonetheless. Flesh, blood, and will.'
'So what do I call the thing his people already are?'
Her eyes went back to the newest line in the Records.
Keeper of Eternal Suffering.
A domain.
The word had been sitting in plain sight, and she had read past it because it had no business being there. Domains belonged to gods. Domains were what she was standing in.
Lilyanna reached through the starlight, took hold of the newest thread in the world's weave, and looked down into the hell of the Demon of Vengeance.
Heat came up through the scrying and touched her face.
That alone should have been impossible. A goddess's mirror carries image, never weather, and this one was sweating.
Black metal ground ran away under a sky the color of banked coals, and the whole country was breathing, slow and hot. It held one resident.
The sound arrived first. It crossed dimensions along with the heat, a wet, doubled scream that reached her sanctum with terrible clarity, and it did not stop.
Then her eyes resolved what was making it.
In the middle of that world stood a crooked pillar of scabbed, glowing metal, and a fat man hung threaded on it with his boots off the ground.
The tapered point stood out of his gaping mouth, white-hot, and around it the scream still found room to happen.

He was descending. His own palms pressed flat against the metal above his head and pushed, driving him down a hand-span at a time, forcing the thickening glow through the whole cooked length of him. The pillar had gone in through his ass, and by now it owned everything from there to his jaw.
Blood boiled up around the point and left him in bubbles. They swelled at his lips, burst, ran hissing down the glow, and new ones rose gurgling to replace them with every push.
Damp gathered along the goddess's hairline, and she never thought to wipe it.

Everything soft inside him burst against the widening girth as he sank, organ after organ. The domain rebuilt each one snug around the metal in the same breath, tender and thorough, so the next hand-span could burst them new.
His skin cooked where it gripped the pillar, stuck, tore free, and was remade smooth. The remaking never once got ahead of the burning.
The goddess watched with one hand pressed hard over her mouth. "How cruel!"
When his boots at last found the ground, he held still for a single heartbeat, run through from ass to mouth on metal as thick as his own chest, standing upright on his own two feet.
Then his hands turned over and began to climb. The ruined length of him tore in the opposite direction, and the scream that had never stopped climbed with him.
"That's so terrible..." Lilyanna breathed. "The villain's handprint all over it..."
The domain healed him as she watched, tenderly, so that nothing would ever dull.
The Records, courteous as always, provided the deed to what she was seeing.
[A world born of the Primordial Villain's authority and the Demon of Vengeance's vow, fueled by vengeance itself.]
[Should she fall, the domain shall endure.]
Lilyanna read the second line twice.
Her legs decided on their own.
