The planes crept back into alignment, and the scorched tiles of the sanctum paled, one by one, back to silver.
Lilyanna stood in the middle of it, bent forward, heaving.
Her breath came in gulps no goddess should need, and it took a long moment before she trusted her legs enough to straighten.
Her fingers rose and found her cheek.
The stain sat where it had sat for far too long now, clamped back behind its old border, quiet again.
Then the Goddess of Purity stamped her foot.
The stomp cracked a plane of layered starlight clean across.
It repaired itself immediately and said nothing about it.
"He corrupts me, and then I have to do this for him!" She stamped again, harder.
"Divine war!
In my own home!
I fight for him whether I like it or not, bleeding in my home, and he doesn't even know!"
"What am I, his slave girl?!"
The question echoed off the silver structures of her sanctum.
She heaved once more, pushed her chin up, and smoothed the front of her robe with both hands.
"...Well.
He is the Subjugator."
"What a terrible man.
I don't even want to see what he's doing right now."
She turned her back on the scrying mirror to prove it.
She retrieved her complaint notebook from where the battle had thrown it, sat very straight upon her throne, and set her pen to a fresh page.
'Complaint #24,318: Evil Boy forced a divine war upon me.
He never once apologized or thanked me.'
Her pen stopped after one line.
The resistance lasted the length of a held breath.
Then the Goddess of Purity set the notebook down and spun on her throne.
She checked anyhow.
The scrying surface gathered itself out of starlight and turned its face toward Thalorind.
A burned record-house in the human kingdom.
Smoke still crawling in the rafters, soldiers pressed along the walls, and the Evil Boy standing in the middle of the wreckage with the red-eyed girl at his side.
Then the fresh ink of the Soul Records surfaced across the image, lines written that very night, and Lilyanna stopped hearing her own thoughts.
[Class Evolved: Demon of Vengeance.]
"The Demon of... what?"
She leaned in until her nose nearly touched the starlight.
"What?
How?!"
[Iris Ravenclaw, the Demon of Vengeance.
Shield of the Innocent.
Scourge of the Vile.
Keeper of Eternal Suffering.]
The red-eyed one.
The little swordswoman forever orbiting him with a scowl, the one whose mouth belonged on a dock worker.
Then the Records gave her the rest.
[The Primordial Villain has taken his justicar.]
Lilyanna shot to her feet.
"His justicar?!"
Her voice cracked across the sanctum.
"He is nowhere near divine!
That seed of his has achieved exactly one thing in all these months, and it was assaulting my perfect skin!"
She began pacing the dais, robe snapping at every turn, counting on her fingers.
"An enforcer of the divine requires a seat." One finger.
"A domain for the oath to anchor in." A second.
"A covenant the Soul Records have ratified." A third.
"And the authority to countersign the remaking of a mortal soul."
Her fourth finger stopped in the air.
Nobody alive on Thalorind held that fourth authority.
She held it.
Her peers held it.
It was the exact power that separated a god's arch priestess from every self-anointed prophet shouting in a market square: the signature.
The starlight mirror scrolled one more line.
[Witnessed and countersigned: Bloodfather.]
"A class," the goddess said, in a very small voice.
"The Records accepted a countersign from a class."
She did not remember crossing the dais.
The complaint notebook was simply in her hands again, and she was tearing backward through her own entries fast enough to bend the pages.
'Complaint #23,882: Gave the samurai water.
Why water?'
'Complaint #23,990: Governor girl still hasn't been given the ritual.
The foul creature keeps neglecting her!'
'Complaint #24,102: The serpent woman's victims rise and fight for her.
This is necromancy by proxy.
He has found a way to commit sacrilege through other people's hands.'
Her pen-hand went slack.
Entry after entry, the same shape stared back at her out of her own tidy grievances: mortal women wearing power with no divine source behind it, granted, anchored, and growing.
Then she realized: 'They were already his blessed.
All of them.
All this time.'
'I have been keeping the registry of his faith for months, and I called it complaints.'
Her own word snagged her mid-thought.
Wrong word.'
'Faith, as the divine understand it, is a covenant with divinity.
A seat above, worship rising to meet it, and the Records keeping count between.'
'He has no divinity.
He has never carried a single drop of it.'
'That is the anomaly sitting in my registry.'
'He is a primordial.
Even now, after the physique, after the classes, after transformation upon transformation... a primordial nonetheless.
Flesh, blood, and will.'
'So what do I call the thing his people already are?'
Her eyes went back to the newest line in the Records.
Keeper of Eternal Suffering.
A domain.
The word had been sitting in plain sight, and she had read past it because it had no business being there.
Domains belonged to gods.
Domains were what she was standing in.
Lilyanna reached through the starlight, took hold of the newest thread in the world's weave, and looked down into the hell of the Demon of Vengeance.
Heat came up through the scrying and touched her face.
That alone should have been impossible.
A goddess's mirror carries image, never weather, and this one was sweating.
Black metal ground ran away under a sky the color of banked coals, and the whole country was breathing, slow and hot.
It held one resident.
The sound arrived first.
It crossed dimensions along with the heat, a wet, doubled scream that reached her sanctum with terrible clarity, and it did not stop.
Then her eyes resolved what was making it.
In the middle of that world stood a crooked pillar of scabbed, glowing metal, and a fat man hung threaded on it with his boots off the ground.
The tapered point stood out of his gaping mouth, white-hot, and around it the scream still found room to happen.
He was descending.
His own palms pressed flat against the metal above his head and pushed, driving him down a hand-span at a time, forcing the thickening glow through the whole cooked length of him.
The pillar had gone in through his ass, and by now it owned everything from there to his jaw.
Blood boiled up around the point and left him in bubbles.
They swelled at his lips, burst, ran hissing down the glow, and new ones rose gurgling to replace them with every push.
Damp gathered along the goddess's hairline, and she never thought to wipe it.
Everything soft inside him burst against the widening girth as he sank, organ after organ.
The domain rebuilt each one snug around the metal in the same breath, tender and thorough, so the next hand-span could burst them new.
His skin cooked where it gripped the pillar, stuck, tore free, and was remade smooth.
The remaking never once got ahead of the burning.
The goddess watched with one hand pressed hard over her mouth.
"How cruel!"
When his boots at last found the ground, he held still for a single heartbeat, run through from ass to mouth on metal as thick as his own chest, standing upright on his own two feet.
Then his hands turned over and began to climb.
The ruined length of him tore in the opposite direction, and the scream that had never stopped climbed with him.
"That's so terrible..." Lilyanna breathed.
"The villain's handprint all over it..."
The domain healed him as she watched, tenderly, so that nothing would ever dull.
The Records, courteous as always, provided the deed to what she was seeing.
[A world born of the Primordial Villain's authority and the Demon of Vengeance's vow, fueled by vengeance itself.]
[Should she fall, the domain shall endure.]
Lilyanna read the second line twice.
Her legs decided on their own.

chapters.title: Chapter 1883 The Secret Ingredient
paragraphs: Her legs decided on their own.
The backs of her knees found the throne, and the Goddess of Purity sat down hard in her own sanctum, eyes wide, while the wailing of a nameless mortal went on faintly through the starlight.
A hell that outlives its keeper.
Permanence was the ink her own sphere rationed above every other. She had petitioned for less and been refused.
A mortal girl had spoken it tonight as a promise, and her class had simply kept it.
"It's not possible," she told her empty sanctum.

'He cannot use that seed. It is dormant. It is a knot of raw entropy that would burn him hollow if he so much as pulled on it. I have watched him not use it for months. That is the single reassuring thing about the man.'
And yet.

She made herself file the evidence as she filed everything: plainly. The seed had moved tonight. She had felt it move, every scrap of ash in her cheek leaning toward Thalorind, and the Withered Flame had come hunting.

'Somehow, the seed helped that girl evolve. A sliver of it went into her remaking. Any true draw would have hollowed him where he stood, so it gave exactly as much as was needed and settled back down... as if something meted it out.'
Then the older truth arrived, and it was worse.
'No. This is not the first sign. It is only the loudest.'

'Ever since that Bloodfather class of his, his women have been wrong. Blessed-wrong. Marks that read their bearers and author fitting gifts. A reservoir that moves his strength into their bodies across any distance. Boosts with no divine source, day after day, in my own handwriting.'
Her eyes narrowed further. 'His blessed.'
There was that. 'The [Blessed Seed].'
The methodology.
Triple growth, arrested aging, delivered by... She declined to complete the thought, alone, in her own sanctum, where it was safest.
Drafting the relevant complaint had required a cold compress.
'But the red-eyed girl...'
Lilyanna sat up and looked at the girl properly through the mirror.
No seed. She checked twice; on that subject her thoroughness was a matter of record.
The pills came back nearly as bare. The girl had swallowed one, once, gaining half a day of borrowed speed that burned out of her before the next dawn, and it left nothing of him behind.
Which left the mark on her spine, one sliver of sleeping corruption, and nothing else at all.
The stain on her cheek went cold.
'His physique.'
Her cosmic eyes went distant. She had his entire blasphemous portfolio memorized. It was for the complaints.

'The Abyssal Genesis Physique. It was the Primordial Breeding Physique once, before he conquered the demoness and it changed with her. It had to become what it is to let him keep his anomalous growth speed up, and in the process, it became what allowed him to house the Bloodfather class.
'A reservoir seated over his heart, moving his essence out along every bond he owns.'
'A pump.'
Her hand came up and pressed flat over her own sternum, over the place her grace rose from whenever one of her blessed called on it.
'Like me. It works like me.'
"He has a me." She heard herself say it aloud. "He grew himself a me."
True agitation took the Goddess of Purity then, and it was a different creature from her tantrums entirely.
He had grown an organ to do a seat's work, taught his blood to write blessings as marks, and let his class sign the Records in place of a covenant.
He did not even know he was doing it.
On instinct, on appetite, on love, the boy was assembling, piece by blind piece, a path that ran beside divinity, paid none of its tolls, and answered none of its restrictions.
And it was arriving.
Her radiance had begun to flicker in time with her breathing, dawn-bright and dim by turns. She pressed both hands together in her lap to stop them from moving.
'A path without restrictions.'
She had heard hunger for such a path before, voiced long ago, in a brighter hall than this one. Her hand was at her cheek before she noticed it had moved.
Lilyanna put the memory down carefully, face-down, and did not look at it again.
"...But no." She breathed in deep. "Let me be fair."
"He is talented. Genius, even. I admit it freely, into this empty room, where he cannot hear me."
"The instincts. The luck. The grit, the willpower, the affinity. All of it exceptional, all of it real."
Her breathing went heavy again. "But nobody builds a road beside the divine because he feels like it. Nobody keeps a road like that standing by accident."
'That realm of his is crude. It is young, it strains, and it should tear a little every time he performs one of his impossibilities. The seed alone should have soured it by now. So why...?'
The question finished itself in a direction she did not like.
'Unless one of his impossibilities is mending the others. Or...'
Her cosmic eyes narrowed to slits. 'Or somebody is.'
'Her.'

The file arrived with the thought: the Primordial Demon of Lust, progenitor of demons, conquered by the boy and coiled inside his soul ever since. Lilyanna had kept records on her since before the first kingdoms existed, and the records were property damage from end to end.
'Her? Mending? Tending?' Lilyanna nearly laughed at her own hunch. 'Impossible.'
But the hunch would not lie down.
The Goddess of Purity scooted forward on her throne, set both hands flat on the starlight, and went to check.
She looked all the way in.
Past the mortal shell, past the crimson lattice scripted across his heart, down into the dark of the villain's soul realm.
She found a decorated sky.
Constellations no Records had ever issued hung painted over the dark, arranged to be seen from the door. Beneath them, every seam she had expected to find torn was bound.
She looked closer. Old essence, older than the seed it caged, ran along every fault line in neat dark stitches. Some of the repairs had healed so long ago they had become structure.
And the seed, the famous, terrible, dormant seed whose single achievement was her cheek, lay at the bottom of that realm the way an old hound lies by a hearth: fed, warm, watched.
A little dryad slept curled against it, nails freshly painted, and even in sleep one small hand rested on the seed's shell.
Beside them, on a throne that matched nothing else in that realm because she had clearly built it to her own taste, sat the demoness herself.
Pink eyes, half-lidded, luminous in the dark.
A long tail hung off the armrest, swishing lazily. She was petting the sleeping dryad's head with one idle hand, and she was chuckling under her breath at a joke she had shared with nobody.
The hunch had come looking for a mender. It had found a keeper.
Nyxara, breaker of ten thousand homes, was keeping one.
The whole picture reassembled itself around that throne in one silent turn.
'The stitches are hers. The sky is hers. The little warden at the seed keeps a schedule, and the schedule is hers.'

'He tears holes in the world's order every other week, on instinct, without ever once looking down. And billions of years of patience sit in the dark behind him, closing every one of them by hand, without ever once telling him.'
'It is her. She is how the impossible road stays standing. The secret backer, mending the path behind the man while he walks it looking only forward.'
Quinlan Elysiar walked a road no being had ever walked, and she had finally met the reason he had never once fallen off it.
The tail stopped swishing.
In the dark of the soul realm, the demoness's chin lifted. The pink eyes opened the rest of the way, unhurried, and found Lilyanna through every careful layer of a goddess's scrying.
Nyxara smiled.
"Kukuku..." The chuckle crossed dimensions without asking permission. "Peeping into other women's homes, little goddess~? And they call you the pure one..."
She waved the way adults wave at a child caught at a keyhole, small fingers folding one after another.
Lilyanna moved faster than she had moved in the entire battle.
The scrying tore shut under her palm. Starlight scattered across the dais, and the Goddess of Purity found herself pressed into the back of her own throne with both hands clamped over a dead mirror.
"Scary. This woman is scary."
But then her curiosity quickly overwhelmed her shock.
"Evil Boy..." she muttered under her breath, scrying already underway. "Just what are you up to now...?"
And just like that, under a hypocrite woman's scrutinizing gaze, it was time for the Primordial Villain to take over the continent!

chapters.title: Chapter 1884 Rampaging Through Ravenshade
paragraphs: Iris Ravenclaw stood in the burned record-house exactly where the night had left her.
The stones lay whole and unmarked beneath her feet. Under them, in a separate dimension, Count Corvane was climbing.
She could feel him doing it.
That was new. Her hell hung off her like a second heartbeat now that she'd gotten a bit acclimated to it, and every push of the count's ruined hands arrived in her chest as a warm coal.
'One,' she thought. 'One is not enough.'
Boots crossed the scorched floor behind her, careful of the ash, and she knew them without turning.
"Iris. Before you start." Felicity had the king's seal out of its case and a fresh warrant flat on the reading table, and she was dripping the wax onto it herself. "We need this on paper."
"Corvane was sentenced in front of a royal commission," Iris said. "It's done."

"It's done for Corvane." The princess pressed the seal down with both gauntlets and held it there until the wax took the impression. "It isn't done for the next one, or the fifty after him. Because you're not done just yet, are you?" she smiled.
"I'm not."
"Good!" Felicity beamed. "Then let's do it like this. I'm not having some lawyer in the capital stand up and call it murder."

Stormlord read the warrant over her shoulder without a word, and whatever the commander of the Aegis Vanguard thought of the thing he was reading, he passed it down to the clerks and kept it behind his teeth.
"Every man your evidence convicts," Felicity said. "My seal, my father's name on it, the whole commission watching. And you get to do it however you want!"
Iris looked at the wax. It was still soft.
"...You thought things through."
"Hehe! I did!" Felicity admitted, joyous.
A short breath left Iris's nose. From anyone else it would have been a laugh.
Against the broken doorframe, arms folded, the Primordial Villain watched his justicar take the paper and left the night to her.
"Let's begin," said the Demon of Vengeance. "We have a long night ahead."
The seam opened in the middle of the record-house floor, wide as a grave, and heat rolled out of it with the smell of cooked iron.
The scream arrived a heartbeat later.
"Corvane," Iris called.
His body stopped climbing.
The sound he made around the metal was a plea worn down to its gums.
"No," she said. "Talk."
In the world above, men hid things in ciphers, in cousins, in bought silence. Down there, in a land made of her promise, his whole life lay open like a gutted fish, and she simply looked.
The names came up through the heat. He didn't even need to part his lips.

"Write," Iris said, and behind her the crown's clerks bent over their boards. "The tax farmer of the eastern crossing is called Odam. The assessors above him answer to a cipher, a wheel with nine spokes. The wheel collects at the Silver Hollow granary on the first frost of every month."
The Mediator unrolled his map with great serenity and set a bony finger on Silver Hollow. "Fascinating. We had that granary listed as a smuggler's rest. It seems we undersold it."
Corvane was weeping now, wet and doubled around the point, and she read him anyway, item by item, brick by brick, name by name.
His machine had one great cleverness. No man in it could name the man above him. Every thread ran upward into a cipher, and every cipher into smoke.
Every man in that machine knew almost everything below himself and some things beside himself, and the moment one of them fell into her domain, all of it was hers.
'They built a ladder no one could climb,' Iris thought, rising from the crouch. 'Fine by me.'
'I'll drag them down it instead.'
What followed was a harvest.
Quinlan opened gate after gate, and the duchy stopped being a distance.
The eastern crossing, an hour past full dark: the doors came off the strongroom, and the tax farmer Odam stood on his own false floor with a shovel.
"I only counted!" he screamed, backing into his own hidden silver. "Coin, only coin, I swear on my mother's grave, I never touched a soul, the count made us..."
"You did more than that," Iris said. "You can keep counting for the rest of time."
The floor opened.
[Resident: 7.]
Her domain had grown a new district while she walked to his door, and it took him screaming.
A counting-house of black iron stood roofless under the ember sky, and at the middle of it a crucible the size of a coffin tipped molten silver down into the open hands of him and his cronies.

Odam's palms went first. The metal ate through them, kept going, and cooled somewhere past the wrist, leaving him two fistfuls of glowing slag in a cage made of his own finger bones. He could feel every coin of it.
He had to count them.

The domain wanted columns, neat ones, and it would not let his arms stop until the tally came out right. So he stacked. The silver welded his fingers shut around the stack, the stack went over into his lap, and it opened both his thighs to the bone in two straight hissing lines on the way down.
"Forty-one!" Odam shrieked up at the sky of that place. "FORTY-ONE, IT'S FORTY-ONE, I COUNTED IT, I-"
It wasn't. Something in the pile ran, or fused, or cooled wrong, so the tally came up one short, and the crucible tipped again.
His hands grew back around the metal still inside them. That was the kindness of the district. New skin, new nerves, old silver cooking underneath, and a fresh pour already coming.

By the fourth tally he had stopped making words and was only making a number-shaped noise, wet at the edges, because his own screaming had torn something loose in his chest and the domain had not seen fit to mend that part.
Silver Hollow in the small hours: the chief clerk of the circuit had written nineteen years of dissolution orders in a fine, patient hand.
"I wrote what they gave me!" he wept onto the crown's warrant. "Word for word! That was all of it, that was my whole crime, I never chose a single name..."
"No."
Iris didn't even entertain the claim, for she knew the truth. The count himself had shown her that these people were more than forced hands.
The deep district took him at the desks, and it began skinning him alive.

His back came off first. It lifted away in long cured sheets with the meat steaming underneath, and each sheet was trimmed square, smoothed flat, and hung to dry on a line strung above his own head, where he could watch his skin stiffen.
He screamed the whole time he watched it dry.
"I wrote what they gave me!" It came out of him wet and torn, over and over, at a sky that had no interest in it. "I ONLY WROTE WHAT THEY GAVE ME!"

sentences.text: Iris Ravenclaw stood in the burned record-house exactly where the night had left her.
The stones lay whole and unmarked beneath her feet.
Under them, in a separate dimension, Count Corvane was climbing.
She could feel him doing it.
That was new.
Her hell hung off her like a second heartbeat now that she'd gotten a bit acclimated to it, and every push of the count's ruined hands arrived in her chest as a warm coal.
'One,' she thought. 'One is not enough.'
Boots crossed the scorched floor behind her, careful of the ash, and she knew them without turning.
"Iris.
Before you start." Felicity had the king's seal out of its case and a fresh warrant flat on the reading table, and she was dripping the wax onto it herself.
"We need this on paper."
"Corvane was sentenced in front of a royal commission," Iris said.
"It's done."
"It's done for Corvane." The princess pressed the seal down with both gauntlets and held it there until the wax took the impression.
"It isn't done for the next one, or the fifty after him.
Because you're not done just yet, are you?" she smiled.
"I'm not."
"Good!" Felicity beamed.
"Then let's do it like this.
I'm not having some lawyer in the capital stand up and call it murder."

Stormlord read the warrant over her shoulder without a word, and whatever the commander of the Aegis Vanguard thought of the thing he was reading, he passed it down to the clerks and kept it behind his teeth.
"Every man your evidence convicts," Felicity said.
"My seal, my father's name on it, the whole commission watching.
And you get to do it however you want!"
Iris looked at the wax.
It was still soft.
"...You thought things through."
"Hehe!
I did!" Felicity admitted, joyous.
A short breath left Iris's nose.
From anyone else it would have been a laugh.
Against the broken doorframe, arms folded, the Primordial Villain watched his justicar take the paper and left the night to her.
"Let's begin," said the Demon of Vengeance.
"We have a long night ahead."
The seam opened in the middle of the record-house floor, wide as a grave, and heat rolled out of it with the smell of cooked iron.
The scream arrived a heartbeat later.
"Corvane," Iris called.
His body stopped climbing.
The sound he made around the metal was a plea worn down to its gums.
"No," she said.
"Talk."
In the world above, men hid things in ciphers, in cousins, in bought silence.
Down there, in a land made of her promise, his whole life lay open like a gutted fish, and she simply looked.
The names came up through the heat.
He didn't even need to part his lips.
"Write," Iris said, and behind her the crown's clerks bent over their boards.
"The tax farmer of the eastern crossing is called Odam.
The assessors above him answer to a cipher, a wheel with nine spokes.
The wheel collects at the Silver Hollow granary on the first frost of every month."
The Mediator unrolled his map with great serenity and set a bony finger on Silver Hollow.
"Fascinating.
We had that granary listed as a smuggler's rest.
It seems we undersold it."
Corvane was weeping now, wet and doubled around the point, and she read him anyway, item by item, brick by brick, name by name.
His machine had one great cleverness.
No man in it could name the man above him.
Every thread ran upward into a cipher, and every cipher into smoke.
Every man in that machine knew almost everything below himself and some things beside himself, and the moment one of them fell into her domain, all of it was hers.
'They built a ladder no one could climb,' Iris thought, rising from the crouch. 'Fine by me.'
'I'll drag them down it instead.'
What followed was a harvest.
Quinlan opened gate after gate, and the duchy stopped being a distance.
The eastern crossing, an hour past full dark: the doors came off the strongroom, and the tax farmer Odam stood on his own false floor with a shovel.
"I only counted!" he screamed, backing into his own hidden silver.
"Coin, only coin, I swear on my mother's grave, I never touched a soul, the count made us..."
"You did more than that," Iris said.
"You can keep counting for the rest of time."
The floor opened.
[Resident: 7.]
Her domain had grown a new district while she walked to his door, and it took him screaming.
A counting-house of black iron stood roofless under the ember sky, and at the middle of it a crucible the size of a coffin tipped molten silver down into the open hands of him and his cronies.
Odam's palms went first.
The metal ate through them, kept going, and cooled somewhere past the wrist, leaving him two fistfuls of glowing slag in a cage made of his own finger bones.
He could feel every coin of it.
He had to count them.
The domain wanted columns, neat ones, and it would not let his arms stop until the tally came out right.
So he stacked.
The silver welded his fingers shut around the stack, the stack went over into his lap, and it opened both his thighs to the bone in two straight hissing lines on the way down.
"Forty-one!" Odam shrieked up at the sky of that place.
"FORTY-ONE, IT'S FORTY-ONE, I COUNTED IT, I-"
It wasn't.
Something in the pile ran, or fused, or cooled wrong, so the tally came up one short, and the crucible tipped again.
His hands grew back around the metal still inside them.
That was the kindness of the district.

His back came off first.

chapters.title: Chapter 1885 Grand Gathering
paragraphs: They didn't.
So the floor opened, mid-plea, every time. The fabricated tales cut off like a snuffed wick, and the woman in black was already walking to the next door.

Her domain only took the proven, as she found out. She couldn't just decide to judge a man for being guilty; she needed the proof of it. But every man she caught carried the proof of the next four, so the deeper she went the faster she moved, and the machine fed her its own arrests.
And as more and more scum was sentenced under her judgment, Iris felt her class slowly, relentlessly increasing her strength.
That's how the Demon of Vengeance worked.
Terror ran ahead of her up the duchy's roads all night, and mercy came behind her exactly never.
The counts came an hour before dawn.
Ostrev tried to buy passage with his own vaults through the shrine door he was hiding behind, and the floor drank him mid-offer.

Orvath of the Weirs, whose family name sat on eleven salvage deeds, was dragged in bellowing about peerage, saw her eyes, and went down howling that he could give them the others if they let him off the hook.
Unluckily for him, he could do that perfectly from hell.
Below, at a long iron table laid out with the terrible courtesy of a lord's own study, the counts of the inner circle were being collected.

Each of them sat in a high-backed chair with a pen in his fist, and the pen fed itself. The nib went into the wrist and stayed there, drawing up through the vein until the whole arm went the color of tallow. Then the hand signed, whether or not the man attached to it wanted it to.
What it signed was an inventory of himself.
"Lot the first," said the auctioneer, warm and unhurried, in the seller's own recorded scream. "The right hand. Sound. Well-used."

The hand came off at the wrist with the pen still in its fingers. The stump was sealed against the table's edge with a hiss and a smell, and a new hand was growing before the old one finished twitching.
"Sold."
"Lot the second. The skin of the back. One piece, unmarked."

Ostrev came out of his chair screaming, and it made no difference at all. The sheet was taken off him whole, rolled while it still steamed, and stamped with his own signet. Then the count went face-down onto the iron with everything under his shoulder blades open to an air that ran hot.
"Sold."
"Lot the third. The tongue."
They screamed through every lot, all of them, all night, and it changed nothing, because the auction only wanted the signature, and it owned their hands.

One man very nearly came back out of that night alive: a ferry clerk with two pages against his name, maybe a rat, maybe a man with a knife at his neck. The residents of hell didn't know, so neither did she.
Quinlan's Subjugation helped solve the case.
He wasn't innocent.
[Resident: 38.]
As the sun began to come up, Quinlan turned the finished master list around with two fingers.
Long years of this shadowy syndicate's history had a shape now: the wheel of nine spokes, the granary, the salvage deeds, the fee for tidy administration.
Every line of coin walked up out of the counties and vanished, in writing, into one house on the northern border.
Iris read the last line twice.

She had spent years working up through syndicate scum, every rung swearing the next one up was the answer, and every rung had run out into smoke. Now the smoke had an address. The address sat in a clerk's tidy hand, under a king's seal.
Paperwork. She had hated every hour of it.
It had just handed her a duke.
Quinlan felt the heat of her from three steps away, and her eyes still carried some of that other sky home with her. Neither thing worried him in the slightest.
"Every trail, the same landlord," he said. "I'd call that enough."
"Yes," Iris agreed.
Felicity looked up from the wax she was dripping, the king's seal heavy in her gauntleted fist, and asked the question the whole night had been building toward.
"Then we have enough to summon the duke?"
"No, Your Highness," Stormlord corrected. "You have enough to summon the defendant."
Six hundred miles north, in a study warmed against the frost, Duke Tharion Ravenshade was listening to silence.

It had a texture, this particular silence. He had spent every hour mapping it. The eastern crossing had not reported. The Weirs had not reported. Silver Hollow, which had never once in generations missed the first frost of the month, had let the frost come and go.
They were being taken in for questioning, according to the official response he received through the correct channels.
What kept him at the map was a conclusion he refused to phrase, even inwardly.
Old instruments had one duty when caught, which was to be caught slowly: to bury the commission in statute for a season, to cough, to stall, to demand daylight and certified inventories.
Corvane had gone silent between one sunset and the next.
Nothing about that was slow.
'The old arrangement is quiet,' he allowed himself, at last. 'This isn't one bit how an investigation of this magnitude should be unfolding... Things are moving far too quickly.'
His teeth bared. "Alexios, you treacherous bastard... you're forgoing procedure to appeal to a man called Primordial Villain?!"

Behind him, his secretary cleared her throat from the door. She had been standing there for a while, holding a scroll case at arm's length, visibly hoping not to be remembered as the one who carried it in.
The wax was royal, and the seal in it was the king's personal ring, pressed by his own hand.
Tharion read it once.
The language was flawless, which he expected, and brief, which he did not.
The crown requests and requires the attendance of its beloved Duke of Ravenshade at the royal palace, before the assembled peerage, to answer matters touching the governance of his duchy.
Answer, before the assembled peerage. The verb did the whole letter's work by itself, and the venue did the rest. They had invited an audience.
His outrage arrived properly then, clean and well-made, with the masonry of a founding house under it.
A duke of the realm had been summoned like a granary clerk caught with his thumb in the scale. His blood sat on the throne beside Alexios. His blood ran in every royal child.
A founding house of Vraven, whistled to heel in front of counts and merchants. On the strength of what? A season of suspicion?
"Ready the column," he said. "Full colors. The good carriage."
The secretary blinked. "Your Grace will... attend?"
"A summons is a stage," Tharion said, already choosing the rings for his hands. "They have built mine at the crown's expense. It would be rude to leave it empty."
And under the outrage, in the place where he did his real thinking, the duke touched the one seal in Vraven that outranked any writ the old man could wave.
A promise, sworn on blood, years before the world had heard the word Villain.
Alexios had bought Ravenshade's peace with it, and had apparently forgotten that a leash like that has two ends.
'Come, then,' Tharion thought, calm again, watching his banners come down off the wall. 'Convene your peers, old friend. Stand me before every noble eye in the kingdom.'
'Let us see which of us can afford the audience.'
The great hall of the Vraven palace had not held the full peerage in living memory, and the full peerage had come anyway.

Every banner in the kingdom hung from the gallery rails. Below them, packed shoulder to shoulder in winter velvet, stood the counts and barons of five duchies, and the question they had all arrived with moved through the hall in a low, endless murmur.
"A closed summons, under the personal seal..."
"They say the commission took thirty men in just an hour... They're wrecking Ravenshade lands like pillagers."
"Where? Which cells? My cousin rode past the Corvane seat and swears the gibbets are empty..."
On the high throne, above all of it, sat Alexios Valorian, and he had not spoken one word in an hour.
The old king wore full regalia for the first time in years. He didn't even wear it for his thousandth birthday.
The great crown of Vraven sat on his grey head, the sword of state lay naked across his knees, and his face was carved out of the same stone as the hall.
Princess Felicity stood at the dais's right hand in her polished armor, visor up, the royal seal hanging over her breastplate. Stormlord stood at her shoulder.
At the dais's left, alone, in plain black, stood a red-eyed woman that not one noble in that hall could name.
The murmur broke on her like water on a rock. Everyone had heard of the crown's new investigator. Nobody had a name, a house, or an explanation, and the not-knowing had grown teeth of its own.
"And the Villain..." a baroness whispered, tilting her head at the western gallery. "Why is the Villain here?!?!"
The western gallery had been given, without one written word of explanation, to the Primordial Villain and his family.
Quinlan Elysiar lounged on the rail like a man at a horse race, arms around his gorgeous women's shoulders.
Ayame sat at his right with her katana across her lap, and Jasmine on his left. Black Fang stood behind him in the shadow of a pillar.
Kitsara had taken the rail and brought a ledger to a murder trial, visibly invested in the drama. Lucille sat beside her, entirely at home under six hundred banners.

chapters.title: Chapter 1886 Accused
paragraphs: The rest of the family filled the gallery in a warm, murmuring row. A blonde head among them kept popping up over the rail to wave at Felicity and Iris until Lucille gently pulled her back down by the tail.
Felicity, who was on duty and being very serious, waved back with two fingers, low, where her father couldn't see.
He saw. He said nothing.
The royal children had the eastern gallery. Prince Elias, first of his name, three hundred years of unhurried dignity, stood at the rail with his hands folded.

Prince Caelum leaned beside him. Between the brothers, in the white and gold vestments of the Goddess's church, stood the Arch Priestess Elisabeth, called Dawn Breaker, and her calm was the professional kind that took effort.
"Sister," Caelum murmured. "What does our father's face say to you?"
Elisabeth studied the carved stillness on the throne.
"It says someone in this hall is already dead," she said.
At the correspondence table set discreetly below their gallery, Queen Morgana read letters and acknowledged nobody.
Many wondered why she wasn't seated next to Alexios, on her throne as monarch.
One table over, in scuffed adventuring leathers that had scandalized the heralds beyond speech, Lilith of the Scarlet Lilies had put her boots up on the crown's furniture and was eating an apple.
Duke Zaren of Duskmere had the place of honor among the peers, white-haired and pleasant, with Calienne on his arm. Duke Alastair of Greenvale stood grey and obedient in front of his twin daughters.
And near the back stood Kaede Fujimori, dressed for the occasion, representing the Duchy of Silverwind, with Chizuru at her side.
The horns sounded at the doors.
"His Grace, Tharion, Duke of Ravenshade!"
The doors swung, and the cold came in wearing black and silver.
Tharion Ravenshade crossed the hall without hurry, in full ducal colors, six retainers at his back. His rings caught the light. His face was courteous, mildly puzzled, faultless.
He stopped at the center of the floor, before the dais, and bowed to the throne with exactly the depth the law required of a duke and not one degree more.

"Your Majesty." His voice filled the hall without effort. "You summoned, and Ravenshade answers, as Ravenshade has always answered. Though I confess myself curious what matter requires my presence before..." His gaze traveled the packed galleries with mild amusement. "...the entire realm."
Alexios looked down at him and said nothing at all.
The silence stretched past courtesy, past protocol, into insult, and the duke's pleasant expression held through every second of it.
Then the king moved one finger, and Stormlord stepped forward to unroll the charge.

"Tharion of House Ravenshade." The commander's voice came out iron-flat, pitched to reach the last row. "The crown charges you with the creation and mastery of a covert organization operating across the lands you administer. You are charged with the levying of an unwritten toll upon the crown's roads."
"With the engineered ruin and seizure of the lands of vassals outside your inner circle, and the enrichment of those within it."
"With extortion, arson, blackmail, the trade in children, and high treason against crown and commons."
The hall stopped breathing.
"The crown will hear your defense."
For three heartbeats, the Duke of Ravenshade did not move.
Then he laughed.
It was a single, disbelieving syllable, and it cracked off the marble like a whip. What came up behind it had nothing amused in it at all.
"Defense." He said the word as if tasting spoiled wine. "Defense?"
His voice rose, and the temperature of the hall rose with it.

"Thousands of Ravenshade men and women have held the northern border of this kingdom. We bled the Elvardian invasions white while half these banners hid behind their walls. My grandfather's bones are mortared into the fortresses that let this hall stand and hold... this farce."
His hand cut at the assembly.
"And the crown of Vraven summons ME, before the peerage assembled, to answer for... what did the soldier recite? Tolls? Arson? The trade in CHILDREN?"
The last word detonated out of him, and the nearest nobles flinched back a step.

"As you like," said the king.
His finger moved again, one degree, toward the woman in black at the dais's left.

The duke's gaze followed it, found her, and for a moment the towering fury broke on simple confusion, because what stood there was a girl, clearly not old enough to speak up in these halls. She was a full head and a half shorter than his retainers, no house sigil anywhere on her.
"...The clerk?" Tharion said.
"The investigator," said the king.

Something moved behind the duke's face and was gone. Months ago he had burned a cipher that described this woman exactly, young, red-eyed, carrying no house name, and he had paid well since to learn what it would not tell him.
Iris came forward off the dais steps, unhurried, and her boots were loud in all that silence.
"No matter what this woman wants, you're holding my vassals on mere suspicion," the duke bit out. "A word that dissolves in any honest court!"
"They're not being held on suspicion." Iris stopped at the center of the floor, ten paces from him, and looked up into his face with eyes like banked coals.
Her hand opened at her side.
The floor of the great hall of Vraven tore open.
The stone stayed whole. That was the obscenity of it. The seam opened in the air above the marble, wide as a war banner, and it poured heat, ember light, and sound into the seat of the nation.
"What in the Goddess?!"
Hundreds of shouts sounded in the great hall, each more shaken than the last.
Tharion took one step back before he caught himself, and his face did not move at all.
The sound came through first, and it was the sound of thirty-eight men.
Every voice down there had a lifetime of practice at screaming and no way to stop. The galleries of Vraven's peerage got all of it at once, doubled, wet, and enormous.
Underneath the screaming ran the patient noises of industry: the clink of coin, the scratch of a pen, a warm voice saying, "Sold."
Half the hall was on its feet before the light stopped moving.
Through the seam, laid out below like a province seen from a low cloud, burned the hell of the Demon of Vengeance.
Black metal ground under a sky of banked coals, breathing. And on it, laid out with the tidy logic the machine itself had taught her, stood an economy.
The counting-house came first, roofless, where nine men caught molten coin with the raw bone of their hands, stacked it, lost it, and stacked it again, weeping numbers.
Beyond it stood the long desks, where careful men wrote their own skins into ledgers, reviewed them for errors, and screamed without once spoiling the penmanship.

At the signing table, candle-lit and courteous, lords in the rags of wine-dark cloaks signed and paid, signed and paid, while the auctioneer's voice announced each collection in the seller's own scream.
And behind it all, remote as a watchtower on a border, a crooked pillar glowed. The fat silhouette threaded on it was climbing.
Up and down, up and down, never once pausing, never once ceasing the constant scream of pain.
Sound broke the hall.
A count of the middle rows vomited down his own velvet.

At the correspondence table, Queen Morgana turned a letter over and began the next one. One table away, Lilith of the Scarlet Lilies looked down into her brother's future, took another bite of her apple, and chewed.

Three barons' wives went down in dead faints, and their husbands didn't notice, because they could not look away. Somebody, quietly, urgently, had started reciting scripture, and it was one of the clerks of the royal chancery.

chapters.title: Chapter 1887 Final Defense
paragraphs: In the eastern gallery, Arch Priestess Elisabeth had come to the rail like a drawn blade, both hands white on the railing, and her professional calm was gone. What stood in her face was doctrine meeting a thing that had no chapter.
"Goddess, tell me... Should I..." She was ready to change into battle mode.
"Steady," Prince Elias said quietly, to his own hands.
In the western gallery, the mood was vastly different.

"Oh, now that's organized!" Jasmine leaned forward with her chin on her knuckles, nodding slowly at the counting-house. "Intake, processing, review, collection. She built a working ministry and she doesn't even know she did it. I'm soo jealous!"
"That fire looks damn hot," Serika grinned with professional envy.
Kitsara whistled, low and long, five tails going at once. "And she gets to keep them forever~"
"Kaelira." Seraphiel leaned over the rail beside her, entirely too delighted. "Serious question. Is that hot enough to work steel?"
Kaelira studied the glow under the distant pillar with her arms folded, and gave it real thought, because she gave everything real thought.
"What nonsense is that question?" the tomboy elf asked dryly. "Of course they're hot enough."
"Excuse me for not knowing these things!" Sera scoffed, then growled. "You better drop your attitude, young lady, or else..."
Kaelira merely grinned and ignored the pouting blonde.
The rest of the family watched a duchy's worth of criminals scream in the ember light, and got comfortable about it.
Somewhere in the middle rows, a baron who had been staring down into the seam turned and stared at the western gallery instead.
"...They're having fun like this is a family picnic," he said, to nobody who wanted to hear it.
And Duke Tharion Ravenshade stood alone at the center of the floor of the seat of the nation, ten paces from a woman in black, and looked into the seam with his rings hanging forgotten at his sides.
The hall watched him find the faces.

Orvath. The Weirs' colors were unmistakable, even in rags, even from above. Ostrev beside him, signing. The tax farmer Odam in the counting-house, black to the elbows, shrieking his way through the second toll one coin at a time.
His men. His circle. His machine, running, forever, in a hell that had not existed nine days ago, owned by a girl whose name he did not know.
"What," said the Duke of Ravenshade, "is this."
"Hell," Iris said. "Scum go in, and they don't come out."
"This is an ATROCITY!" The word came out of him in a blast that guttered every torch in the hall, and he rounded on the throne with his cloak snapping.

"You sit there, under the law of a million years, and you let a nameless creature show me sorcery and call it evidence?! Peers of the realm, in a pit, tortured before the assembly like a carnival, and I am to, what, to confess at the sight of it?!"
He flung a hand at the seam without looking at it.

"Forced testimony. Every word those wretches have screamed came out of them under compulsion, and every court in this kingdom's history has burned such testimony unread. You know this, Alexios. Your own ancestor wrote the statute. Nothing those men say has legal standing, and nothing they say touches me!"
His voice steadied as it found the old road, the good road, the road of paper and precedent his house had walked since the kingdom's first stones.
"So I ask the crown again." The court-smooth register came back down over the fury.
"Where is the evidence a court may touch? Show me one document bearing my seal, one order in my hand, one witness who is not screaming in a witch's oubliette."
"Show me anything at all, or by every law this hall was raised on, this ends with the crown paying reparations to Ravenshade for the gravest insult a king of Vraven has ever offered a loyal house."
Silence.
The seam breathed heat into it, the screaming went on underneath, and the old king on the high throne looked down at the duke for a long, long moment.
"...That's your defense, then," Alexios said at last, dry as a winter field. "Deniability."
"It is not a DEFENSE, it is the LAW!"
"Mm." The king's thumb moved once along the flat of the sword of state. "The law. Is there anything else you'd like to say to the crown?"
The nonchalant dismissal stopped Tharion Ravenshade mid-breath.

The two men looked at each other across thirty feet of winter air, a lifetime of dealings in marriages, borders, and debts standing in the space between them. The hall watched the duke's face change as he arrived, at last, at the bottom of his purse.
One coin was left, the oldest he owned, and he spent it.

"You would let it come to this," he said quietly. Then, louder, with his spine straightening into ceremony: "Then the crown leaves me no choice but to remind it of its own word, here before the peerage, as the old oaths demand witnesses."
"Tharion," Alexios said, low. "Think carefully."

"I have thought of nothing else for days." The duke turned to face the assembled nobility of Vraven, and his voice rang off the banners. "Peers of the realm! Hear what your king swore, and judge what his justice is worth!"

"Three years ago, Alexios Valorian came to my hall. Not I to his. The king of Vraven, dying, came north to Ravenshade, because his crown was a beggar's crown, because his dukes ruled him and not the reverse, and he needed the one house strong enough to hold the realm's spine straight while he set it."
The hall had gone very still.
"And a bargain was struck, sworn, and sealed in the king's own blood."

Tharion's hand rose, one ringed finger pointing up at the throne. "Ravenshade's full support, for the rest of his reign, in every decision the crown should make. My armies at his call. My voice behind his edicts. My coin behind his wars. And Ravenshade delivered! When Greenvale burned for its corruption, and for letting those filthy criminals-"
He screamed, pointing at Quinlan himself.

"-ravage his lands?! Whose banners rode? When his unfair reforms gutted half the privileges in this hall, whose voice held the counts in line? EVERYTHING this king has built for the last three years, he built standing on Ravenshade's shoulders, by the terms of that oath!"

"So that was why..." somewhere in the middle rows, an old count breathed it out loud to nobody. "The Greenvale conflict... Ravenshade rode to help with an army, but it wasn't big enough to win the competition, as Alastair's and Kaede's armies were much grander. It made no sense for him to participate... We all wondered why..."
Duke Alastair of Greenvale stared at the floor of the hall and did not look up, and his twin daughters each took one of his arms.
"And the price!" Tharion's voice rose over the murmur and crushed it. "The price the king of Vraven swore, on his blood, before the Records above, in exchange for my house carrying his crown!"
He let it hang. He was a master of halls, whatever else he was, and he made the whole realm lean in before he laid it down.
"That his third daughter, Felicity Valorian, would be named heir to the throne of Vraven and crowned its queen."

chapters.title: Chapter 1888 Wagered Daughter
paragraphs: "That his third daughter, Felicity Valorian, would be named heir to the throne of Vraven and crowned its queen."
The hall detonated.
Half the peerage came up shouting. The other half turned as one to stare at the eastern gallery, at the princes, and the words flew over the floor like crossbow bolts.
"The third princess..."
"...passed over both princes? The king had gone senile..."
"...sold the succession, the succession itself, to Ravenshade..."
At the foot of the dais, Princess Felicity Valorian stood absolutely still, and her face had gone white as her armor.
And the deal was exactly what the duke said it was.
Three years ago, a dying king had traded his youngest daughter's future to the most dangerous house in his realm, buying the strength he needed to rule.
Tharion had chosen her himself: the youngest, the sweetest, the one who would come to her throne knowing nothing, owing everything, reaching for the first steady hand offered.
Her dear uncle's hand. Both men had sworn to it, and it had sat under three years of Vraven's history like rot under a floor.
Felicity's lips moved twice before sound came out of them.
"...What?"
Nobody answered her.
"Father, what is he..." Her voice cracked up an octave, and her gauntlet was gripping the royal seal on her chest like it had grown too heavy to carry. "What is he talking about?"
In the eastern gallery, Prince Elias had not moved at all, and his stillness had stopped being dignity.
"Named heir," the first prince said, to no one, in a voice like a door coming off its hinges. "We were told it was merit!"
Beside him, Caelum had begun, helplessly, horribly, to smile. "Brother. Brother, breathe."
"Do not tell me to breathe, Caelum!"
At the place of honor among the peers, Calienne Valorian, first daughter of the king, wife of Duskmere, had gone bright-eyed over a grin that was wide, mad, and entirely her father's.
"Oh, this old fox father of mine..." she whispered, delighted, while her husband looked back and forth between his wife and the throne in complete, honest bewilderment. "You didn't."
Tharion felt the hall in his hand, and he turned back to the throne to close it.
"So judge, peers of Vraven!" Tharion spread his ringed hands wide, the picture of a wronged pillar of the realm. "Your king charges my house with conspiracy, on the word of a pit! Very well!
"Then let the crown stand in the light beside me. Let the realm see every deal made in the dark. And let my king remember..."
He turned back to Alexios, lowered his voice, and made sure every soul in the hall could hear him lower it.

"...that a man who breaks an oath sworn on his own blood is only a liar with an army. Charge my house, Alexios, and you must first tear up your own sworn word... and every banner in this hall will watch you do it."
He straightened, magnificent, finished.
"That is my defense."
And on the high throne of Vraven, for the first time since the charge was read, the old king moved.
He chuckled.
It was a low, dry sound, a few grains of gravel turning over, and it did to the great hall what no herald's staff could have done.
"This defense... is far too outdated."
"What?" Tharion gasped, confidence disappearing from his face.
"Blackmailing me with this information would've worked a few months ago, but now..."
Alexios shrugged.
Every voice died. Every eye went up.
Alexios Valorian sat on the high throne of Vraven, under the weight of his own crown, and chuckled at the ruin of his reign being read aloud. The peerage did not know what to do with that at all.
"Your Majesty..." somebody began, in the middle rows.
"It's the truth."
The king said it plainly, at speaking volume, and it reached the last banner anyway.
"Every word of it. The winter, the oath, the blood. The price." He looked out over his hall, unbent.

"Three years ago I rode north to Ravenshade as a beggar with a crown on, and I sold my youngest daughter's future to the strongest house in my realm. Tharion asked for Felicity by name. I knew exactly why but I swore anyway."
At the dais's right, a white gauntlet closed around the royal seal until the metal edges bit.
The hall's murmur rose, broke, and died, because the king was still speaking.

The princess flinched like the name was a thrown stone.

chapters.title: Chapter 1889 Terrible Father
paragraphs: She had not moved through any of it. She stood at the dais's right in her white armor with the seal hanging on her chest, and her face had been through six kinds of weather in a quarter hour. The whole assembled realm turned to look at her at once.
"I..." Her voice came out tiny. She cleared it. It came out tiny again. "Father, I don't..."
Her eyes went, helpless, over the floor, past the duke, up to the western gallery. To Feng Jiai, who was gripping the rail with both hands.
"Stop shaking, dummy!" the young jade beauty of Zhenwu called down, into the silence of the entire peerage. "I'll give you a few headpats afterward."
A wet little laugh broke out of Felicity. "Who wants your headpats?"
Her eyes found Quinlan next. The Primordial Villain had not moved from the rail, hands still on his girls' shoulders, and he did nothing at all except look back at her.
Then he nodded.
That was enough.
Princess Felicity Valorian crossed her father's hall with her shoulders back, and if her gauntlets rattled faintly the whole way, the hall generously failed to notice.
She stopped in front of the king. "...Yes, Father."
Alexios looked down at her for a long moment.

Then he took her face in both hands, bent, and kissed her on the forehead in front of the assembled peerage of Vraven. He held her steady after it, because she had begun, much more visibly now, to tremble.
"I am sorry," the king said. "You have a terrible father."
"I sold your future for a gamble of mine."
His thumbs moved once across her cheekbones. "My advisors would all tell you it was one of the greatest trades in the history of the kingdom. But that doesn't make your father any less terrible."
Felicity stared up at him.
Her mouth opened, closed, opened. The tears arrived all at once, and with them, out of nowhere at all, fury.

"But... but the concoction!" She grabbed his wrists with both gauntlets. "You just said it! You never planned to die, you never planned to leave me to him, you were going to..." The realization built as she said it, word over word, faster.
"You were going to live until it was safe. You were always going to live until it was safe to pass the crown!"
"Yes," said Alexios.
"Then it was never real!" She stamped her feet on the marble, armor ringing, tears running freely now, fourteen years old in front of six hundred nobles and completely done caring.

"The bad part was never going to happen! You were going to fix everything first, that was the whole point, so don't stand there and call yourself terrible when the entire scheme was you refusing to leave me a broken kingdom, you, you absolute..."
"Felicity."
"Don't 'Felicity' me!" Another stomp. "Take it back! If it's like that, then don't call yourself terrible!"
The old king looked down at the crying, furious, shining girl gripping his wrists, and the frost in his face gave way by degrees to old, tired warmth.
He freed one hand and stroked her hair, tenderly, ruinously, in front of everyone.

"I still bet you on my gamble," he said quietly. "Had the Fujimori medicine stopped working. Had they stopped supplying. Had Ravenshade outmaneuvered me. Had I misjudged the continent's geopolitics. I could go and on. Had any of it gone wrong, you would have paid for my choice, and you'd have had no say in the wager. A father who plays his daughter as a card deserves the title. I'll keep it."
"You... that's..." She swiped her arm across her eyes, furious. "That's NOT..."
"However."
The word came out with a different weight, and the whole hall felt the ground shift under it.
"When I swore that oath, naming you heir was strategy. A coin I paid a schemer, nothing more."

His voice climbed, dry, iron, and absolutely clear, to fill the seat of the nation to its rafters. "Since then, I have watched you walk alone into a war camp to stop a war. I have watched you hold ground at fourteen that broke soldiers of five hundred."
"I have watched you fight and valiantly save the people you cherished. I have watched you choose conscience over your comfort. You made me proud with every single choice when one was offered."
He took a breath.

"I made that call for strategy. By now, I stand by it wholeheartedly. There is nobody in this realm, of any age, of any house, better fit to bring Vraven into the next era than Felicity Valorian. And so..."
The king of Vraven reached up with both hands and lifted the great crown off his own head.
Six hundred people inhaled at once, and the sound was too big to be a gasp.
"Father..." Felicity's eyes had gone perfectly round. "Father, what, wait..."

"Tharion of Ravenshade." Alexios did not look at the duke. He looked at his daughter, and the corner of his mouth had already curved. "You invoked the oath before the peerage. The oath never had a time limit attached to it, but very well. You may witness its fulfillment."
"That is not..." The duke had gone grey. "You cannot... a coronation requires the conclave, the temple, the writ..."

"The law requires the sovereign's word, the heir's blood, and the realm as witness," said a clear voice from the eastern gallery, and Arch Priestess Elisabeth, Dawn Breaker, chosen of the Goddess, stepped to the gallery rail with her white and gold vestments falling straight as scripture.
"The temple has read the same statutes the duke has. The temple finds the hall sufficient."
Alexios glanced up at her, one look, wordless.

His third child looked back at him for a moment, and whatever passed between them had no words in it either. Then Elisabeth descended the gallery stair to stand at the dais and raised her right hand, and dawn-colored light gathered on it like the first sun of the year.
"Kneel not, Felicity Valorian," the Arch Priestess said, warm and enormous, "for a queen kneels to no one in her own hall."
"I don't... sister, I can't..." Felicity was crying again, or still, looking from her father to Elisabeth to the crown in her father's hands. "It's too... I'm fourteen..."
"I was seven when the Goddess chose me," Elisabeth said. "Fate does not check your age, little star. It only checks whether you'll carry it."
"By my word," said Alexios Valorian, "before this realm assembled."
He raised the great crown of Vraven.
"I name Felicity Valorian queen of Vraven, sovereign of its crown lands, keeper of its law, and shield of its commons. My reign ends where hers begins, and it begins now."
He lowered the crown.

It was made for a warrior-king in his prime, that crown, forged for a man who had carried a longsword at his hip for a milennia. It went past her ears. It came to rest on the bridge of her nose and the tops of both eyebrows.

The newly crowned queen of Vraven stood before her entire peerage holding it up off her face with both gauntlets, eyes enormous underneath the rim, looking exactly like a fawn that had wandered onto a tourney field.
"Um," said the queen.
The Goddess's light came down on her anyway.
It fell from Elisabeth's raised hand in a golden veil, and where it touched the too-big crown the old gold woke and shone.
The Arch Priestess spoke the blessing of the faith over her baby sister in the voice that had broken undead hosts.
"The Goddess lights the reign of Queen Felicity Primrose Amabelle Valorian. May it be long, just, and kind."
The light hung there, gold and patient, while the peerage of Vraven watched, and then it faded.

What had just happened landed on Duke Tharion Ravenshade without mercy. The hall watched him understand, in full view, that the greatest coin in his treasury had just been paid out to the last copper.
This was what he wanted. What he'd been salivating about since Morgana's womb held its first resident.
A child of Ravenshade blood held the throne now. His niece, extremely young and malleable, ready to be shaped into the puppet he needed to rule the realm from the shadows.
Or so it should've been.
The crown he had bought for his puppet sat on the head of a crying girl who belonged, body, soul, and choice, to everyone in the world except him.
The peers of Vraven began to kneel to their new queen, rank by rank, house by house, a tide of velvet going down across the great hall.
Duke Zaren of Duskmere knelt to her beaming, with Calienne sinking beside him in a reverence of vicious elegance, her mad grin hidden in the folds of her bow.
Prince Caelum knelt to his sister. Prince Elias stood one heartbeat longer than everyone around him, looking at the girl under her ridiculous crown.
Then the first prince of Vraven knelt too, to his queen, and if his bow was stiff, it was also, unmistakably, real.
"Long live Queen Felicity Primrose Amabelle Valorian!" someone shouted, the hall took it up, and the roar of it shook dust off banners that had not moved in a century.
In the western gallery, Quinlan sat. The look on the Primordial Villain's face had nothing villainous in it at all.
Instead, he tenderly smiled, looking like a proud uncle who was invited to his niece's graduation ceremony.
"Long live Queen Felicity Primrose Amabelle Valorian."

chapters.title: Chapter 1890 Sentenced
paragraphs: Instead, Quinlan tenderly smiled. "Long live Queen Felicity Primrose Amabelle Valorian."
But he did not bow to her.
Then his whole family was up and cheering with zero royal decorum, a blonde tail wagging madly over the rail, and the noise they made rode clean over six hundred nobles.
"Long live Queen Felicity Primrose Amabelle Valorian!"
Felicity, queen of Vraven, holding her crown off her nose with both hands, went scarlet to the ears and beamed through her tears at all of them, and for one moment the seat of the nation was warm.
Alexios let the roar crest and settle.

Then the old man, bareheaded, turned back to the center of the floor, where the Duke of Ravenshade stood alone in the wreckage of his last card. The hall went quiet behind him like a blade going back to a sheath.
"Now then," said Alexios. "Where were we... ah. Yes."
Tharion Ravenshade had been many things across eight hundred years, and every one of them had fought to its last breath.

He rebuilt himself in front of them. The grey left his face by force of will alone, the spine reset itself vertebra by vertebra, and when he spoke again his voice had found its way back to the courtroom.

"My stance stands unchanged." He straightened his rings, one by one. "The crown has shown me a pit and called it proof. Compelled testimony is ash in every court since the founding statutes. That law did not change with the wearer of the crown."
"No," Alexios agreed. "It hasn't."

The old man gestured. Stormlord came forward, and behind him came the crown's clerks carrying ledgers in pairs, stacking them on the great floor of the hall between duke and dais, stack after stack after stack.

The old man gestured. Stormlord came forward, and behind him came the crown's clerks carrying ledgers in pairs, stacking them on the great floor of the hall between duke and dais, stack after stack after stack.

"Generations of toll schedules came in under seal from nine crossings," Stormlord recited, iron-flat. "The crown's own schedules sit beside them. The difference between the two columns, year on year, coin for coin, matches the deposits recorded in these." Another stack. "The private ledgers of the granary at Silver Hollow."
"Ledgers written by criminals," Tharion said contemptuously.

"Ledgers written by careful men," said the king. "You taught your inner circle bookkeeping wonderfully. It kept them honest with each other while they robbed everyone else. Every coin that walked north is written down twice by men who never met."
"Nonsense. I don't know what they are, but not one page of it bears my hand, my seal, or my name given in order," the duke said.
"Because I gave none. A duchy is vast. If clerks and counts built a trough under my roads, then try the clerks and counts. Ambition is not treason, and neither is other men's coin flowing uphill."
"Forget the coin," Iris spoke and looked at Stormlord.

The commander took up the recital: eleven holdings seized for engineered debts in one county alone, every one escheated up to the duchy on dissolution, every one granted back down to the duke's circle as a fee for loyal administration, and every grant sealed under the duke's own signet.
"A long history of stolen land," Stormlord spoke slowly. "Every grant with your seal on it."
"Grants of escheated land are routine!" Tharion began, and for the first time all day his voice reached for volume.
"The motion is heard," said Alexios Valorian, mildly. "And declined."
"On what grounds?!"
"On the grounds that the pit of Iris Ravenclaw is not your evidence of innocence." The mildness dropped out of the old man's voice on the way through, and what was left was bedrock.
"The paper convicts you on its own. The tolls, the schedules, the deposits, the deeds, the grants under your signet. None of them are proof enough alone, but I have decided that together, they hold."
"Which statute allows you that exactly?!" Tharion screamed.
The hall went very still, awaiting the king's response.
"Stop hiding behind statutes. They will help you no longer. You're guilty, I'm sure of it. That's enough."
"No, it isn't!" Tharion was going blind with utter rage. "This is RIDICULOUS!"
"For the whole of my reign I have ruled this realm by its own rules, and men like you built your machine inside those rules and called it law. I am done with them."
The king's eyes moved onto his vassals, observing them slowly.

"With the passage of the crown, the Vraven Kingdom embraces a new future. A great many rules will be changed in the following days. If you're unwilling to change with the nation, then you have no place inside its borders."
"So let me ask. Who here disputes the legitimacy of the Valorian family's claim on the crown, and our right to revisit its laws?"
Six hundred peers stood in their velvet and said nothing at all.

And just like that, the king who spent his entire reign restrained by the rules his ancestors signed, finally behaved like the tyrant he worked to one day be: someone who could dictate how his own nation was to behave, and whose subordinates would have no choice but to bow.
"NO! I REFUSE-" While Tharion was screaming, Alexios turned, and inclined his head to the young queen.
"Your Majesty. The crime is far older than your reign. By your leave, the old reign will sweep its own floor."
Felicity looked at her father. Whatever was still storming in her face, she put it down, all of it, and the nod she gave him was slow, grave, and completely royal.
Alexios Valorian turned to face the Duke of Ravenshade, and the great hall arranged itself into the shape of an ending.

"Tharion of House Ravenshade. On the evidence of your vassals' records, cross-proven and sealed, the crown finds you guilty of mastering a covert machine of extortion, ruin, and seizure upon the vassals of this realm."
"Guilty of the unwritten toll."
"Guilty of the engineered destruction of houses outside your circle and the enrichment of those within it."
"Guilty of high treason against crown and commons, sustained across a generation."
Each count came down like a course of masonry.
"House Ravenshade ends today. Its lands revert to the crown, entirely. Its armies pass to the crown's marshals."
"And for the lives," continued Alexios Valorian, quieter, "priced, ruined, carried off in boxes, written out of the books... the crown takes yours."
He let one breath pass.
"The execution belongs to Iris Ravenclaw. She may render it however she wants, for as long as she wants."
The hall exhaled, and the girl with no house began to walk.

She came at him unhurried, boots loud on the marble, a plain figure crossing the last of the crown's velvet and heraldry. Every banner she passed under belonged to a bloodline with a seat in this hall.
Hers had a grave, and a hell.

Her entire backing on this earth lounged in the western gallery, watching her with open villainous pride. He stayed exactly where he was, because this walk had been hers alone since before he ever met her.
The Duke of Ravenshade watched her come, and the last thing he had left rose up in him.
"Stop," he said, and it came out as an order, because everything always had. She kept walking. "Stop. Before this... whatever this is... ends. I will have one answer."
Iris did not stop.
"[Undying Damnation]."
The air above the marble tore at her feet, wide as a grave. Ember light climbed out of the cut and lit six hundred faces from below, and the heat came with it, carrying the smell of cooked iron.
Below the rim there was no cellar and no earth. Black metal ground ran away in every direction under a sky the color of banked coals, and the whole of it breathed.
"Who are you?!"
The question came out of Tharion with terrible, honest bewilderment, the first fully honest thing the hall had heard him say all day.
"What house sent you?!"
The smile on Iris's lips arrived slowly.
It was small, it was delighted, and there was nothing sane anywhere in it.
"You actually don't know." Her voice came out warm.
"Know WHAT?"
"He said my name just now."
Her head tilted.
"Nothing, huh?"
The duke went back for it. His eyes went up and left, the courtroom memory raking through the last ten minutes for a word it had thrown away on arrival.
"...Ravenclaw," he said. "Ravenclaw..."
The name went around his mouth twice and caught on nothing. Then his eyes stopped moving.

"The barony." It came out slow, hauled up from the very bottom of the ducal records. "The little barony. Insignificant border trash. There was..." He stopped, remembering. "...There was a daughter unaccounted for."
